author: Administrador
title: Zapatistische Vorbereitungen für das umarmende Treffen mit den Familien Sucherinnen. Teil 6: GESCHENKE
content:
Musik: „Es que yo te quiero a ti“, Kevin Kaarl Bilder, Schnitt und Produktion: Terci@s Compas Zapatistas

Ich glaube, es war im Juli, als Subcomandante Insurgente Moisés den Beginn der ersten Etappe der „Reise für das Leben – Kapitel Mexiko“ ankündigte. Ich glaube, er sagte damals in etwa, dass die suchenden Mütter wie unsere Mamas seien. Damit nahm das Problem seinen Anfang, wie es so schön heißt.

Denn wir alle aus der Truppe dachten: „Oha, das sind unsere Mamas, und wir werden sie besuchen. Auf keinen Fall können wir da ankommen und einfach sagen: ‚Bin da, Chefin, was gibt’s zu essen?‘“. Nein, wenn wir so ankommen, bekommen wir nur die Sandale, einen Klaps oder einen fiesen Kniff (denn nette gibt es ja auch) zu spüren. Denn die oder der Freund:in – na ja, das geht vorbei, dann ist es wieder gut und fertig. Aber wenn die Mamas sauer werden, lieber Gott im Himmel, da gibt’s kein Entkommen.

„Wir sollten ein Geschenk mitnehmen“, sagte einer. „Ja“, antwortete eine Insurgenta (*), „so wie wir Mutter Erde unsere ehrliche Arbeit schenken.“ Der Capitán meinte: „Ja, als vorbeugendes Geschenk. Also noch bevor die Standpauke losgeht, hast du das Geschenk schon parat, und wenn der Sturm losbricht, holst du das Geschenk raus, lächelst und machst ein Gesicht wie: ‚Mama, ich bin‘s, der kleine Marcos, und ich werde keinen Unfug anstellen.‘“

„Das glaubt dir doch kein Mensch“, mischt sich SubMoy ein und fügt hinzu: „Außerdem steht in allen sozialen Netzwerken, dass du keine Manieren, also keine Mutter hast.“

Die Diskussion ging weiter und alle einigten sich, dass es ein Geschenk geben solle. Aber dann gab es viel Wirbel darum, welches Geschenk das sein sollte. Vielleicht Blumen. „Nein, Compa, die sind schon verwelkt, wenn du in den Bus steigst.“ „Ein Gedicht“, schlägt eine andere Insurgenta vor. Darauf SubMoy: „Die Pueblos werden schon Briefe, Gedichte und Lieder schicken. Obwohl ich nicht weiß, ob die suchenden Mütter Hip-Hop und Rap und sowas mögen.“

Die Diskussion ging weiter. Und zog sich immer weiter hin. Und dann wurde es noch schlimmer, als ein Insurgente (**) vorschlug: „Schenken wir ihnen doch ein Andenken.“

Da kam es zum Tumult. Alle redeten durcheinander: Was für ein Andenken denn, wo sollen sie das hinstellen, das ist keine gute Idee, doch, ist es, denn die Erinnerung ist das Wichtigste, deshalb sind sie ja Sucherinnen. Wenn sie keine Erinnerung hätten, würden sie aufgeben, in Ohnmacht fallen.

Da sagten die Frauen – mit dieser schlechten Angewohnheit, die Frauen haben, Diskussionen zu beenden, gerade wenn es richtig spannend wird: Stickereien und Puppen. „Damit sie wissen und sich daran erinnern, dass sie hier Familien haben.“

Die Insurgentes, angeführt vom Capitán, widersprachen und argumentierten, dass Puppen und Stickereien was für kleine Mädchen seien, dass die suchenden Mütter doch schon groß seien, dass sie gar keine Zeit für Spielereien hätten, und dann noch Stickereien, dass das einfach nicht zu glauben wäre. Die Insurgentas wurden wütend und entgegneten, dass es nichts bringe, so zu denken, weil es sich um Erinnerungen handele, nicht um Spielzeug oder Schmuck.

Und die Diskussion geht weiter, aber jetzt ist alles durcheinander, weil dem Insurgente, der für die Verpflegung zuständig war, die Bohnen angebrannt waren – und das nur, weil er sich in das Gerede um das Geschenk eingemischt hatte. Und einen Moment lang machen Frauen und Männer gemeinsame Front, denn eine Sache ist, sozusagen, der Schlagabtausch, und eine andere sind die angebrannten Bohnen. Aber dann trösteten sich alle mit Tostadas und Reis nach vietnamesischer Art. Doch es war nur ein Waffenstillstand, so unbeständig wie das Temperament von Trump. Und so ging es, nachdem sie das Geschirr gespült und die Hunde und Kätzchen gefüttert hatten, weiter.

Da kam SubMoy hinzu: „Was streitet ihr denn so?“ Alle fingen quasi an, das Problem darzulegen. „Jetzt hört aber auf damit“, rief SubMoy. Es wurde ganz still. Die Männer hofften, dass sich der Sub auf die Solidarität unter Männern besinnen würde. Und die Frauen hofften auf sein gutes Urteilsvermögen.

SubMoy zündete sich eine Zigarette an und dachte nach. Nach einer Weile sagte er: „Macht eine Liste mit dem, was wir besorgen müssen.“

Die Insurgentas applaudierten. Die Insurgentes verzogen das Gesicht, sagten aber nichts, denn die Strafe bestand darin, die angebrannten Bohnen zu essen.

Also machten sich alle Insurgentes, gleich welcher Position, daran, Geschenke zu basteln. In aller Eile, denn bis zur Abreise war nicht mehr viel Zeit.

Und dass sie so spät anfingen, war die Schuld des Capitán, der erst mit dem Nonsens angefangen hatte, dass Puppen und Stickereien gar nicht gingen, weil das was für kleine Mädchen sei. Und außerdem baute er aus den Tischen und Stühlen einen Schutzwall, hinter dem sich alle Insurgentes verschanzten. Denn wie sich herausstellte, attackierten die Insurgentas sie mit Schlammkugeln, deren Herstellung ihnen angeblich vom „Comando Palomitas“ beigebracht worden war. Und dann brauchten sie eine Weile, um alles wieder in Ordnung zu bringen und aufzuräumen.

Also, wenn die Geschenke nicht vollständig sind, geht das auf das Konto des Capitán.

Mich trifft keine Schuld. Ich bin nur ein Käfer und ein fahrender Ritter, der ganz große „Don Durito de la Lacandona. e. V. & Co. KG ohne Haftung und Verstand“ mit seinem phänomenalen Gedächtnis. Und ich hatte nichts damit zu tun. Aber ich habe alles mit angesehen. Und ich will hier keinesfalls tratschen, nein, ich gebe euch nur eine Information weiter.

Also, wenn ihr den Capitán seht, könnt ihr ruhig mit ihm schimpfen, so wie die Mamas mit ihren Kleinen schimpfen, wenn sie sich nicht benehmen. Aber der Capitán ist dickköpfig, da können ein paar fliegende Sandalen und Kopfnüsse nicht schaden.

Das sind alle meine Infos. Wenn es noch mehr Klatsch und … ich meine, noch mehr Infos gibt, die ich euch mitteilen kann, sag ich euch Bescheid.

Aus den Bergen im Südosten Mexikos

Der ganz große Don Durito de la Lacandona Mexiko, November 2026

P.S.: Glaubt ihm kein Wort, ich war gar nicht dabei. Das beglaubige ich: El Capitán (mit einem Fahrradhelm zum Schutz vor Sandalen und mitten in Verhandlungen mit dem Comando Palomitas über eine Beschlagnahmung von Munition bei den Insurgentas) – Wir kommen wieder!

* Insurgenta: weibliches Mitglied der militärischen Selbstverteidigungsstruktur der EZLN; wörtlich: die Aufständische, Plural: Insurgentas – die aufständischen Frauen

** Insurgente: männliches Mitglied der militärischen Selbstverteidigungsstruktur der EZLN; wörtlich: der Aufständische, Plural: Insurgentes – die Aufständischen; hier: die aufständischen Männer

author: ROAPE
title: Who gets to make Ethiopia’s peace?
content:
Ethiopia’s newest opposition alliance contains a remarkable contradiction. The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), the main party in northern Tigray, now shares a coalition with the Amhara Fano National Movement, although their forces fought on opposite sides of the devastating 2020–2022 war.

[1]

 The Oromo Liberation Army and organizations rooted in Somali, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz also appeared in its founding declaration.

[2]




Announced on 20 September 2026 as the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, the coalition seeks Abiy’s removal and an inclusive transitional administration. Its advertised seven-member composition was soon disputed: the Gumuz Peoples’ Democratic Movement denied membership on 26 September.

[3]




Removing a government requires agreement about an adversary. Constructing the political order that follows requires agreement about something much harder: who may exercise power, how that power will be limited, what happens to rival armies, how disputed territory will be governed, which crimes from the previous war will be investigated, and who has the authority to write the rules of a transition.




Opposition to Abiy may be sufficient to create a wartime coalition. It is not, by itself, a postwar settlement. Events have since altered the military balance. Tigrayan forces seized the airports at Mekelle, Axum and Shire in September, actions the African Union described as inconsistent with the Pretoria Agreement.

[4]

 Britain condemned the seizures and rejected the alliance’s objective of overthrowing the government, while calling for an end to hostilities and renewed dialogue.

[5]




By early October, federal and allied forces had retaken Mekelle after the TPLF withdrew. Their allies include the Tigray Peace Force, composed of former TPLF fighters.

[6]

 On 16 October, Abiy announced a six-month caretaker administration for Tigray, tasked with restoring services, facilitating displaced people’s return and preparing elections.

[7]

 Fighting nevertheless continued: ACLED reported clashes in northwestern Tigray on 19 October.

[8]




These reversals change the immediate question. Alongside the alliance’s claim to determine a transition stands the federal government’s ability to reshape Tigray’s administration through military success. Neither battlefield control nor an electoral timetable, by itself, establishes that civilians can freely determine their political future. Military power can determine who cannot be ignored. It does not automatically determine who is entitled to rule.




A coalition united by a common opponent




The alliance presents itself as an answer to a profound political crisis. Its members accuse Abiy’s government of centralizing power, producing insecurity and restricting political space.

[9]

 Some concerns overlap with independent findings. Human Rights Watch has documented arrests of journalists, newsroom raids and regulatory pressure on independent outlets.

[10] 

But opposition to the federal government does not erase the histories separating the coalition’s members.




Fano forces fought alongside the federal side against Tigrayan forces during much of the 2020–2022 war, before entering their own confrontation with the federal government in 2023.

[11]

 

The TPLF, which dominated Ethiopia’s ruling coalition

 before Abiy took office in 2018, signed the Pretoria Agreement and subsequently alleged federal failures to implement it; the Oromo Liberation Army has pursued a separate insurgency in Oromia.

[12]




Their present cooperation rests chiefly on agreement about what they oppose. Reuters reported when the coalition was announced that its members remained divided over territorial and political questions.

[13]

 These disagreements concern how the Ethiopian state itself is organized. Ethiopia’s constitution links regional boundaries to language, identity, settlement patterns and consent, while protecting communities’ right to self-government.

[14]




The clearest example is the territory commonly called Western Tigray by Tigrayans and Welkait-Tegede by many Amhara claimants. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International documented competing claims, earlier abuses under TPLF-led rule against Amhara and Walqayte communities, and wartime ethnic cleansing of Tigrayans under Amhara-controlled authorities.

[15]

 Hundreds of thousands of displaced Tigrayans remained unable to return when Human Rights Watch reported continuing persecution in April.

[16] 

A military alliance can postpone that dispute. A postwar government cannot.




Pretoria was more than a ceasefire




The 

Pretoria Agreement

, signed on 2 November 2022, was negotiated between the federal government and the TPLF under African Union mediation. It is often described simply as the agreement that ended the Tigray war. But the document attempted something broader: to connect the end of hostilities to a political and institutional framework for restoring authority and resolving disputes.




The TPLF committed to respect federal constitutional authority, refrain from assisting armed groups, end mobilization for renewed conflict and cease attempts at unconstitutional government change.

[17]

 The federal government undertook to halt operations targeting TPLF combatants, restore essential services and facilitate humanitarian assistance.

[18]




The agreement provided for federal control of major infrastructure, including airports, and restoration of federal authority alongside Tigray’s representation in federal institutions.

[19]

 It required political dialogue over an interim regional administration and provided for elections, transitional justice and constitutional resolution of contested territories.

[20]




Yet Pretoria’s importance should not be confused with evidence that it was fully implemented. Human-rights reporting has documented continuing abuses and unresolved displacement in Western Tigray.[

21]

 The European Union’s September statement also expressed concern about Ethiopian military drone strikes, rather than assigning responsibility exclusively to Tigrayan forces.

[22] 

Even substantial breaches of an agreement by one side do not automatically confer on the other side the right to determine Ethiopia’s constitutional future by force.




When battlefield gains become claims to rule




War does more than destroy. It redistributes political power. A force that captures territory gains leverage. An armed organization capable of shutting airports, disrupting transport or opening a new front becomes harder to exclude from negotiations. A military coalition capable of threatening the survival of a government can acquire a degree of political relevance that peaceful opposition organizations may lack. But it also creates a problem: bargaining power derived from violence can quietly become a claim to the right to govern.




Armed groups may require seats at peace talks because they possess the capacity to continue fighting. That pragmatic necessity does not establish that they are the exclusive representatives of the populations in whose name they act, or that their relative military strength should determine their share of constitutional authority.




Research on civil-war settlements emphasizes credible commitment: whether former enemies can trust one another to honour a peace agreement. Combatants may resist disarmament because it leaves them vulnerable.

[23]

 Political, territorial, economic and military power-sharing can provide reassurance.

[24]

 Implementing military arrangements, rather than merely signing them, also matters.

[25]




Ethiopia’s difficulty is particularly acute because the question is not simply how many ministries each faction might receive. It is what state they would be sharing. The coalition joins organizations with different regional bases, different experiences of federal authority, different armed structures and different understandings of Ethiopia’s unresolved territorial and constitutional conflicts. A bargain sufficient to hold those movements together against Abiy could prove insufficient once they had to decide which armed forces disarm, which commanders answer to whom, what becomes of contested territory and how authority is distributed between Addis Ababa and the regions.




The coalition’s regional breadth does not resolve this difficulty. Organizational diversity is not the same thing as democratic representation. A movement’s ability to mobilize armed followers does not establish that civilians have authorized its political project. Nor does the participation of Tigrayan fighters on the federal side establish a mandate to speak for all Tigrayans.




The civilians between the armies




One of the most consequential questions in Ethiopia’s next political phase may therefore be who is absent from the bargaining table. They include civilians who oppose the federal government but reject armed regime change; Tigrayans resisting renewed mobilization; displaced communities; independent parties, journalists and rights organizations; and women whose experience of war differs radically from that of military elites. Their political preferences cannot be inferred from whichever armed organization controls their locality.




Human Rights Watch’s 6 July 2026 report documented forced recruitment by Tigrayan authorities since at least April, including boys as young as 15. It described roundups, house searches and pressure on relatives. Tigrayan officials disputed the allegations and described recruitment as voluntary.

[26]




October brought another indication of war-weariness. Associated Press reported former fighters registering in Mekelle for reintegration into civilian life, with some expressing reluctance to return to combat.

[27]

 Those choices deserve protection irrespective of which force controls the city. If coercion determines who fights, territorial control determines who administers communities, and military organizations determine who negotiates, then the range of choices available to civilians can narrow long before anyone convenes a constitutional conference.




A negotiation may later look inclusive on paper while endorsing outcomes imposed through war. Territory illustrates the problem. Pretoria committed the parties to resolving contested areas constitutionally.

[28]

 Yet territorial possession affects who lives where, which officials exercise authority, which displaced people can return and which claims acquire the appearance of permanence. By the time negotiators formally address a territorial dispute, violence may already have changed the population whose wishes the negotiations are supposed to reflect.




The accountability bargain




The 2020–2022 conflict was marked by grave abuses attributed to multiple forces. Human Rights Watch’s warning about renewed fighting explicitly pointed to the warring parties’ history of atrocities and continuing impunity.

[29] 

Pretoria calls for accountability, truth-seeking, remedies for victims, reconciliation and healing, with input from stakeholders and civil society.

[30]




The new alliance creates a difficult question: what happens to accountability when former enemies become political partners?Their cooperation does not prove that they have agreed to suppress investigations into wartime conduct. Former adversaries often have to reconcile if wars are to end. But tactical reconciliation can create powerful incentives for mutual silence.




A coalition that depends on former enemies may find it easier to defer investigations into each side’s abuses. Leaders may conclude that reopening the past would fracture the alliance needed to fight the present war. Victims can then become inconvenient to political cohesion. The same danger applies to a victorious government protecting its forces or allies. An arrangement that requires silence about the previous war would carry its unresolved violence into the next political order.




Peace and accountability are often presented as competing imperatives. The more difficult reality is that impunity can itself shape the peace. A settlement constructed by actors who know that political power protects them from scrutiny can reproduce the conditions under which coercion becomes a lasting source of political power.




Can force succeed where diplomacy failed?




Supporters of renewed military pressure can contend that governments and insurgencies often compromise only when battlefield conditions change their calculations. If peaceful appeals, diplomatic pressure and incomplete agreements fail to resolve fundamental grievances, the threat of force may create incentives for negotiations that did not previously exist. Military pressure can therefore produce bargaining leverage.




Once violence becomes the most effective route to political inclusion, it risks becoming not the failure of politics but a method of entering politics. Armed organizations discover that territorial control yields negotiating status. Commanders learn that military mobilization generates international attention. Civilian movements discover that disciplined nonviolence may give them less influence over a transition than control of an armed formation. The immediate negotiation may end one war while reinforcing incentives for another.




That is why the question is not whether force can produce negotiations.  If greater military strength buys more influence over the country’s rules, then every future faction confronts an uncomfortable incentive: political relevance may be easier to obtain by becoming militarily indispensable than electorally persuasive.




Regime change is not a constitutional settlement




Abiy’s opponents argue that removing him would change Ethiopia’s political possibilities. Criticism of restrictions on political space and human-rights abuses remains substantial.

[31] 

But the departure of a political leader and the creation of a legitimate political order are different events. Removing Abiy would answer the question of who no longer governs. It would not determine who should exercise power next; whether a transitional government could command rival armed groups; how federal and regional authority would be divided; what limits would constrain it; or how ordinary citizens could peacefully replace those in power.




The alliance promises an inclusive transitional government, participatory constitutional dialogue and peaceful resolution of differences.

[32]

 Those commitments matter, but inclusiveness cannot be measured simply by counting armed organizations inside a coalition. The more fundamental question is whether the transition would leave Ethiopia’s political future open to peaceful challenge and change.




The caretaker administration must face a related test. A six-month election pledge is meaningful only if displaced people can participate, opposition groups can organize safely and voters can choose freely. Pretoria envisaged dialogue over interim authority.

[33]

 Federal appointment following military advances cannot substitute for that political task. Territorial gains therefore sharpen, rather than settle, the question of legitimate regional government.




The war may settle questions before the negotiators do




External involvement has become more immediate. Ethiopia and Eritrea severed diplomatic ties in early October. Ethiopia subsequently accused Eritrea of an invasion; Eritrea rejected the allegations as a pretext for Ethiopian aggression. Reuters also reported witness accounts of Eritrean soldiers in northern Ethiopia.

[34]

 Ethiopian troops then advanced to Zalambessa on the Eritrean border.

[35]




On 14 October, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged de-escalation, dialogue and respect for neighbours’ sovereignty in a call with Abiy.

[36]

 In a speech on 19 October, Abiy warned Eritrea of severe consequences if it continued supporting Ethiopian rebels.

[37] 

These developments connect the internal conflict more directly to the danger of interstate war. Foreign backers can provide resources, sanctuary or diplomatic support, while acquiring influence over a conflict’s objectives and duration. Federal gains against domestic opponents can also bring the fighting closer to an international border.




Territorial seizures can establish facts on the ground. Forced displacement can alter who is present to claim land. Wartime bargains can create obligations among factions. External assistance can create debts to foreign patrons. Each development can reduce the outcomes that remain politically possible. A peace conference may therefore begin with delegates formally free to negotiate while much of the underlying distribution of power has already been determined outside the room.




The alliance’s setbacks have weakened its immediate challenge to the government. They have not resolved Ethiopia’s territorial disputes, questions of accountability or the exclusion of civilians from decisions made in their name. Nor do federal advances establish that renewed war is over. A war can remove leaders, redraw zones of control and compel negotiations. It can also narrow political choice, empower armed elites, entrench territorial facts and make yesterday’s atrocities inconvenient to tomorrow’s rulers.




The alliance’s members have demonstrated that former enemies can identify a common adversary. They have not demonstrated a common answer to the harder question: what political order would replace the one they seek to overturn, and by what authority would it bind Ethiopians who never chose the war?




The federal government’s military recovery poses the corresponding question: will restored authority reopen political choice, or allow the victors to determine its limits?




Those questions cannot be answered by battlefield arithmetic alone.




That is the problem confronting Ethiopia’s peace, whatever happens next on the battlefield.

author: Jesse Staniforth
title: Kebaowek First Nation turns to Supreme Court to rule on UNDRIP, consultation and a nuclear waste dump
content:
Kebaowek First Nation (KFN) intends to ask the Supreme Court to hear its legal case against Canadian Nuclear Laboratories (CNL) according to a release Monday.




In October, the Federal Court of Appeal ruled that CNL and the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission were not required to consider the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples when consulting or developing a project for a low-level nuclear waste dump near KFN’s ancestral territory.




KFN announced today it is filing a leave to appeal the Federal Court of Appeal’s Oct. 16 decision, and also filing a motion to expedite the application, since construction on the nuclear-waste site could begin as early as next year.




“The legal challenge goes far beyond a single nuclear waste project,” KFN’s council argued in the press release. “At its heart is a question of national importance: Does Canada’s commitments in its federal legislation on the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) require federal administrative bodies to consider and apply UNDRIP now in their consultation processes and decisions affecting Indigenous lands and rights?”




Kebaowek is located in the far west of Quebec, roughly 400 kilometres north of Oshawa.




More than a debate over the nuclear-waste facility, KFN said the Supreme Court must clarify how UNDRIP, incorporated into law through the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, must shape government decisions and Indigenous consultation processes.




Kebaowek First Nation Chief Lance Haymond said his Nation’s fight has never been about preventing the nuclear-waste disposal facility alone, but about whether Canada is welling to respect Indigenous rights in action.




“When decisions affecting our lands, waters and future generations are made without our free, prior and informed consent, reconciliation remains an empty promise,” Haymond said. “We are turning to the Supreme Court because First Nations across this country deserve clarity, accountability and meaningful respect for their rights.”




Haymond was supported by Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak as well as by Assembly of First Nations Quebec–Labrador Regional Chief Francis Verreault-Paul.




“I commend Kebaowek First Nation for this brave decision,” Verreault-Paul said. “Rights cannot exist only on paper. They must shape the decisions governments make when our lands, waters and rights are at stake. That means honouring the duty to consult and giving real effect to the principle of free, prior and informed consent. First Nations should not have to go to court time and again to compel governments to respect rights they have already committed to uphold. Yet the Chalk River case shows that, far too often, this remains our only recourse.”




In February 2025, a Federal Court found in favour of KFN’s argument against a plan for a low-level nuclear-waste facility to be located at the Chalk River Nuclear Laboratories campus in Deep River, Ont., located about 180 km west of Ottawa.




The Federal Court found that since Parliament had adopted the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples into law, demands on administrative tribunals like the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission (CNSC) to meet the duty to consult and accommodate had increased. The Federal Court ordered CNL and CNSC to carry out further consultation with First Nations prior to moving ahead on the waste facility.

Kebaowek First Nation turns to Supreme Court to rule on UNDRIP, consultation and a nuclear waste dump

author: Randi Beers
title: New Nunavut minister takes on energy, environment portfolios
content:
Fred Pedersen is minister of environment, energy, and minister responsible for Qulliq Energy Corp. following his selection to cabinet on Nov. 5.




Nunavut Premier John Main announced the assignments in a news release Monday morning.




The Cambridge Bay MLA was 

chosen

 by his colleagues to replace former minister Brian Koonoo, who 

stepped down

 from cabinet Nov. 2, citing personal reasons.




Koonoo held four portfolios. He was minister of environment, energy, languages, and culture and heritage.




Human Resources Minister Annie Tattuinee now has the languages and culture and heritage portfolios.




David Akeeagok will remain minister of education, but his role as minister responsible for Nunavut Arctic College will move to Gwen Healey Akearok, who was minister responsible for QEC prior to Monday’s announcement.

author: Charlotte England
title: Mamdani Abolishes Violent Police Protest Unit
content:
Zohran Mamdani is set to disband a controversial New York City police unit known for using excessive force against protesters.




The New York City mayor laid out plans on Monday to scrap the Strategic Response Group (SRG) in favour of a “civilian-led approach” to policing protest that will put “communication, de-escalation” and “coordination” front and centre.




In a joint statement with the city’s police commissioner, Jessica Tisch, Mamdani said his plan would involve replacing 600 SRG officers with a civilian team and a small specialised police unit to handle protests. 




Abolishing the SRG – a highly militarised police unit that became notorious for its violent and racist policing of Black Lives Matter protests – was one of Mamdani’s core 2025 campaign pledges. 




Under Mamdani’s reforms, the use of tear gas, rifles, painfully loud noises above 90 decibels and kettling – the surrounding and trapping of protesters, usually before mass arrest – will all be banned.




The mayor also endorsed a council bill that would ban the New York Police Department (NYPD) from ever reviving the SRG or its tactics.




The SRG has been subject to countless misconduct claims over the years. In 2020, Human Rights Watch accused the unit – which handles both protests and counter terrorism – of “serious violations of international human rights law” after officers trapped around 300 peaceful protesters in the Bronx neighbourhood of Mott Haven, then beat and arrested them for breaking a curfew they had been prevented from obeying. 




More recently, the SRG has been accused of using excessive force against pro-Palestine and anti-ICE protesters, including punching people who are already pinned to the floor, heavy use of tear gas and mass arrests. 




In October, Mamdani ordered the NYPD to conduct its first comprehensive review into use of force in more than a decade, and appointed a new chair of the Civilian Complaint Review Board to increase police accountability. 




“New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat,” Mamdani said in a statement on Monday. “Protecting New Yorkers’ rights and keeping our communities safe go hand in hand.”




In March, Mamdani created the Mayor’s Office of Community Safety, which he said would strengthen violence prevention, change how the city responds to mental health crises and tackle the root causes of crime. Under the new plans, an unarmed civilian unit within the office, with no powers of arrest, will take the lead in engaging with protesters from 2028.




Within the NYPD, meanwhile, a new First Amendment Support Team (FAST) will respond to protests. Named after the constitutional amendment that protects freedom of speech and the right to peaceful assembly, the team of 30 armed officers will be trained to de-escalate tensions and communicate with demonstrators. They will be backed by a new Patrol Support Division, trained in crowd management, which will either accompany them to protests or be stationed nearby.




Under the new structure, the SRG’s counterterrorism functions will be separated from protest policing and instead consolidated within the NYPD’s Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau.

author: ACG
title: When Anarchism Ceases to Be Anarchist: Liberalism, Subjectivism and the Loss of the Revolutionary Horizon
content:
Below is the second of two texts produced by Spanish libertarian writers., this time from a member of the Spanish anarchist organisation Liza, based in  Granada and Madrid. We reproduce these texts, not because we necessarily agree 100 per cent with their arguments, but because they make valuable and stimulating arguments, necessary for the strengthening and development of anarchist  communism.




There is a discussion within anarchism that for too long has been relegated to the background. It is not a question of determining who possesses an anarchist certificate of authenticity or of establishing a doctrinal orthodoxy. It is a question of examining what conception of society, freedom, power, conflict and social transformation really sustains a given position and what political consequences follow from it.




Table of Contents




Anarchism is not only a negation of the state, an abstract defence of individual freedom, a cultural sensibility, or a collection of horizontal practices. In the anarchist tradition, emancipation implies transforming the social relations of domination and developing forms of self-management capable of replacing them through a revolutionary process. Felipe Corrêa has synthesised this conception through three articulated elements: revolution, critique of domination and defence of self-management.




This definition allows us to establish a fundamental starting point. Anarchism cannot be defined only by what it rejects. Its specificity also lies in the social relations it seeks to build and in the forces capable of making them possible. The question is not only whether a position is anti-state, anti-capitalist or pro-freedom, but also to determine what it means by these concepts, what social relations it identifies as the foundation of domination and how it intends to transform them.




It is from this perspective that it becomes important to examine the liberal and subjectivist influences that run through certain sectors of contemporary anarchism. The problem is not the intellectual origin of each concept considered in isolation. This is what happens when certain categories modify the way in which society is understood to the point of displacing the analysis of social relations, organisation and revolution.




1. Liberalism does not necessarily enter through the front door




When one speaks of liberal influences within anarchism, the most immediate reaction is to seek an explicit defence of the market, private property, or the minimal state. That search can overlook much deeper forms of influence.




Luigi Fabbri already warned about the so-called “bourgeois influences” within anarchism. The problem was not necessarily that the anarchists affected by them consciously became defenders of the bourgeoisie. It consisted of the incorporation of categories produced by bourgeois society that could alter the understanding of organisation, solidarity, social struggle and revolution.




Liberal influence can operate, therefore, by preserving the libertarian vocabulary while transforming the categories through which reality is interpreted. Autonomy, freedom, resistance or emancipation can maintain a radical appearance while detached from the material relations that provide them with political content.




Displacement appears when the individual becomes the privileged unit of analysis, when autonomy is separated from collective organisation, when immediate resistance replaces strategy, or when subjective will begins to explain phenomena determined by historical relations. It also appears when identity displaces material positions, when personal transformation is presented as equivalent to social transformation, or when the critique of the State replaces the analysis of the relations of domination in which it is inserted.




It is not a question of affirming that every defence of individual autonomy is liberal. Nor is it a question of reducing anarchism to a sociology of classes. The question is different. The individual and the collective are not confronting realities. They are in a historical relationship of mutual constitution. The individual acts within social relations that he has not created and these relations can be reproduced or transformed through conscious and collective action.




Ideological filtering becomes problematic precisely when this relationship breaks down and one of its terms goes on to explain the other. When society appears as the result of autonomous individuals who subsequently relate, social structures cease to be the starting point of analysis. When, on the other hand, the collective becomes an abstraction placed above those who compose it, individual autonomy is also annulled. A coherent anarchist perspective needs to reject both reductions.




2. The problem of the abstract individual




Vladimir Benoit’s critique of the so-called “anarchist liberalism” is useful in specifying this problem. Its central concept is methodological individualism, understood as the tendency to take the isolated individual as a fundamental unit to explain society.




From this perspective, classes, organisations, unions, and social movements end up appearing as aggregates of individuals. Society is explained on the basis of the particular decisions of its members rather than on the basis of historical relations that determine the conditions under which those decisions can occur.




This does not imply denying the individual or his autonomy. Nor does it mean that every individualistic conception of freedom is necessarily liberal. The problem arises when the isolated individual becomes a sufficient explanation of phenomena that possess a relational existence.




Exploitation is not the sum of personal experiences of precariousness. Wage labor is not simply a choice repeated by millions of individuals. Property is not a private preference. The State cannot be understood as the cumulative result of particular administrative decisions. All these realities express historical relations that condition the action of individuals and that, at the same time, are reproduced or disputed through their activity.




Reversing this relationship has political consequences. A social structure can end up being translated into the language of individual experience. Exploitation becomes personal precariousness. Domination becomes interpersonal relationships. Organisation appears as a matter of preferences. Social conflict becomes a problem of conscience, identity or behaviour.




The result is an impoverished conception of politics. Society ceases to appear as a historical totality traversed by power relations and material antagonisms and begins to be conceived as the sum of particular experiences whose subsequent articulation would produce the collective.




The problem is not to recognise the individual dimension of oppression. The problem is to turn it into the fundamental explanation of relationships that exist before each individual and that require collective intervention to be transformed.




3. From social analysis to psychologism




When the individual occupies the centre of the analysis, the will inevitably acquires an increasing weight. If social phenomena are explained mainly by the decisions and dispositions of the subjects, politics ends up concentrating on what they do, think or represent.




From this arises a form of radicalism focused on the permanent evaluation of individual coherence. It examines whether a person is sufficiently autonomous, whether he or she reproduces authority, whether he or she maintains horizontal practices, whether he or she uses appropriate language or whether his or her interpersonal relationships reproduce certain forms of domination.




These issues can be politically relevant. The transformation of everyday relations and the critique of the forms of power that run through social life are part of the anarchist tradition. The problem begins when this level replaces the analysis of the social relations that make these behaviours possible.




A material perspective demands different questions. What relationships produce a certain situation? Who controls the resources and the means of production? How is exploitation reproduced? Which institutions guarantee its continuity? What social forces can confront it? What organisational capacity exists to intervene on it?




The difference is not merely methodological. A policy focused on subjective coherence tends to turn conflict into a moral issue. A policy oriented to the analysis of social relations seeks to identify forces, interests, structures and organisational capacities.




The will is indispensable for any conscious transformation, but it does not explain by itself the conditions under which it can act. Revolutionary consciousness does not exist outside of history. It is formed within certain social relations and acquires transformative capacity when it is articulated with a collective practice capable of intervening on them.




Emancipation therefore requires subjective transformation and social transformation. The former may contribute to the latter, but it cannot replace it.




4. When Anarchy Becomes an Ideal Type




There is another form of abstraction that operates in a seemingly opposite direction. It consists in converting a certain representation of “Anarchy” into the criterion by which every concrete practice is immediately judged.




In this case, anarchy ceases to function as a political horizon and set of guiding principles to become an idealised model against which organisations, demands and experiences are evaluated. That which does not coincide with the model appears to be insufficiently anarchist, while that which reproduces certain formal features can be elevated to an expression of anarchy.




The relationship between theory and reality is thus inverted. Instead of using principles to guide the analysis of concrete historical situations, an abstract image of the future is used to judge reality from outside its contradictions.




A revolutionary policy demands something different. A demand, an organisation or a collective experience must be analysed in terms of the social relations they express, the forces they mobilise, the interests they confront, the contradictions they contain and the possibilities they open.




This does not mean abandoning principles. On the contrary, principles are necessary precisely because they make it possible to determine the emancipatory meaning of a transformation and to distinguish anarchism from other forms of radicalism. What must be rejected is to turn them into a finished description of every historical experience.




The difference is decisive. Principles guide practice. The ideal type is intended to replace concrete analysis. The former allow us to intervene without losing sight of the revolutionary horizon. The second can turn anarchy into a morality external to history.




Anarchism does not need to find experiences that perfectly reproduce an imagined future society. It needs to understand existing conditions, intervene on their contradictions and develop the forces capable of transforming them.




5. Classes as social relations




This question appears with particular clarity in the conception of social classes. Formally recognising the existence of workers and capitalists is not enough. It is also necessary to understand what makes them class.




A class is not a statistical set of individuals who share income, professions, or economic characteristics. It is a historically determined social relation. The existence of the working class depends on certain relations of property, production, work and appropriation. The capitalist class occupies the corresponding position within these same relations.




The capitalist is not simply a wealthy individual. The worker is not simply someone who receives a salary. Both occupy social positions determined by a structure that conditions their possibilities of action and whose reproduction depends on concrete practices.




Therefore, the class struggle cannot be reduced to a psychological conflict between groups of individuals. Its foundation lies in objective social relations that produce differentiated positions within the reproduction of society. Individuals participate in them and can face them, but they do not produce them through their isolated decisions.




Nor does this imply reducing all domination to the economy. The state, gender, racism, culture, and ideology all have specific dynamics. A rigorous materialism does not consist in converting all contradictions into a mechanical reflection of the economy, but in situating them within the historical and material relations that condition its development.




The issue is the same again. Where the relational dimension disappears, structures can end up being interpreted as effects of individual consciousness. Social transformation is then subordinated to the modification of the attitudes of the subjects.




But a social relationship does not disappear because the subjective dispositions of those who participate in it change. It requires a transformation of the conditions that allow it to be reproduced.




6. Liberal freedom and anarchist freedom




The difference between the liberal and anarchist conceptions of freedom cannot be reduced to affirming that one defends freedom and the other seeks to expand it. Both traditions contain different positions, but there is a fundamental difference in the way of understanding the social conditions of freedom.




A liberal conception can understand freedom as the existence of a sphere of action protected against external interference, particularly against political power. The central problem is then to determine which restrictions must be eliminated in order to preserve individual decision-making capacity.




Anarchism introduces an additional question. It is not enough to ask what interference the individual is formally protected from. It is also necessary to ask under what material conditions he can effectively exercise his freedom.




Legal equality does not eliminate inequalities arising from property relations. A worker can be legally free and materially dependent on the sale of his labor power. He may enjoy the same formal rights as the owner of a company and yet lack equivalent capacity to decide on the conditions of production.




From an anarchist perspective, freedom cannot be separated from the social relations that allow it to be exercised. It does not only consist of having a private space in front of authority, but of participating in relationships where no one is subject to a separate power and where the conditions of existence can be decided collectively.




Freedom thus acquires a material and social dimension. It is not only a matter of limiting political power, but of transforming the relations that produce dependence and subordination. Hence the question of freedom leads directly to self-management.




7. Self-management, organisation and anti-statism




Self-management does not mean that each individual manages his or her own affairs in isolation. It means that those who participate in a social activity can collectively control the conditions in which it takes place.




That is why it presupposes organisation. Production, distribution, deliberation and collective life require coordination. The anarchist problem is not to eliminate any organisational structure, but to prevent coordination from becoming a separate body capable of imposing decisions on those who constitute it.




Autonomy and organisation are not, therefore, contradictory terms. An organisation can expand the effective capacity of individuals precisely because it allows the coordination of forces that would remain isolated without it. The decisive question is how functions are distributed, who controls decisions, how delegations are revoked and what mechanisms prevent the formation of a separate power.




Federalism expresses this logic at the level of articulation between different social units. It is not simply administrative decentralisation. It involves coordinating organisations and communities through structures subject to the control of those who constitute them. But neither can political decentralisation be reduced to a sufficient solution. Territorially distributing power does not in itself eliminate exploitation or transform property relations.




This explains why isolated anti-statism is not enough to define anarchist politics. Opposing the state can coexist with very different conceptions of property, the economy, and social organisation. Reducing state functions does not necessarily equate to abolishing the relations of domination that structure society.




The anarchist problem is not simply to determine how much power the state should have. It consists of transforming the social conditions that make possible the separation between those who govern and those who are governed.




Therefore, abolishing an institution without transforming the relations that reproduce domination can leave intact the conditions for it to reappear in another form. Anti-statism acquires its revolutionary meaning when it is articulated with the transformation of property relations, social equality, collective organisation and self-management.




Self-management thus constitutes the positive dimension of anti-statism. It responds not only to who should not govern, but to how the conditions of social life can be organised without producing a separate instance of power.




8. From Stirner to the Politics of Subjectivity




Max Stirner’s critique introduces a question that deserves to be treated more precisely. To reduce his thought to a simple radical liberalism would be insufficient. A central part of his work is to question the abstractions that acquire authority over the individual. The state, citizenship, morality, humanity, or “man” can become entities to which people must subordinate themselves.




This critique retains an obvious utility for anarchism. No collective category should be transformed into a sacred entity placed above those who constitute it. But it does not follow that every collective category is an illegitimate abstraction.




A class can express a real social relation without becoming a metaphysical essence. An organisation can perform a political function without becoming a sacred entity. A society can be the object of collective transformation without being elevated to a transcendent subject.




The problem is not in using collective categories, but in substantiating them and separating them from the concrete relations that provide them with content.




This question acquires special relevance in certain contemporary currents that have developed critiques of fixed identities, universal subjects and essentialist categories. There is no linear continuity between Stirner, Nietzsche, Foucault, Deleuze, Derrida and the so-called “post-anarchism”. However, certain theoretical concerns have acquired considerable influence in sectors of contemporary libertarian thought.




These tools can be productive when they question naturalised forms of power or rigid conceptions of subjects. The problem arises when the critique of identity becomes a critique of concrete social positions. The fact that an identity is not an immutable essence does not mean that the social relations associated with it lack reality. The fact that class is historically changing does not mean that class relations disappear. The fact that an organisation can produce power relations does not mean that all organisation is equivalent to domination.




Displacement becomes politically problematic when revolution comes to be conceived primarily as a transformation of subjectivity. Everyday resistance can then acquire a centrality that displaces stable organisation, strategy and structural transformation.




Here it is important to distinguish revolution and insurrection. An insurrection may imply a break with existing forms of subjectivity and authority. A revolution, on the other hand, also involves a transformation of social relations and institutions. Both dimensions can be part of the same process, but they are not equivalent.




Transforming subjectivity can contribute to an emancipatory practice. It cannot replace the transformation of relations that reproduce exploitation and domination.




The problem is not to recognise the importance of subjectivity or to deny that power runs through everyday relationships. It is to prevent this analysis from completely absorbing the terrain of revolutionary politics. A multiplicity of resistances can produce cultural and subjective changes without substantially modifying property, work, production or institutional forms of power.




The revolutionary question remains intact. What forces can transform existing relationships? What forms of organisation can articulate them, and what strategy can turn these dispersed capacities into a historical force?




9. From liberal filtration to the loss of the revolutionary horizon




Liberal influences can also be produced through the co-optation of the libertarian vocabulary itself. Shelagh Roxburgh’s research on 

so-called soft anarchism

 is illustrative in showing how concepts associated with anarchism can be incorporated into liberal frameworks, particularly in the theory of international relations.




Networks, decentralisation, cooperation, resistance, and non-state actors can be integrated into governance discourses without necessarily retaining their anti-capitalist content. The effectiveness of this co-optation lies precisely in the fact that it does not need to eliminate radical language. It can preserve words while modifying the conceptual relationships that gave them meaning.




Autonomy can be detached from ownership. Cooperation can be separated from exploitation. Resistance can be reduced to a permanent practice without a revolutionary horizon. Decentralisation can become an administrative technique. Participation can exist without effective control over resources.




Here Fabbri’s notion of “bourgeois leaks” becomes important again. Its usefulness lies not in classifying people as bourgeois or revolutionary, but in analysing how categories produced within bourgeois society can be incorporated into an emancipatory theory and modify its presuppositions.




Bourgeois society does not produce only certain economic relations. It also produces historical conceptions of the individual, freedom, property, competition, responsibility, and autonomy that can be presented as universal. When these categories organise political analysis, essentially social relations can end up being interpreted as individual problems.




The same displacement can affect the conception of class and organisation. If structures are translated into personal experiences, class ceases to appear as a social relation. If every organisation is treated primarily as a potential source of hierarchy, the need to build collective capacities can become a problem in itself.




The critique of rigid identities can serve to combat essentialisms. It does not justify, however, abandoning social relations as an object of analysis. Similarly, recognising that organisations can produce power does not imply that organising is tantamount to reproducing domination.




The result of these successive reductions can be a policy focused on local resistances, subjective practices and daily ruptures. Such experiences can be part of a revolutionary strategy. They become a substitute for revolution when they are no longer linked to the transformation of social relations.




The problem then reaches its clearest form. Revolutionary language can survive after that which made it revolutionary has disappeared. Autonomy, cooperation, participation, decentralisation and resistance can coexist with the existing order if they are separated from ownership, exploitation, social conflict and self-management.




The question is not whether certain practices are radical enough. It is whether they contribute to the development of the forces capable of transforming the social relations that produce domination.




10. Towards a social and revolutionary reconstruction of anarchism




Recovering the revolutionary horizon does not require building a closed doctrine. It requires the re-establishment of a coherent relationship between freedom, material conditions, social relations, organisation and collective capacity.




Anarchist freedom cannot be reduced to the absence of interference or to legal equality. Its exercise depends on specific conditions such as access to resources, time, education, decision-making capacity and control over living conditions. Therefore, emancipation requires transforming the relations that produce dependence, including the ownership of the means of production and the organisation of work.




Self-management expresses this transformation in positive terms. It does not mean simply participating in decisions, but collectively exercising control over the social conditions that determine one’s existence.




Nor can anti-statism constitute a separate program. Abolishing the State requires transforming the relations that make possible the separation between rulers and ruled, but also those that produce economic dependence and concentration of power. The question is not only which institution should disappear, but what social forms can make its existence unnecessary.




This places organisation at the centre of the revolutionary problem. Organisation does not mean authority by definition. What is decisive are the power relations it establishes, the mechanisms of control over its functions, the participation of its members and the possibility of revoking delegations. An organised structure can reproduce domination or expand the collective capacity of those who make it up.




Malatesta linked revolution to conscious action, organisation, and the creation of new social relations. The militants of 

Dyelo Truda

, starting from their interpretation of the Russian Revolution, also insisted on the problems arising from the absence of an anarchist organisation capable of coordinating a coherent revolutionary intervention. This does not make platformism a mandatory model. Its relevance lies in a more general question: a revolutionary force needs mechanisms capable of coordinating action without separating the political leadership from those who produce it.




The same perspective allows us to distinguish reform and reformism. A partial claim can improve living conditions and strengthen the organisation. It becomes reformism when it ceases to be part of a strategy of transformation and becomes the definitive horizon. Nor does the revolution need be reduced to a single insurrectionary moment. It can develop through a prolonged process of conflict, organisation, self-management, and social transformation, provided that the partial struggles maintain a conscious relationship with that horizon.




Murray Bookchin’s critique of 

so-called lifestyle anarchism

 is pertinent here, even if his opposition between “social anarchism” and “lifestyle anarchism” is too rigid to encompass the historical plurality of anarchism. Individual practices can contribute to an emancipatory culture, but they do not in themselves replace the transformation of social structures. The problem is not personal transformation. It is to make it the main terrain of revolutionary politics.




Defending a social perspective does not mean sacrificing the individual to an abstract collectivity. Individual and society are inseparable dimensions of human existence. Cooperation can expand individual freedom when it allows for collective control over material living conditions. Anarchist communism does not conceive of the community as a negation of individuality, but as a condition for its development without subordination.




The historical plurality of anarchism does not oblige relativism either. It is not necessary to construct a closed canon or to establish a definitive definition of anarchism. But recognising diversity does not mean considering all conceptions of freedom, domination, organisation, and revolution as equivalent. Different diagnoses produce different strategies.




The relevant criterion is not doctrinal purity, but coherence between the analysis of social relations, the emancipatory horizon and the means proposed to achieve it.




Contributions from other intellectual traditions can be incorporated critically. A revolutionary theory does not need to isolate itself intellectually. It needs to retain the capacity to subject any conceptual tool to its own emancipatory objectives and reject those categories that end up hiding the relations it seeks to transform.




The social and revolutionary reconstruction of anarchism therefore involves recovering a perspective capable of linking autonomy and collective capacity, freedom and material conditions, anti-statism and social transformation, concrete struggles and revolutionary strategy.




It is not a question of preserving a doctrinal identity in the face of all external influence. It is a matter of preventing concepts such as freedom, autonomy, resistance or participation from being separated from the social relations that provide them with political content.




The fundamental question remains open, but it is not ambiguous. What relations of domination must be abolished, what social forms can replace them and what collective capacity is necessary to make this transformation possible.




Don Diego de la Vega, militant of Liza.

author: Phill Gittins
title: Rethinking Defense: World BEYOND War Joins International Conference in Strasbourg
content:
By Phill Gittins, World BEYOND War, November 16, 2026







World BEYOND War’s

 Europe Organizer Annachiara Canetta and Education Director Dr. Phill Gittins joined around 150 participants from across Europe and beyond in Strasbourg, France, for the 

international conference 

Comprehensive Defence: The Contributions of Unarmed Civilian-Based Defense (UCBD) to Whole-of-Society Defence

.




Held at the Centre Culturel Saint-Thomas on November 13–14, 2026, the 

conference

 aimed, in the organizers’ words, to explore “the value, the feasibility, and the limitations of unarmed civilian options in the field of defence.”




Across the two days, presentations, roundtables, and workshops ranged widely, from the history, theory, and strategies of unarmed civilian-based defense (UCD) to civilian resistance and resilience in Ukraine, responses to authoritarian regimes and armed groups, information warfare, deterrence, and preparedness. The conference also included a video address from Ukrainian human rights defender Oleksandra Matviichuk of the Nobel Peace Prize-winning 

Center for Civil Liberties

. Participants came from a range of organizations, including 

FLACSO Ecuador

, 

NOVACT

, 

Greenpeace

, 

Nonviolent Peaceforce

, and other research and civil society organizations.




Despite the range of topics and perspectives, one question ran through the conference: what does it mean — and what does it take — to defend a society? What are civilians already doing, and what more could they do?




Different understandings of defense




There seemed to be broad agreement that civilians have a role in defense, but much less agreement about what that role should be. Some saw UCD as a complement to military defense. Others argued that UCD should be developed as an alternative, not simply an addition, to military defense. For some, the question was not just about effectiveness, but about what we are trying to defend. Military force can devastate the very people, communities, cultures, and environments it is meant to protect. Nonviolent action offers ways to defend them without resorting to that destruction.




Military defense remains the dominant approach in much security thinking, policy, and planning. Governments increasingly speak of comprehensive or whole-of-society defense. Yet UCD and its distinctive logic and strategies receive far less attention than military approaches. Practical training in how nonviolent civilian defense works is also far less established than military training, including across much of civil society.




A society’s greatest strength lies in its people and their capacity to act together, not in the latest and most lethal weapons systems. Communities, schools, local authorities, trade unions, and civil society organizations have knowledge, relationships, and skills that should be central to how we understand and pursue security.




Another important theme was the need to build defense from the bottom up, through cooperation, collective action, and shared decision-making — what might be called 

power with

, rather than 

power over

. There is a fundamental difference between involving civilians in existing military-led arrangements and supporting them to develop alternatives of their own. As I argued during the roundtable, this is the difference between renovating the existing system and transforming it: moving beyond reliance on military force and building a system in which peace is pursued by peaceful means.




Friday’s roundtable








































Annachiara and I explored these questions during Friday’s roundtable on cooperation between institutions, civilians, and the military. The discussion brought together sharply different views. We argued for war abolition and nonviolent alternatives, while others saw military force as necessary alongside greater civilian involvement.




Annachiara discussed growing militarization in Europe, military spending, conscription, conscientious objection, and youth mobilization. She emphasized the importance of protecting the independence of civil society, including the right to refuse to kill or take part in military service. This raises another question: what opportunities are available for people who refuse military service to learn, organize, and contribute to protecting their communities through nonviolent means?




I drew on World BEYOND War’s research and education work, including our 

growing list of successful nonviolent actions used instead of wars

. One distinction I raised was between responding to the “wars of the day” and addressing the wider War System: the institutions, political and economic interests, assumptions, and cultures that sustain the preparation for, financing of, and reliance on war. Responding to particular wars is necessary, but not sufficient. If we do not also address the systems that sustain war, we are likely to keep confronting new ones.




Some of the most interesting conversations took place outside the formal sessions. Over the two days, several people approached us to say that they had been thinking along similar lines. One woman said she had wondered whether she was at the wrong conference, given the arguments being made for military responses at an event devoted to UCD. Another felt that some discussions were not going far enough in questioning the wider War System.




Disagreement was to be expected, and it was worth having. We may agree that people need to be safe while disagreeing sharply about how best to protect them. Yet, as one participant asked during a session, what do we do when people simply refuse to listen? This raises a wider challenge for the peace movement: how do we engage people who believe military force is necessary and encourage them to consider nonviolent alternatives?




From knowing about alternatives to preparing for them




UCD should not be mistaken for passivity. It requires courage, discipline, and commitment, often in dangerous circumstances. But knowing that alternatives exist, or believing they can work, is not the same as being prepared to use them.




People need strategies, relationships, communication, training, and opportunities to practice making decisions and coordinating actions under pressure. Military institutions invest enormous resources in planning and preparation. UCD also requires serious preparation, yet it receives far less sustained attention and investment. We would not expect an army to improvise all its plans when a crisis begins. Why do we so often expect civilians to do so?




World BEYOND War’s six-week online course, 

Unarmed Civilian Defense Instead of War

, was developed to help address this gap. Across three offerings, more than 500 people from over 20 countries and territories have registered. In our 

crisis simulations

, participants take different roles and work through questions of civilian protection, noncooperation, communication, and coordination as a crisis escalates — without relying on military force.




Our next course is planned for February 2027.




Connections across the movement




Strasbourg was also a chance to reconnect with colleagues, meet others working in the field, and explore possibilities for future collaboration.




We caught up with Hans Hedrich, 

World BEYOND War’s Romania Co-Coordinator

. Earlier that week, Hans and Annachiara had supported a 

submission to the International Criminal Court in The Hague

 concerning alleged U.S. complicity in crimes in Gaza, with Annachiara also speaking at the accompanying press conference.







I reconnected with Dr. Christine Schweitzer, a researcher and practitioner in nonviolent defense who contributed to an earlier offering of our UCD course. Her work includes 

research on unarmed civilian protection and its lessons for social defense

.




It was also good to spend time chatting with Felip Daza Sierra, learning more about his research on civilian resistance and community resilience in Ukraine, including his recent report, 

Democratic Resilience in Ukraine: From Emergency to Transformation

. We discussed ideas for a related course and a possible larger research collaboration.

























With Dr. Christine Schweitzer




With Felip Daza Sierra













We also spoke with Xavier Major Roca, a longstanding conscientious objector and participant in our 

War and the Environment

 course, Martí Olivella of NOVACT, and other colleagues about conscientious objection and anti-war organizing in Catalonia.




Dr. Cécile Mouly and María Belén Garrido of FLACSO Ecuador shared 

research on community-led peace initiatives in Colombia

. Having previously collaborated with colleagues from FLACSO on a webinar series about peace and security in Latin America, we discussed possibilities for further cooperation.

























With Xavier Major Roca.




With María Belén Garrido and Cécile Mouly of FLACSO Ecuador.













What should happen next?




























The closing discussions brought an important reminder: “Do not only speak to ourselves.” Participants also called for “larger international and intergenerational exchanges” beyond established networks.




A phrase I heard several times during the conference was “broaden the scope of possibility.” It stayed with me and reminded me of peace researcher Elise Boulding’s observation: “We can’t work for what we can’t imagine.”




This matters for how we think about defense. If military force is the only response we can imagine, it is likely to remain the only one we seriously prepare for. That means questioning familiar assumptions, examining the evidence, acknowledging limitations, and preparing credible alternatives. It also means bringing different people and perspectives into the conversation, including policymakers, military professionals, researchers, activists, and the communities whose security is at stake.




Participants also called for more in-person training, closer links between universities and civil society, and greater involvement of young people. The last point came up repeatedly, with one participant describing it as “the elephant in the room.”




After Saturday’s program, Annachiara and I joined steering committee members Dr. Alexandre Christoyannopoulos and Dr. Cécile Dubernet, other colleagues, and a group of young people to explore possible collaboration on UCD and related issues by, with, and for young people.




Looking ahead, a 

workshop at Loughborough University

 on March 22–24, 2027, will bring together researchers and practitioners to explore the barriers to wider adoption of civilian-based defense and how these might be overcome. I look forward to contributing to those discussions.




Strasbourg did not resolve our different understandings of peace, security, defense, and violence, nor was that necessarily the aim. Concepts such as these, alongside democracy and justice, illustrate what philosophers call 

essentially contested concepts

: we may use the same words while disagreeing deeply about what they mean and how they should guide our actions. The point is not necessarily to agree on a single definition, but to listen carefully, understand what others mean, and be willing to question our own assumptions.




What matters now is whether these conversations build stronger relationships, encourage further research, and, most importantly, help people prepare to use nonviolent alternatives — and actually use them. For World BEYOND War, defense must mean more than preparing for the next war. It must mean developing the knowledge, relationships, institutions, and capacities needed to prevent wars, end those underway, and ultimately abolish war itself.




World BEYOND War thanks the conference organizers — 

Mouvement pour une Alternative Non-violente (MAN)

, 

Institut pour la Paix (IPP)

, 

Institut de recherche sur la Résolution Non-violente des Conflits (IRNC)

, 

Organization for Nonviolent Movements (ONM)

, and 

Center for Nonviolent Conflict Research (CNCR)

 — together with the steering committee, volunteers, speakers, and everyone who contributed.

Rethinking Defense: World BEYOND War Joins International Conference in Strasbourg

 appeared first on 

World BEYOND War

.

author: Chris Walker
title: Over 50 Incoming Dem Lawmakers Demand House Ban on Congressional Stock Trading
content:
Despite midterm wins, the incoming Democrats noted the party has “a long way to go to earn back the trust of voters.”

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Dozens of incoming Democratic representatives-elect have signed on to an open letter demanding that leaders of their party within the House of Representatives support new rules that will prohibit stock trading by lawmakers.

The incoming lawmakers — fresh off their enormous victories in midterm election races across the United States earlier this month — noted that voters elected them to end “corrupt self-dealing” in Washington. Democrats can deliver on that promise “the day the new Congress is sworn in,” the letter-writers stated.

“We are calling on our Democratic leaders in the House to quickly adopt a rule barring members and their spouses from owning or trading stocks, commodities, futures, derivatives, and other related securities, with limited exceptions such as a diversified mutual fund or an investment held in a qualified blind trust,” the letter said.

The letter was signed by over 50 Democratic representatives-elect, more than half of whom flipped their districts’ seats from Republican control. The incoming lawmakers also come from 23 different states across the country.

The letter-writers recognized that Democrats “may have won the election,” but the party has “a long way to go to earn back the trust of voters across the country.”

“A stock trading ban alone will not fix Washington, but it is the fastest way to show voters we heard them. … We promised our communities we would clean up this place,” they added. “In January, we should do just that.”

There wasn’t an immediate response from Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York), who is poised to become the next Speaker of the House. Jeffries has supported stock trading bans in the past and has indicated support for the idea in the next congressional session.

Americans largely back such a ban, with the issue being supported across the political spectrum.

A PRRI poll conducted this summer showed that 80 percent of Americans believe it should be illegal for “elected officials to buy or sell individual stocks while in office.” Only 15 percent said they disagreed with the idea.

Among Democratic respondents, 84 percent said they supported banning elected officials from stock trading. Eighty-three percent of independent voters said the same, along with 79 percent of Republican voters.

House Democrats are likely to adopt rules on the matter. They could also attempt to introduce legislation banning stock trading for lawmakers in both houses of Congress, as well as for the executive branch. Though such a bill could potentially be blocked by a Senate filibuster, efforts to block such legislation may be unsuccessful due to the popularity of a ban among the American public.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $28,000 in the next 72 hours. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.
