author: Wendy Bacon, Cathy Peters
title: Time to reassess the antisemitism envoy’s role
content:
Civil liberties and Palestinian supporters are calling for the Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism, Jillian Segal, to be sacked after her latest report accused them of using “human rights” to hide their antisemitism.

Segal’s Plan to Combat Antisemitism appears designed to raise the pressure on all levels of government as well as the forthcoming final report of the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion in December.

Segal is an active player in an international network, coordinated by key pro-Israel Jewish bodies as well as the United States State Department. Indeed, if it had not been for pressure from the US government, Segal might not have the job at all.

Segal is one of 32 Special Envoys in North America, Europe, South America, Israel and Australia.

The position of the US Special Envoy to Combat and Monitor Antisemitism was established in 2004, when New Jersey Republican congressman Chris Smith, who has a history of advocating for Israel and a record of accusing organisations including UN bodies of rampant antisemitism, successfully pushed to pass legislation creating the position.

Following the US lead, the European Union appointed an Envoy in 2015, followed by Canada, Greece, the Organization of American States and Britain. Israel’s envoy is part of its Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

In 2021, Smith, by then a strong supporter of Donald Trump, successfully pushed for an amendment which strengthened the position of US Special Envoy to the level of ambassador. They report directly to the Secretary of State, are appointed by the President and, crucially, can access foreign governments.

The ambassador’s mission is to promote US foreign policy by developing and implementing policies and projects to support action against antisemitism.

The office uses the controversial International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition, which directly links Jewish people with Zionism and the State of Israel, and conflates criticism of Israel with antisemitism.

The current US Antisemitism Ambassador is far right winger Rabbi Yehuda Kaploun. He has boasted about influencing governments and recently described his office as supporting Trump’s policies by having 250,000 visas cancelled to keep campuses “‘safe”, interfering in foreign educational curricula and initiating prosecutions of what he describes as “hate crimes”.

This is echoed in Segal’s plan, which include compulsory training for Home Affairs staff responsible for certain visa applications and a new task force to review existing visas.

While it was initially reluctant, the Anthony Albanese Labor government appointed Segal in July 2024, after intense lobbying from the US State Department, which the Australian media did not cover.

FOI releases show that in May 2024, Aaron Keyek, the then US deputy antisemitism envoy, met with Australian officials in Foreign Affairs and Trade and the Attorney General’s Department to pressure the Albanese government to appoint an envoy.

Keyek also met with Deborah O’Neill, the Co-Chair of Labor Friends of Israel.

The crunch came with an ultimatum regarding a meeting of special envoys in Argentina, in July 2024, to sign US-drafted global guidelines to counter antisemitism.

A former senior US official told Jerusalem News Syndicate: “We were all diplomatic about it, but we told Australia, essentially, ‘It’s going to be glaring’. We didn’t want to repeat the situation, where one of our closest allies didn’t stand up to one of the top foreign-policy priorities when it comes to human rights that the United States is pushing internationally… So we told them that they could only attend if the delegation was led by a special envoy.”

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade sent a cable to the US State Department on July 4 advising of the imminent appointment of an envoy who would report directly to the Prime Minister.

Segal was appointed on July 9, just 10 days before the meeting in Buenos Aires, which she attended. According to that cable, she had already approved the guidelines and her tickets had been booked before she was appointed.

Australia’s Ambassador to Argentina was permitted to sign off on the guidelines which refer to the IHRA definition as a key tool for fighting antisemitism, as a result of Segal’s hasty appointment.

In 2019 the New York based World Jewish Congress (WJC), the central governing organisation of Jewish organisations, which “defends the Jewish state of Israel”, established the Special Envoys and Coordinators Combating Antisemitism (SECCA) Network to coordinate “responses to antisemitism”.

Segal’s work is partially dictated by this body. Since her appointment, Segal has worked closely with SECCA. In July last year, Rabbi Yehuda, the US Special Envoy in the State Department Ambassador thanked her for hosting an online forum.

In her first 15 months, Segal took five overseas trips, costing $85,000, and in May she travelled to Geneva to sign another SECCA joint declaration.

The 15th meeting of SECCA was held last month in Dublin, organised by the WJC in partnership with the European Commission. The conference aimed to look at ways to implement strong measures to “confront online hatred and turn government promises into concrete action”.

It heard reports from delegates from 28 countries, including Australia, and included visits to the European headquarters of TikTok and Meta. It included representatives from the WJC’s Technology and Human Rights institute, which focuses solely on lobbying governments, international bodies, and tech companies on policy, monitoring and control within the digital realm.

Maram Stern, WJC Executive Vice President and SECCA Co-Chair spoke at the forum emphasising the need to urgently enforce “practical solutions” to antisemitism.

Stern linked the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack to a worldwide surge in antisemitism, rather than to the worldwide revulsion with Israel’s genocide in Gaza.

Segal. who spoke via video to the Dublin conference, urged stronger institutional accountability, education and enforcement against antisemitism.

Referring to the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion (which heard many unchallenged allegations of antisemitism), Segal noted that its proceedings had brought into focus “concerns about antisemitism in universities, cultural institutions, and healthcare”.

These are key areas where we have seen false claims of antisemitism and lawfare used against academics, artists and healthcare workers.

Segal was not the only Australian who spoke. Her close partners from the Executive Council of Australian Jewry (EJAC), Peter Wertheim, EJAC co-CEO, called for “more proactive regulation of technology companies and effective legal avenues for people harmed by online content”.

Daniel Aghion, ECAJ president and WJC vice president, emphasised the importance of active special envoys, sustained government engagement and coordination between Jewish organisations.

Before the conference had started, it emerged that one of Dublin’s prestigious hotels had refused to accommodate the SECCA delegates and alternative accommodation and a conference venue had to be found.

This went unreported until Maurice Cohen, chairman of the Jewish Representative Council of Ireland, told a pre-conference event that the 4-star Herbert Park Hotel in Dublin, which had taken the SECCA booking for 70 rooms in April, had abruptly cancelled this booking after a meeting with the conference organisers and the hotel’s general manager.

Cohen was asked by the hotel manager whether the event had any ties to the Israeli Defence Force (IDF). He told Fox News Digital, “I was completely taken aback by that question. I said, ‘What would the IDF have to do with a conference on antisemitism?’.”

It was revealed that the hotel’s general manager subsequently consulted the hotel owners before the cancellation was made.

This was immediately characterised by the organisers as a major antisemitic event.

The World Jewish Congress published an opinion piece by Maurice Cohen on October 14 titled: “Ironically, an antisemitism conference falls victim to Jew-hatred”.

Although the Herbert Park Hotel refused to make public comment, it is clear it chose not to be associated with an event that had ties to the IDF.

The links between SECCA and support of Israel and members of the IDF are strong. SECCA representatives work with pro-Israel organisations, that have key personnel directly connected with the Israeli state, and past and present members of the IDF.

Conflating this refusal with antisemitism is yet another example of how peak pro-Israel Jewish organisations continue to wrongly link antisemitism to protest actions such as the Herbert Park Hotel boycott.

One of the major organisations participating in the SECCA conference in Dublin was the Combat Antisemitism Movement (CAM), which is based in the US and has spread internationally. Its advisory board members and its CEO are directly linked to Israel.

CAM works globally to pressure governments to not only endorse the IHRA definition of antisemitism but to enforce it. It reported that it was recognised as a “trusted US State Department partner” at the SECCA conference, where it reiterated the coordinated push to get governments to enforce the IHRA antisemitism definition — a point which was emphasised by US Special Envoy Ambassador Rabbi Yehuda Kaploun.

CAM also has strong links with the IDF.

The J50 forum, founded by Israel’s foreign ministry, includes 50 Jewish organisations internationally. Its third meeting in Jerusalem last September issued its hard line and contentious Declaration on Zionism and Antisemitism, which stated unequivocally that “Zionism is part of Jewish identity”.

It defined anti-Zionism as a form of antisemitism when used to “marginalize or deny Jewish self-determination”.

Daniel Aghion’s presentation summarised ECAJ’s work since the Bondi terrorist attack. He offered some unguarded insights into how this organisation mobilised around the royal commission: “It has been a massive exercise over the last year. The Jewish community has spent millions of dollars, and many millions more in pro bono legal and non-legal work. This was to make sure that our voice is heard properly, both inside and outside the Commission, and to ensure that the Commission has run as well as it can.”

MWM asked ECAJ about whether any of ECAJ’s large government grants had been used on the royal commission work but not not receive a response.

On November 19, the Israel-based Jerusalem Post Group’s first Asia-Pacific Summit will be held in Sydney. It will feature many Israeli speakers, including Israel’s president Isaac Herzog’s wife Michel Herzog, who will speak online, the Israeli ambassador to Australia, former senior IDF members, as well as President of Zionist Federation of Australia, Jeremy Liebler.

The focus is on “countering hostility” to Israel and building business links, something which many anti-genocide Australians do not support.

Ten days later the 2026 CAM conference for mayors and councillors will be held in Sydney. These events reinforce the global messaging of SECCA, WJC and J50. They are designed to add impetus Segal’s agenda leading up to the first anniversary of the Bondi massacre, and prior to the release of the royal commission report in December.

Segal’s overreach into all aspects of our civil life is not just angering human rights activists, and those who are unfairly being labelled as antisemitic, but large sections of Australian society who do not support Israel and do not want to be policed at the service of this rogue state.

Albanese buckled to pressure in creating the position of antisemitism envoy and made a striking error in appointing the Israel lobby’s choice to that position.

As anger grows about Segal’s appointment, it is time to reassess the legitimacy of the position itself in light of the facts surrounding its creation.

We have existing anti-discrimination legislation and strong National Anti-Racism Framework guidelines that are yet to be implemented.

Bending to US, Israel and the local Israel lobby’s demands will only intensify public anger.

title: Gaza versus Ucrania: la diferencia entre un genocidio y una guerra, en cifras
content:
Hay números que no necesitan adjetivos. Ponemos una al lado de la otra las cifras de Gaza y de Ucrania, las de las fuentes oficiales y las de los organismos internacionales, y dejamos que hablen. Todas son terribles, porque cualquier guerra es una tragedia humana. Pero no todas las muertes responden a la misma lógica.




Los niños, el primer termómetro.




En Ucrania, desde febrero de 2022, la ONU (OHCHR) ha verificado 820 niños muertos y 3.126 heridos. Son 820 vidas truncadas que nunca deberían haberse perdido.




En Gaza, desde octubre de 2023, las cifras oficiales indican que el ejército israelí ha matado a más de 21.000 niños y ha dejado unos 44.500 heridos hasta principios de abril de 2026. UNICEF eleva el cómputo a más de 64.000 niños muertos o heridos, incluidos unos 300 fallecidos en los 300 días posteriores al alto el fuego de octubre de 2025. Es decir, más de 25 veces el número de niños muertos en Ucrania y más de 14 veces el de heridos, en un territorio que cabe en un puñado de comarcas gallegas y en menos tiempo.




Los civiles: dos guerras, dos lógicas.




La ONU ha verificado en Ucrania al menos 16.874 civiles muertos y 51.273 heridos.




El Ministerio de Salud de Gaza cifra los muertos en 74.645 y los heridos en 175.978, según los datos más recientes, del 10 de noviembre de 2026. Mujeres y niños representan aproximadamente la mitad de las víctimas. Desde el alto el fuego de octubre de 2025 se contabilizan unos 1.600 muertos más, y siguen quedando víctimas bajo los escombros sin recuperar. Un alto el fuego en el que se sigue matando.




Quién muere en una guerra y quién muere en un exterminio.




En una guerra, la mayoría de los muertos son quienes combaten. En Ucrania, Zelenski habló en febrero de 2026 de 55.000 soldados muertos, según las cifras oficiales, mientras que el CSIS estadounidense calcula entre 125.000 y 150.000 muertos en combate hasta junio de 2026. Del lado ruso, Mediazona y la BBC han confirmado, con nombres y apellidos, unos 283.000 militares muertos, y los servicios británicos estiman la cifra en unos 500.000. Los ejércitos, quienes decidieron o acataron la guerra, ponen la inmensa mayoría de los muertos.




En Gaza, el ejército israelí reconoce 970 muertos entre soldados, reservistas y agentes de seguridad desde el 7 de octubre, 472 de ellos durante la ofensiva terrestre y 85 por fuego amigo o accidentes (el Ministerio de Defensa eleva la cifra a 1.152 con otro método de cómputo). Frente a eso, más de 74.000 palestinos muertos: unos 77 por cada militar israelí caído, según las cifras del propio ejército.




Israel afirma haber matado a más de 24.000 combatientes en Gaza. Sin embargo, una investigación de +972 Magazine y The Guardian, basada en datos de la inteligencia militar israelí, señala que, en mayo de 2025, esa misma inteligencia solo contabilizaba 8.900 combatientes de Hamás y de la Yihad Islámica como muertos o probables muertos. Israel rechaza esa interpretación. Aun así, incluso aceptando su cifra más alta, queda un número enorme de muertos que no empuñaban un fusil.




Lo que dicen los juristas.




El genocidio consiste en la comisión de determinados actos con la intención de destruir, total o parcialmente, a un grupo nacional, étnico, racial o religioso. No es una cuestión de palabras gruesas: es una categoría jurídica, y cada vez más voces con autoridad para hacerlo la aplican a Gaza.




En septiembre de 2025, la Comisión de Investigación de la ONU concluyó que Israel es responsable de genocidio en Gaza, tras constatar cuatro de los cinco actos genocidas recogidos en la Convención de 1948 y una intención de destruir a los palestinos de la Franja. Un centenar de penalistas españoles del Grupo de Estudios de Política Criminal han denunciado crímenes de guerra, de lesa humanidad y de genocidio, y reclaman a España y a la Unión Europea que se personen en los procesos penales internacionales y rompan las relaciones comerciales y diplomáticas con Israel. El caso de Sudáfrica sigue abierto ante la Corte Internacional de Justicia, y la propia Fiscalía española ha abierto una investigación.




Israel rechaza todas estas conclusiones. Que lo haga no las borra, y quienes las suscriben no son precisamente propagandistas. Quien siga poniendo en duda lo que muestran las cifras y lo que dicen los expertos será recordado por la historia como cómplice.




La diferencia no es de grado, es de naturaleza.




En una guerra, por brutal que sea, el objetivo principal no son los civiles y mucho menos los niños: mueren por la lógica criminal del conflicto, por los bombardeos y por el desprecio a las leyes de la guerra. En un genocidio, el objetivo es la aniquilación de un pueblo, su exterminio. Por eso, los niños, que son su futuro, y los civiles, que son su sustancia, no son un «daño colateral», sino la diana.




Las cifras hablan por sí solas. Lo que no puede hacer nadie con dignidad es seguir mirando para otro lado.




¡Hasta la victoria siempre!




André Abeledo Fernández

Indymedia Argentina Centro de Medios Independientes (( i ))

title: Horizontes Postcapitalistas
content:
Horizontes Postcapitalistas




Argentina 2026-11-14 – enviado por Andrés L R: andresenbsas@gmail.com 




Es un gusto presentar este audiovisual, en pleno estreno.


Integro el grupo de personas que, desde diferentes países, en forma colectiva, construimos este proyecto.




La Red de Estudios en Postcapitalismo busca aportar al pensamiento y la práctica para el postcapitalismo.




[ 

Nueva revista: 

https://rep.enesmerida.unam.mx/revista-horizontes-poscapitalistas

/

 ]




Es decir, pensar imaginar compartir estudiar cuidar, qué y cómo, crear hacer construir tejer sembrar ese modo de mundo ya no capitalista, esas formas de autonomía, que, desde abajo, recuperan lo comunitario priorizando la defensa y protección de la biodiversidad que integramos.




Este audiovisual, hace foco en las circunstancias dadas que atravesamos como humanidad, analiza las artimañas y los avasalladores golpes que el sistema capitalista ejecuta, a traves de sus operadores, para traspasar las crisis profundas que padece.




Sobre la base del análisis y observación, del profesor William I. Robinson, veremos la crisis institucional en curso, el surgimiento del nuevo complejo económico hegemónico mundial y la oleada de expansión capitalista que padecemos.




Que sea un aporte para el pensar y el hacer.


Intentar ver dónde estamos paradxs y a qué nos enfrentamos.




Y también abrir la pregunta ¿Con qué herramientas contamos?




«Hora Cero; Crisis de Época del Capitalismo Global»




https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bUjk9rptWXI




.







REVISTA HORIZONTES POSCAPITALISTAS




/rep.enesmerida.unam.mx/revista-horizontes-poscapitalistas/




EDITORIAL Número 2. Noviembre, 2026. Precisiones y límites del concepto postcapitalista.




Tras haber sembrado en nuestro primer número una cartografía de experiencias vivas, les invitamos a recorrer las páginas de este segundo número de la revista Horizontes Postcapitalistas, titulado Precisiones y límites del concepto postcapitalista. Este proyecto editorial nace de la profunda convicción de que el conocimiento no es un ejercicio académico abstracto, sino un acto ético y político de co-construcción y cuidado mutuo.




En tiempos donde las lógicas de la competencia y el individualismo tienden a aislarnos, apostamos por pensar y escribir en común como una forma genuina de resistencia. Nuestro objetivo para esta entrega es dar continuidad a la labor de documentar el hacer postcapitalista, proponiendo un ejercicio de diálogo crítico que abone al desarrollo conceptual desde la experiencia, la escucha y la reflexión situada. Creemos firmemente que es en ese encuentro donde logramos ensanchar las grietas por las que ya germinan otros mundos posibles.




Este número abre con un texto colectivo elaborado por el Grupo de Investigación Colectiva del Semillero de Saberes de la REP, el cual ofrece delimitaciones fundamentales sobre las praxis y filosofías milenarias no capitalistas y los buenos vivires en las ciudades, las selvas y los campos. A partir de ahí, las páginas se despliegan como un mapa en movimiento para asomarnos a las geografías de lo posible, un tránsito por las orillas de un sistema que se resiste a morir pero que ya no tiene el monopolio del porvenir.




Este viaje no busca certezas acabadas, sino rastrear las grietas donde los pueblos ensayan la vida en común. Así, al andar por la experiencia de la cooperativa Acapatzingo en Iztapalapa y la política subalterna de los Panchos de la mano de Libertad Castro Colina, o al beber de la sabiduría maya ancestral para perfeccionar la comunalidad con el plan de vida junto a Franklin Velasco García, comprendemos que el postcapitalismo no es una teoría fría, sino un caminar guiado por la memoria y el arraigo.




Ese mismo pulso nos lleva a detenernos, con Raquel Méndez Villamizar, en los apuntes decoloniales del banco de tiempo Kual Kan de Yhali Rosa Lombera, y  a reflexionar con Víctor Hugo Bonilla Muñoz sobre las monedas comunitarias y la autodependencia compartida a partir de la propuesta de Claudia Yadira Caballero, recordándonos que medir el tiempo y el valor de otra manera es fracturar la lógica del capital.




El camino se expande hacia horizontes más amplios al encontrarnos con el Tejido Global de Alternativas con la reseña de Saharai Martínez Arellano, o al conocer  los derechos de la naturaleza leídos por Valentina Campos Cabral a partir de la propuesta de Alberto Acosta. Este tramo se enriquece con una introducción a la caja de herramientas audiovisuales de Territorios de Vida, también comentada por Valentina Campos, y concluye con las Pluritopías reseñadas por Stella Cárdenas Agudelo.




Continuamos la marcha atravesando la experiencia de Tejiendo Imaginarios en Colombia con René La Torre, el estado de la cuestión en la economía social en México a cargo de Ricardo Contreras Soto, y la mirada crítica plasmada en el video realizado por Débora Manchón Lerma, Dani Sevillano y Andrés R. López Ramírez a partir de la conferencia Hora Cero de William Robinson.




Más que un inventario de iniciativas, este trayecto funciona como una brújula que nos obliga a tantear el terreno: interrogar los alcances y las fronteras de nuestras propias prácticas, rozar los límites conceptuales del término y preguntarnos qué tanto de lo que nombramos como postcapitalismo está transformando el suelo pisado o se queda en la superficie de la promesa. Cada uno de estos trabajos encarna el esfuerzo colectivo del Semillero de Saberes de la REP, visibilizando las praxis y reflexiones actuantes que sostienen alternativas concretas frente al neo-extractivismo y los obstáculos onto-epistémicos.




Como muestra de un ejercicio riguroso de transparencia, corresponsabilidad y ética poscapitalista, se solicitó a todas las autorías declarar explícitamente el uso de herramientas de inteligencia artificial en sus procesos de escritura. En un contexto donde la tecnología suele mercantilizarse para enajenar y vigilar, asumir colectivamente su uso con franqueza es también una forma de politizar la herramienta, recordando que la emancipación tecnológica se construye desde la rendición de cuentas abierta y el cuidado común de la palabra.




Que este número sea la prueba viva de que otra forma de habitar el pensamiento y los territorios es no sólo necesaria, sino posible. Sigamos tejiendo las grietas del presente con la certeza de que el horizonte postcapitalista se construye andando, preguntando y escuchando…




Delta Argelia Torres Rivera

title: ENERGIA NUCLEARE: opportunità o speculazione? – Un approfondimento de I Saperi Maledetti su Radio Blackout
content:
Bollette alle stelle, spesa sempre più cara, stipendi che non bastano più. Dietro al carovita si cela una parola chiara: 

energia

. Mentre l’aumento dei prezzi riguarda l’afflusso di carburanti, il dibattito sull’energia sta venendo spostato, intorno alla questione 

nucleare

. 







Partendo dalle interviste in università, emerge come l’energia nucleare sia ritornata di petto nel dibattito pubblico, mentre il 

disegno di legge sul nucleare

, 

approvato dal Senato in data 23/09

, mostra il 

tentativo del governo

 di proporlo come panacea alle crisi globali.




I Saperi Maledetti tornano quindi con una puntata densa di analisi, spunti e polemiche per cercare di rispondere a una domanda semplice, solo in apparenza:

 Cos’è davvero l’energia?

 Abbiamo ricostruito come funziona la sua compravendita, chi e cosa ne stabilisce i prezzi e determinandone l’aumento disastroso in termini di carovita.




Qualcosa non torna: perché se l’aumento dei prezzi riguarda l’afflusso di carburanti, il tema dell’energia sta slittando oggi intorno alla questione del nucleare? Cosa stanno cercando di venderci? Quali interessi si mostrano dietro all’investimento in questa fonte? 




Per entrare nel vivo del dibattito intorno all’energia nucleare vi proponiamo il confronto a due voci, da una parte un rappresentante del comitato 

Nucleare e Ragione

, dall’altra 

Alessandro Ferretti, professore di fisica nucleare

:







Purtroppo, per impegni logistici degli intervistati, non vi è potuto essere un vero e proprio botta e risposta. Rimane quindi un dibattito aperto, per questo vi invitiamo a seguire le prossime puntate dei Saperi Maledetti, ad interagire e polemizzare con noi, sintonizzandovi sulle frequenze gli 

ultimi due lunedì del mese alle 13:00

!




dalla trasmissione 

I Saperi Maledetti

 in onda su Radio Blackout

title: Solidarietà alle compagne e ai compagni colpite/i dalle misure cautelari
content:
Ripubblichiamo il testo di 

Associazione a Resistere Pisa

. 




Contro la criminalizzazione delle lotte sociali. Askatasuna vuol dire libertà! 







Associazione A Resistere Pisa esprime solidarietà alle compagne e ai compagni di Askatasuna, di Torino, Cosenza e di altre città colpite/i dalle misure cautelari per la manifestazione nazionale del 31 gennaio 2026.




Quella giornata ha espresso una ribellione popolare allo sgombero di Askatasuna e alla volontà di cancellare uno spazio sociale costruito in decenni di attività e lotte. Gli scontri sono stati parte dell’esito di quella mobilitazione, della rabbia e della determinazione di chi non ha accettato passivamente l’ennesima imposizione. Cinquantamila persone hanno attraversato Torino per difendere Askatasuna e contestare il Governo Meloni. Non si possono processare poche persone per una rivolta sociale, né cancellare il significato collettivo di una giornata di partecipazione di massa.




Lo sgombero di Askatasuna, il 18 dicembre scorso, è stato una scelta politica: colpire uno spazio sociale e le decine di migliaia di persone che si erano attivate con una vitalità incredibile a Torino e in tutta Italia nelle mobilitazioni di Blocchiamo Tutto contro il genocidio in Palestina. 

Una risposta violenta e antisociale di un governo che taglia servizi, impoverisce le persone e finanzia il riarmo, mentre cerca di reprimere chi costruisce opposizione sociale e cambiamenti reali.




Le compagne e i compagni oggi colpite/i non sono professionisti della politica, ma persone che mettono a disposizione tempo, corpo e intelligenza per cambiare lo stato delle cose. Non accettiamo che vengano trasformati in capri espiatori di una mobilitazione di massa.  E’ grazie a questi compagni e compagne che i movimenti crescono e si affermano. In tutta Europa, dalla Spagna, Francia, Germania, Belgio, Albania, quello che sta succedendo è una ripresa dell’iniziativa militante di nuove generazioni, e questo vento è inarrestabile!




Il 31 gennaio è stato anche una cerniera tra la sequenza della solidarietà alla Palestina e dell’opposizione alla guerra con il presente di lotte sociali contro il carovita, la precarietà e i tagli allo Stato sociale. Dalle proteste di agricoltori e autotrasportatori nel Sud alle mobilitazioni studentesche e universitarie nel Nord, fino agli scioperi, quelli diffusi e quelli generali, emergono conflitti diversi che hanno bisogno di riconoscersi e costruire legami. Mentre le risorse vengono dirottate verso il riarmo e l’economia di guerra, peggiorano le condizioni materiali di vita. È dentro questo scenario che si moltiplicano le forme di rifiuto e di ribellione. Per questo leggiamo la repressione come parte di quella dialettica del Potere volta a restaurare lo status quo, utilizzando forme meschine di manipolazione, divisione e repressione.




Anche Pisa conosce questa dinamica. Il 23 febbraio 2024, le piazze studentesche scesero in strada contro il genocidio palestinese e la violenza degli Stati che, per mantenere il proprio dominio sui territori e sulle risorse energetiche, non esitano a ricorrere a occupazioni, bombardamenti e massacri. Le cariche e i manganelli contro studenti e manifestanti produssero uno scandalo nazionale. Oggi, mentre emergono indagini sulle condotte di alcuni agenti, si tenta di ricondurre la vicenda alla responsabilità di singole mele marce e di utilizzare la condizione dei minorenni come elemento di una narrazione rassicurante. Ma la questione non riguarda soltanto gli abusi individuali di alcune forze di polizia: è la volontà politica del Governo e dei suoi apparati di restringere progressivamente l’agibilità delle piazze e il diritto al dissenso che deve essere messa in discussione. Non c’è una generazione di studenti da una parte e una generazione di cosiddetti spaccavetrine dall’altra: è la stessa generazione che rifiuta di normalizzare la violenza e l’ingiustizia.




D’altro canto la lotta e le barricate del 30 settembre 2026 nel carcere Don Bosco, con le proteste dei detenuti diffuse anche attraverso una diretta TikTok, sono state un altro sintomo di un sistema di criminalizzazione che sta mostrando tutta la propria inadeguatezza. La società esprime un rifiuto crescente del peggioramento delle condizioni di vita, della marginalizzazione e dell’abbandono. Le politiche punitive, l’ingabbiamento delle nuove generazioni e l’espansione del sistema carcerario non sono strumenti in grado di reggere il peso delle trasformazioni sociali in corso. Pensare di rispondere con più carcere e più repressione a una crisi che investe lavoro, reddito, casa, futuro e dignità significa non comprenderne le cause.




Associazione A Resistere Pisa

, parte di una rete di supporto contro la criminalizzazione delle proteste e del conflitto sociale, intende trasformare questa solidarietà in iniziativa concreta. L’allargamento delle mobilitazioni contro il carovita, la precarizzazione e l’economia di guerra ci pone la necessità di costruire reti di sostegno per manifestanti colpiti da procedimenti penali, arresti, misure cautelari e restrizioni domiciliari. 

Nelle prossime settimane organizzeremo serate di raccolta fondi, momenti di confronto e iniziative di sensibilizzazione politica, per sostenere chi viene colpito dalla repressione e rafforzare i legami tra le esperienze di lotta

.




Non vogliamo una solidarietà di circostanza, ma una rete capace di organizzarsi, sostenersi e rilanciare le lotte. Una politica di liberazione fatta di tempo sottratto all’alienazione del lavoro, di spazi collettivi, di relazioni e di umanità contro l’individualismo capitalista.




Giù le mani da chi lotta! La lotta continua!




ASKATASUNA VUOL DIRE LIBERTÀ!

title: Big Oil, Climate Change, and a ‘Smoking Gun’
content:
Arnold Obguia did not leave the island. According to the forecast, it was no big deal, just another tropical storm. But a few hours later, the winds escalated rapidly, bringing waves so large they almost pulled him out to sea. Clinging to a piece of broken sea wall, Arnold survived to find his house completely destroyed. Others were not so lucky.






















 
















This story is published in partnership with 

Rolling Stone.













Typhoon Rai, known locally as Typhoon Odette, battered the Philippines in December 2021. With winds of up to 167 miles per hour, extreme rainfall, violent storm surges, extensive flooding, and landslides across the central Philippine archipelago, Odette ripped rooftops from houses and devastated crops, engulfing people and property in torrents of fast-flowing floodwater. A Category 5 cyclone, Odette displaced nearly 

3.2 million people

, killing 400, injuring over 1,000, and causing nearly a billion US dollars in damages.




Now, Arnold and other victims of the typhoon are demanding their day in court, filing a civil 

lawsuit

 against 

oil and gas giant Shell

. Their allegations: Shell helped to make the typhoon more destructive through the company’s contribution to historic greenhouse gas emissions and its funding of climate denial — despite knowing since at least 1965 that the burning of fossil fuels was the primary cause of man-made climate change.




“The forecast had initially said it was going to be a weak storm,” says Arnold from the house he rebuilt with storm debris on the tiny island of Bilangbilangan in the heart of the Philippines’ Cebu Strait. Forty-four years old, Arnold is a fisherman, born and raised on the island, who earns his living catching trevally and bigeye scad, silvery-blue-green fish that swim in large schools around the region’s coral reefs.




“But suddenly the winds were different, they were very strong,” he recalls. “When I looked outside the window it was frightening because the waves were very high.” While his wife and two young daughters had taken refuge on the mainland, Arnold and his 14-year-old son had stayed behind to guard his boat and fishing equipment — the source of the family’s livelihood. “The waves were swelling and I could see the storm surge coming,” he remembers. Calculating that he might have time to better secure his boat, he ran outside only to get caught by the 20-foot waves that nearly swept him away. Terrified, Arnold held tight to the broken sea wall until, bruised and wounded by the debris whirling in the water, he was able to rejoin his son. “Thinking about my family and how much I wanted to see them again gave me the strength to hold on,” he says. Arnold and his son rode out the rest of the storm sheltering in the house of a neighbor. Hours later, when it was over, Arnold discovered his boat was broken but his family was safe. Like everyone else on Bilangbilangan, they had lost almost all their possessions. “Everyone went back to zero,” he explains.




Arnold joined the lawsuit in early 2024 when a coalition of NGOs working with communities ravaged by the typhoon organized a 

civil claim

 on behalf of the survivors. In 2025, British law firm Hausfeld agreed to take up the case in the UK — where Shell is headquartered —submitting full details of the claim against the oil company in July of this year.




Typhoon Rai — known as Odette in the Philippines — had sustained winds of 121 miles (195 kilometers) and gusts of up to 167 miles (270 kilometers) per hour when it made landfall in the archipelago on December 16, 2021. Credit: NASA Earth Observatory image by Lauren Dauphin, using VIIRS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE , GIBS/Worldview , and the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership. Public Domain.




Representing more than 100 of the typhoon’s victims, Hausfeld describes the suit as a “landmark case” that could have “major repercussions for the 

fossil fuel industry,

” potentially paving the way for other hard-hit communities around the world to sue oil Big Oil on its home turf. The firm argues its clients suffered severe losses including serious property damage, personal injury, bereavement, psychological trauma, and loss of earnings. An announcement of the date for the first hearing to be held at London’s High Court is expected sometime early next year, says Greg Lascelles, the Hausfeld partner leading the legal team.




Shell has dismissed 

the lawsuit

 as “baseless,” asserting the company had no “unique knowledge about climate change” in an 

official statement

.




However, evidence uncovered by DeSmog in collaboration with Rolling Stone reveals explosive new details of Shell’s decades of climate research that warned the company burning fossil fuels could lead to worsening storms — including studies conducted at the Climatic Research Unit (CRU), the UK’s first specialist climate research center established by Shell on the campus of a university in eastern England in 1972.




Some of these documents might have been lost forever, had a sharp-eyed faculty member not rescued them from a dumpster where they’d been thrown out after the retirement of the CRU’s first director, the UK’s leading climatologist, Hubert Lamb. Now preserved inside the temperature-controlled archives at the University of East Anglia, a few miles outside the medieval city of Norwich, these and other files contain handwritten notes, official correspondence, and reports that hold secrets of Shell’s early climate research, detailing a program that would give the company advance warning of the numerous threats climate change posed to its business — if not to the people, like Arnold and his island neighbors, liable to suffer the most harm.




Documents from the late 1960s show Shell playing a pivotal role in establishing the center before paying the CRU to carry out an in-depth 

“North Sea Storms Study”

 beginning in the mid-1970s. The findings warned Shell that 

storms in Europe’s North Sea

 — home to the company’s burgeoning offshore drilling business — were increasing. Rising atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) levels due to the burning of fossil fuels might be the most likely explanation, the Shell-funded study concluded.




These discoveries contribute to a growing body of existing evidence demonstrating that by the late 1980s the 

oil majors

, including 

Exxon

 and 

Shell

, knew the dangers posed by fossil fuel-induced climate change. However, a fresh look at documents previously unearthed by other researchers shows Shell receiving further storm warnings. For example, in 1980, a 

Shell-sponsored study

 at the CRU modeling future “Scenarios for a High CO2 World,” calculated that rising CO2 levels from burning fossil fuels would “perturb the whole 

atmospheric circulation system,

” affecting 

rainfall, temperatures, and winds 

all over the world.




By the end of the 1980s, Shell had specifically learned that global warming would likely lead to more frequent and more dangerous storms, especially in tropical regions.




Today, as the world approaches the peak of what promises to be the worst 

El Niño

 cycle in recorded history, supercharging hurricanes, heatwaves, droughts, and other extreme weather events already made worse by climate change, the documents open a rare window into Shell’s early sponsorship of climate science, illustrating how much the company knew about the risks posed by burning its products before supporting million dollar 

PR and lobbying campaigns

 that denied or cast doubt on this climate science in public.




Shell did not respond to a request for comment about the company’s historical climate research.




Geoffrey Supran, an associate professor in the department of environmental science and policy at the University of Miami who is not involved in the lawsuit, but who has reviewed the new documents for DeSmog and Rolling Stone, calls them “a smoking-gun,” containing important evidence of “how the early climate denial machine began to be built — and when.”




“Seen across seven decades, Shell’s research looks less like scientific philanthropy and more like a public affairs strategy of ‘Know Thy Enemy,’” says Supran, “allowing the company to understand climate change early, help shape and stay close to the science, anticipate the physical and economic threats it poses, and stay ahead of policies that might threaten business-as-usual.”




‘A Centre on Climatic Studies’




Sitting at his desk in London’s “Shell Tower,” a 26-story modernist skyscraper with majestic views overlooking the River Thames and Houses of Parliament, R. O. Chalkley had a problem.




It was September 1966. The Beatles’ 

Revolver

 had reached Number One in the album charts but Chalkley was wrestling with something far more changeable: the weather.




As the director of a company-wide planning study, it was Chalkley’s job to help Shell find the most effective way of coping with variations in the demand for oil brought about by an apparently changing climate. Recent European winters had sent temperatures plunging but if Shell invested heavily in storing up larger quantities of oil to heat Europe’s homes only for the weather to turn warmer, it could prove an expensive mistake.




An image from a Shell brochure of the Shell tower in London in the 1960s. Credit: UEA Archives and Library Special Collections, UEA/Jones/40




Luckily for Chalkley, an August 1966 

article in The Times

 by the UK’s leading climatologist, Hubert Lamb, offered a possible solution. “Is our climate changing?” Lamb asked, arguing that improved understanding of the Earth’s climate history was essential for future economic planning. Hoping that the climatologist’s work might benefit Shell, Chalkley 

wrote

 to Lamb inviting him to discuss “the climatic aspects” of the company’s problem in person.




Their meeting was an instant success, launching the idea for a Shell-funded “

Centre

 on Climatic Studies

” — Lamb would search for a university to host his research, while Chalkley pitched the idea to his bosses inside Shell.




Slowly, the proposal moved up the ranks at Shell Tower and, on October 1, 1969, Chalkley arranged 

a meeting 

between Lamb and a handful of high-level Shell executives.




Present at the meeting was Monroe Spaght, a former country boy from Eureka, California, now president and chairman of Shell Oil (the company’s United States subsidiary) and the first American managing director of Shell’s parent company, Royal Dutch. Joining Spaght was Lord Victor Rothschild, director of Shell Research, scion of the famous banking dynasty, scientist, and World War II spy chief. Both held key positions on 

Shell’s grants committee

 and were “visibly enthusiastic” about Lamb’s proposal for the UK’s first specialist climatic research center, to be housed at the University of East Anglia under the aegis of Professor Keith Clayton, dean of its brand new School of Environmental Sciences.




Letter dated August 26, 1968, from R. O. Chalkley to Hubert Lamb, stating that Shell was interested in providing “some financial support” to the creation of a “Centre on Climatic Studies.” Credit: UEA Archives and Library Special Collections, UEA/Jones/40




No record of Lamb’s 1969 pitch to Shell has yet been found but a 

proposal

 for the center written around the same time reveals that, in addition to providing enhanced weather forecasting, investigating the climate impact of burning fossil fuels was one of the center’s founding ambitions, DeSmog and Rolling Stone can reveal.




This excerpt from a 1969 document containing a proposal for Centre for Climactic Studies acknowledges the link between fossil fuels and climate change. Credit: UEA Archives and Library Special Collections, UEA/Jones/40




“Climatic history is particularly important because man is now disturbing the atmosphere so much (e.g. by increasing 

the CO2 level

 by burning fossil fuel) that it is difficult to disentangle long term trends from the effects of man,” stated 

the proposal,

 before promising that the center offered “a hope of long term climatic forecasting,” and would “evaluate the problems posed by such 

man-made changes

 as the CO2 level of the atmosphere.”




‘Beneficial to Shell’s Operations’




This message that burning fossil fuels could be altering the Earth’s climate would not have come as a surprise to either of Shell’s top men.




Spaght represented Shell Oil on the board of the 

American Petroleum Institute (API)

, the U.S. oil industry’s primary 

lobby group

. In November 1965, API President Frank Ikard had briefed the group’s membership on the latest science linking CO2 emissions from “coal, oil, and natural gas” with future temperature increases and “

changes in climate

.”




Meanwhile in London, former intelligence officer Rothschild had already coordinated secret climatic research inside Shell, having commissioned the visionary British scientist 

James Lovelock

 to investigate the atmospheric consequences of burning fossil fuels. Were fossil fuels altering the Earth’s climate or could other factors be blamed? In the summer of 1965, Rothschild had dispatched Lovelock to find out.




Victor Rothschild in 1965. Credit: Bassano Ltd/

National Portrait Gallery

, London/NPG x172039/Non-commercial license




Submitting a report in June 1966, Lovelock had confirmed that pollution from burning fossil fuels “may be responsible for 

large scale phenomena

 affecting the whole of the Earth’s atmosphere.” Although there were uncertainties over the precise impacts of different pollutants, Lovelock told Shell it was important to recognize “the almost certain fact that the climate is worsening and the probability that the 

combustion of fuel

 is responsible.”




As 

several historians

 have recently documented, Shell buried Lovelock’s findings for years, and Rothschild expressly forbade him from talking to “

non-Shell people

” about his work.




By the late fall of 1969, however, Shell seems to have taken Lovelock’s warning seriously enough to sponsor a new climate project.




After his meeting with Spaght and Rothschild, Lamb wrote to the University of East Anglia’s Professor Clayton informing him that Shell wanted to set up a climatic research center for “

their own ends

.” Not only did the company want monthly and seasonal forecasts but also advice on the more “

general climatic prospect

 over 5 to 25 years.”




Letter from Hubert Lamb to Keith Clayton describing his meeting with Shell, October 1969. Credit: UEA Archives and Library Special Collections, UEA/Jones/40




Shell’s Spaght was particularly encouraging, stating that the new project would contribute to “the increase of knowledge” in general and might also be beneficial to “

Shell’s operations

.”




At the end of October 1969, Shell approved an 

initial grant of £10,000

, a contribution it eventually doubled to 

£20,000

 ($370,000 today) — a game-changing amount that, in Clayton’s words, made the Centre “

a real possibility

.” By 1971, 

BP

 had also put forward £3,000 and two 

UK electricity groups

, £5,000. With these sums in the bag, the university agreed to provide the rest of the funding. And, in 1972, the 

Climatic Research Unit

 (CRU) opened its doors with Lamb appointed its first director.




From the outset, the CRU provided its sponsors with general weather forecast bulletins and a newsletter to keep a finger on the pulse of “

world climate

.” But before long Shell would find an even more specific use for the CRU’s expertise.




Obtaining information about storms was about to become one of the company’s top priorities.




‘Increasing Storminess’




“The Texas of Europe” was how the British press described the massive oil fields discovered by Shell and Esso (Exxon’s UK subsidiary) at the start of the 1970s in Europe’s North Sea — a region notorious for its fearsome waves and gale force winds.




Naming the oil fields after local seabirds, Shell operated the enormous “Brent” field and in 1975 paid the CRU 

another £15,921

 [worth $166,000 today] to conduct a “

North Sea Storms Study

” that would help the company future-proof its new facilities.




It was exactly the kind of project Lamb had been waiting for, allowing the CRU to gather records dating back to the time of the Spanish Armada of 1588 — a “

wealth of information

” meticulously recorded by scientists, sailors, merchant traders, and amateur observers across 400 years.




The documents reveal Shell working closely with Lamb on 

a plan

 designed to identify 

specific dangers

 and improve storm prediction techniques. According to Lamb, the research would alert Shell to “

forewarning signals

” indicative of extreme weather events by mapping and analyzing “the 

severest North Sea storms

 of the past.” The study would also look at “

variations of sea level

 in the North Sea region” produced by storms as well as “disastrous sea floods” and “the height of sea defences.”




With its profitable North Sea operations playing an increasingly important role in its business, Shell requested 

regular updates

. In November 1981, Lamb sent Shell an “

Interim Report

,” noting that he was also keeping a watch on “

current weather developments

” including recent storms that had seriously damaged several North Sea oil rigs.




Citing these powerful storms, Lamb sent a further update to Shell in 1982 containing a significant new observation. According to the data, Lamb told Shell in handwritten notes, there was “some indication of an 

increasing storminess

” since the 1950s. In November 1981, winds reaching 120 to 130 knots — equivalent to a Category 4 hurricane — had ripped two oil rigs housing over 200 people from their moorings.




Update from Hubert Lamb to Shell on the North Sea Storms study, April 1982. Credit: UEA Archives and Library Special Collections, H.H. Lamb, Deposit 1




This warning would come almost 10 years before the study was published, giving Shell advance notice of nearly a decade that storms in the North Sea were increasing.




Despite Shell’s appreciation for 

Lamb’s “useful” work

, the company did not approve further funding for the storms study. Undeterred, Lamb, who had retired as the CRU’s director, completed the study in 1991, sending a copy to the head of 

Shell Exploration

 and thanking the company “for the grant which started the project.” In line with his earlier findings, Lamb wrote that his subsequent research had confirmed his observations of 

increasing storminess

 in the North Sea over the latter half of the 20th Century and he concluded that 

rising atmospheric CO2 levels

 could be considered a likely explanation.

Sign Up

All




US/Global team




UK/Europe team




























In the cautious, circumspect style that is typical of his writings, Lamb stated: “It is not easy to point to a firmly established reason for the increase in storminess affecting northern and northwestern Europe, and the off-lying seas, since 1950. Some would probably attribute it with little more ado to 

the greenhouse effect 

expected from the increase of carbon dioxide and other gases in the atmosphere caused by human activities.”




 ‘Scenarios for a High CO2 World’




Over the 1980s, Shell continued to use the CRU as the company’s go-to lab for inside climate information and advance updates.




While Lamb was focusing on historic storms, in 1980 Shell funded 

another CRU study

, “

Scenarios for a High CO2 World,

” investigating what a future, warmer world might look like. Using 20th century temperature records, the CRU researchers modeled four potential future climate impact scenarios.




Specifically, the company wanted to know how changes to temperature, rainfall, and sea levels might affect Europe’s 

energy consumption and agriculture 

— key areas of interest for Shell’s business operations.




The research

 was published in 1983 and extended to 

North America

 in a 1984 report commissioned by the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), tracked down by DeSmog and Rolling Stone. Basing their North American calculations on the methodology they had developed for Shell, the CRU researchers also submitted this second report to the 

oil company

.




In both cases the message was the same. Increasing atmospheric CO2 produced by the burning of fossil fuels would trap 

ever-increasing amounts of heat 

within the earth-atmosphere system. Beyond increases in temperature, however, the CRU’s researchers emphasized that the 

overall impact 

would be “much more fundamental,” that it would “perturb the whole 

atmospheric circulation system

,” affecting rainfall and 

winds

, “indeed all of the meteorological variables,” around the world.




An even more urgent warning was delivered to Shell two years later, in November 1985, when a member of the company’s internal 

“Greenhouse effect working group,”

 M. H. Griffiths, visited the CRU for a 

status update

 on the latest developments in climate science from its new director, Thomas Wigley. Although Wigley briefed Shell’s representative on remaining 

scientific “uncertainties”

 relating to the precise impacts of the greenhouse effect, he was “prepared to stick his neck out” on some key points, wrote Griffiths in a confidential 1985 

internal Shell memo

. This memo, detailing Griffiths visit to the CRU, formed part of a 90-page “confidential” internal company report on “

The Greenhouse Effect

” compiled in 1986 for Shell International, discovered by Dutch journalist 

Jelmer Mommers

 in 2018.




An internal, confidential Shell memo from M.H. Griffiths about his meeting with Thomas Wigley, director of the Climate Research Unit, on November 27, 1985. Credit: 

Climate Files




As Griffiths reported to Shell, Wigley warned him that although “CO2 build-up” had caused a global temperature increase of 0.5 degrees over the last 100 years, “a 

further 1-

2

 degree warming

 over the next 40 years” was expected — a rise “greater than any change in the last 1000 years.” And, while global warming had already caused average 

sea levels to rise

 by “some 15 [centimeters] over the last 100 years,” or about 6 inches, Griffiths noted that they could rise a further 20-120 centimeters (about 8-47 inches) by 2050.




Higher global temperatures would result in higher rates of evaporation, Griffiths informed Shell, meaning “monsoon rainfall ought to increase also as should the 

frequency of tropical storms.

”




‘A Serious Risk’




As the scientific consensus on climate change strengthened over the course of the 1980s, the company joined forces with 

other oil majors

 under the banner of the International Petroleum Industry Environmental Conservation Association (IPIECA), a global oil and gas group that had been established in 1973 to monitor and influence 

environmental protection measures

 that might “affect the oil industry.” In 1988, IPIECA formed a “Working Group on Global Climate Change” tasked with producing an internal report that would brief IPIECA’s members on the newest developments in climate science. Two 

Shell representatives

 were among the working group’s members, as were representatives from Exxon, Mobil, Texaco, BP, ELF, and Saudi Aramco.




“Major populated coastal areas of the globe are at risk from 

rising sea level

, especially in undeveloped countries,” declared the IPIECA report, discovered by Nathaniel Rich, author of 

Losing Earth

: 

The Decade We Could Have Stopped Climate Change

 in 2019. A section of the report authored by Exxon Senior Scientist Brian Flannery also warned “that the frequency and magnitude of 

large storms

 may be higher in a warmer world.” The coupling of sea level rise, and the possibility of enhanced storm surges presented “a 

serious risk

, especially to low-lying coastal areas,” explained Exxon’s scientist.




Typhoon Odette wiped out homes and boats on the island of Batasan, not far Arnold Obguia’s island home of Bilangbilangan in the Philippines archipelago, in 2021. Credit: Greenpeace and The Odette Case




Fast forward approximately three decades when this “serious risk” warning given to Shell was realized in the devastation wrought by Typhoon Odette. Photographs of the aftermath show buildings broken into matchsticks, crops destroyed, livestock animals killed, as well as damage to bridges, roads, ports, airports, and communication lines. In low-lying coastal areas, the strong winds, storm surges, and floods killed people instantly. More than 400 lost their lives with drowning being the most common cause of death.




On Bilangbilangan, Arnold knows he is lucky to be alive, but the trauma of the typhoon stays with his whole family. They are all afraid of another storm. “After the storm, everything was washed out, the houses, the boats and everything,” he says, describing how he lost his fishing rod and other equipment. “For the community, everyone had a difficult life after the storm. Everything was devastated.




“Honestly we are still not fully recovered,” Arnold explains. “All of our appliances, our personal belongings — very few were saved.”




By contrast, in 1989, Shell announced it was redesigning its $3-billion dollar North Sea “Troll” gas platform, raising it by 4 to 6 feet to better protect its operations against damage from the rising sea levels and more powerful 

storm surges

 predicted as a result of climate change. Reported by The New York Times as the first major project to anticipate the impacts of the greenhouse effect, a Shell spokesman told The Times he hoped that gas production from Troll would continue “for up to 70 years.”




But, just as Shell was taking these steps to protect its own operations, the company simultaneously began pouring money into public relations and lobbying campaigns denying the science of human-caused climate change.




1988 had been a trigger year for oil companies. In June, NASA scientist James Hansen had told a U.S. Senate committee that global warming was already changing the Earth’s climate. In August, Republican presidential candidate George H. W. Bush had given a campaign speech promising to tackle the greenhouse effect with “the White House effect.” And, in November, the United Nations had formed the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change to help governments develop policies aimed at preventing climate change by reducing greenhouse gas emissions.




The threat to oil companies was clear. In response, they went after the science.




 ‘No Convincing Evidence’




“No convincing evidence exists to support claims that hurricanes, tornadoes, and other extreme temperature and precipitation events are on the rise,” declared a 1995 

press release

 from the oil-industry funded group, the 

Global Climate Coalition

 (GCC). A fossil-fueled 

engine

 

of disinformation

, the GCC spread climate denial during the 1990s. 

Shell

 was one of its founding members, joining in 1989 — the very same year the company began climate-proofing its North Sea oil facilities.




Working through the GCC for the best part of a decade, Shell and the other oil majors bankrolled the group’s well-documented multi-million-dollar 

public relations

 

and lobbying campaigns

 designed to persuade Americans that 

the science

 of climate change was uncertain and to block national and international measures aimed at tackling global warming — including the introduction of carbon taxes and U.S. ratification of the Kyoto Climate Treaty.




“Oil companies had been at the forefront of climate research right up to the moment when the world actually began to wake up to the crisis,” says the University of Miami’s Geoffrey Supran. “At which point they spent the next 30 years pretending that this was all new, uncertain, unreliable science on the basis of which no policy decisions could ever be made.”




Backed by Shell, a 1995 GCC campaign targeted concerns that global warming was increasing the risk of hurricanes, casting doubt on studies linking rising sea surface temperatures with more intense tropical storms. The campaign’s central reference was a 

GCC-funded report

 conducted by commercial weather-forecasting firm AccuWeather that attributed public fears over increased storminess to “

global warming alarmists

.”




A February 3, 1995 news release from the Global Climate Coalition denied there was a link between climate change and extreme weather. Credit: Stephen Henry Schneider Papers (SC1053). Dept. of Special Collections, Stanford University Libraries, Stanford, Calif.




Like many of the GCC’s publications, the AccuWeather report championed the 

work

 of a 

new wave of so-called climate skeptics

 frequently sponsored by 

Shell

 and other 

oil interests

. While the first wave of industry-sponsored scientists, like Lamb and Wigley, were drawn from the scientific center ground, this new wave of scientists consisted of a small number of outliers, occupying fringe positions from which they waged a relentless contrarian war, variously arguing that computer-based 

climate modeling

 was unreliable, that 

temperature predictions

 were inaccurate, or that high levels of 

atmospheric CO2

 would improve plant growth.




Amplified by the GCC, this 

small cadre

 of 

skeptics

 appeared regularly in 

print

 as well as on 

television

 and radio, successfully marginalizing legitimate scientists and draining public support for climate action.




Releasing the report on the eve of a United Nations 

climate negotiation session

 in New York for maximum impact, the GCC hosted a press conference at the UN Plaza Hotel intended to “provide reporters with an 

overview and background

 of the issues under consideration at the session.” Key 

press releases

 sent out by the lobby group failed to mention that the AccuWeather report had been paid for by the GCC and its fossil fuel industry sponsors, although this information was included in the report.




Shell quit the GCC in 1998 as public calls for action to address climate change intensified. But the damage was done. Proposals for a tax on fossil fuels in the U.S. had been defeated, helped by a $1.8 million campaign by the GCC. And in 2001 the Kyoto Protocol on emissions reductions was rejected by U.S. President George W. Bush — according to an 

internal State Department brief

 this decision was due in part to 

input from the GCC

.




’Four-Dimensional Chess’




Early access to climate scientists like Lamb and Wigley not only gave Shell and other oil companies advance information useful for protecting their own facilities, it also provided another major advantage: a working knowledge of the uncertainties, common to any field of scientific inquiry. In the 1990s, amid international calls for curbs on greenhouse gas emissions, the industry weaponized these uncertainties to sow confusion and stall policy.




For 60 years, “the oil industry has been playing four-dimensional chess with the public affairs of climate change,” says Supran, pointing to what he calls a “four-step” playbook. “First they learn about the dangers of their products, then they scheme, then they deny, and then they delay in any way possible.” 




Despite quitting the GCC, Shell remains a member of the API and other industry lobby groups also accused of carrying out climate disinformation activities on behalf of the oil and gas industry. Along with Shell and other oil majors, the API is facing state-level legal action in the U.S. for its alleged role in promoting climate denial.




Today, 

climate denial

 based on the 

false arguments

 and red herrings popularized by the GCC still persists as a powerful force in the U.S. and around the world, underpinning 

President Donald Trump’s

 withdrawal of the United States from the 2015 Paris Agreement, as well as the administration’s rollback of domestic climate policies and unprecedented attacks on climate science.




“By obstructing climate action, those campaigns exposed all of us — particularly the vulnerable and unborn — to dangers the industry itself had long foreseen,” says Supran.




 ‘The Law Is Catching Up’




“Science has been sounding the alarm on the scale of climate harm for a long time,” says Joie Chowdhury, senior attorney at the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL). “Now, with the different climate litigation cases across different countries, the law is catching up.”




Using the same legal strategy that won record payouts from Big Tobacco in the 1990s and 2000s, the Typhoon Odette survivors’ case against Shell is the latest in a rising number of “

climate deception

” lawsuits being brought against oil and gas companies for actively promoting disinformation about their products through organizations like the GCC. There are currently more than two dozen such cases pending in the U.S. alone, with another filed against BP in New Zealand, according to the 

Climate Litigation Database

 compiled by Columbia University’s Sabin Center for Climate Change Law. Essentially these are fraud cases, explains Chowdhury. “We’ve seen numerous lawsuits alleging that major oil companies knew about the risks for decades, that they misled the public and helped to delay climate action while continuing to profit from fossil fuels,” she says, describing the U.S. as “an epicenter” of 

this type of litigation

.




While the U.S. legal system is particularly well suited to class action lawsuits, 

opportunities for climate litigation

 on behalf of multiple claimants, like the Odette case, are rapidly growing elsewhere. While deception is not always at the heart of these cases, says Chowdhury, the idea that polluters should pay for the 

destruction

 their products cause is gaining traction. To date, hundreds of greenwashing and other climate accountability claims have also been filed against fossil fuel companies around the world.




Since Shell is headquartered in the UK, the Odette claimants are suing the company in London, kickstarted by 

a 2022 finding 

of the Commission on Human Rights of the Philippines, which ruled that major fossil fuel companies can be held accountable for human rights violations caused by climate change and that affected Filipino citizens may pursue civil and legal remedies through other national courts.  




It is not publicly known who is funding the Odette case. In the past, similar legal costs have often been met by philanthropic foundations or charities, but the UK has also seen an uptick in 

litigation funding

 by private investors who see future payouts from such legal battles as a potential business opportunity.




Big Oil, however, is pushing back. Firstly through the age-old legal tactic favored by big corporations: extensive procedural fights about where cases should be heard. On October 5, the 

U.S. Supreme Court

 heard arguments relating to a petition from ExxonMobil and the Canadian energy giant Suncor, both facing a climate deception lawsuit in Colorado, that fossil fuel companies should not be sued in state courts over their role in global warming. A ruling is expected in 2027. Raising the stakes even higher, the API and the industry’s 

Republican allies

 have also been lobbying lawmakers to give fossil fuel companies total 

legal immunity

 from climate deception cases.




“For years, fossil fuel companies have argued that climate claims belong in federal court or are matters for Congress rather than state courts,” Chowdhury says. But the “explosion in climate accountability cases” outside the U.S., including the Odette case, reduces the risk that this accountability depends on the outcome of cases in the U.S. or any one specific country, she says.




“Climate harm does not exist beyond the reach of law,” argues Chowdhury.




According to figures from the International Chamber of Commerce, climate-related extreme weather events are estimated to have cost 

the global economy

 $2 trillion over the last decade — 

costs

 that could spiral to $3.1 trillion 

a year

 by 2050.




Issuing an official response to climate lawsuits, Shell maintains that “

litigation

 aimed at individual companies is not an effective way to reduce global emissions.”




 ‘For the Generations to Come’




Roosters crow and dogs bark as Arnold speaks on a video call via a translator patched in from Manila. It’s late afternoon on Bilangbilangan, a time when Arnold would usually be preparing to go fishing, but today the seas are too rough. “It’s too unpredictable,” he says, looking through his window out to sea.




Every day stuck on the island is a day without income and times are tough. Before Odette, the fish catch was abundant and Arnold was easily able to provide for his family, earning up to 5000 pesos ($80) on a good day. But Odette damaged the coral reefs that support the local fish stocks and for a period after the typhoon he went for months without income. Although things have improved since then, the catch remains smaller. On a bad day he may only catch around 400 pesos’ worth of fish, equivalent to around $6. “I’ll go out tomorrow,” Arnold says, “if the weather improves.”




Arnold Obguia inside his rebuilt work area on Bilangbilangan in 2026. Credit: Greenpeace and The Odette Case




As we talk, 

Typhoon Francisco

 is sweeping north with winds reaching 145 miles per hour. Satellite trackers show Francisco veering away from the Philippines but the effects of its wider storm system are being felt across the region.




Since then, 2026’s 

“Godzilla” El Niño

 has been building in the Pacific with sea temperatures predicted to reach a peak of 39.2 F above the seasonal average at the end of this year, raising the risk of supercharged Pacific typhoons. Already wreaking 

havoc

 around the world, this El Niňo is expected to be the most destructive and deadly since 

records

 began, with climate scientists forecasting “

a string of weather catastrophes

” around the world — from intense heatwaves, wildfires, and drought in some places, to torrential rain and flooding in others. In the U.S., California’s sea levels are rising threatening coastal communities with 

dangerous storm surge

s while an unprecedented series of 

powerful hurricanes

 has been hitting Hawaii since August.




Not only is climate change causing more destructive storms, 

recent studies

 show it is also likely making storms harder to predict. 

A study

 published in December 2025 concluded that Odette’s rapid intensification from a Category 1 to a Category 5 typhoon probably occurred after the storm passed over ocean hotspots — warmer patches of seawater that are occurring more frequently as a result of climate change-induced marine heatwaves. A similar phenomenon occurred in the Gulf of Mexico in 2022, when 

Hurricane Ian

 caused destruction across Cuba, Florida, and the Carolinas.




Arnold Obguia holds small artworks that his daughter painted on the remnants of his fishing boat, which was destroyed during Typhoon Odette. Credit: Geric Cruz/Greenpeace and The Odette Case




“We only knew the storm was different when it was already happening,” says Arnold. “We didn’t have the foresight that it was going to be different.”




Turning to the lawsuit, Arnold says, he joined the case in the hope that it might give his children the chance of a better life. “Whether we win or lose, what’s important for me and the other claimants is that our message is being sent across the world to the UK, to Shell headquarters. We hope this case might encourage Shell to reduce their impact on the environment because at the end of the day it’s people like us who have to face the really tall waves, the really strong typhoons.”




“If we win this case,” he adds, “it isn’t just for us, the typhoon survivors, it’s also for the generations to come.”




The post 

Big Oil, Climate Change, and a ‘Smoking Gun’

 appeared first on 

DeSmog

.
