title: Explosion im Stahlwerk im westtürkischen Aliağa mit 19 Toten und vielen Verletzten: Nicht der erste Arbeitsmord im Industriekonzernn HABAŞ
content:
„… 

Die Explosion ereignete sich am Montagvormittag während des laufenden Betriebs. Nach ersten Angaben des Gouverneursamtes von Izmir brach während eines Gießvorgangs ein Deckenkran ab und stürzte in einen Industrieofen. Die dadurch ausgelöste Explosion verursachte einen Brand, über dem Werksgelände stiegen dichte Rauchwolken auf. Es war bereits der dritte tödliche Vorfall innerhalb weniger Wochen. Im Oktober war der Leiharbeiter Hakan Doğan aus etwa acht Metern Höhe gestürzt und ums Leben gekommen. Am 5. November starb der 20-jährige Leiharbeiter Eyüp Eğinli, als beim Aufpumpen eines Reifens an einer Arbeitsmaschine eine Explosion ausgelöst wurde. Zusammen mit den Opfern der jüngsten Katastrophe sind damit innerhalb kurzer Zeit 20 Beschäftigte bei HABAŞ ums Leben gekommen

…“ 

ANF-Beitrag vom 10.11.2026

 

 („Hatimoğulları: Das ist nicht der erste Arbeitsmord bei HABAŞ“) und mehr Informationen auch zu den anhaltenden Protesten und der Repression dagegen:







Protest gegen tödliche Arbeitsbedingungen bei HABAŞ: „Brechen wir das Schweigen!“




„

Nach einer tödlichen Explosion im HABAŞ-Stahlwerk in Aliağa haben Gewerkschafter:innen und linke Organisationen in Istanbul protestiert. Sie werfen dem Konzern und der Regierung vor, Profite über Menschenleben zu stellen.




Nach der Explosion im Stahlwerk des Industriekonzerns HABAŞ im westtürkischen Aliağa mit 18 Toten und zahlreichen Verletzten haben Gewerkschafter:innen, linke Parteien und Jugendorganisationen vor einem weiteren Werk des Unternehmens in Istanbul protestiert. Unter massiver Polizeipräsenz prangerten sie die systematische Missachtung des Arbeitsschutzes, fehlende staatliche Kontrollen und die Straflosigkeit bei tödlichen Arbeitsunfällen an. Die Protestierenden machten deutlich, dass die Todesfälle keine unvermeidbaren Unglücke seien, sondern das Ergebnis einer Wirtschaftsordnung, in der die Profitinteressen der Unternehmen über dem Leben der Beschäftigten stünden. 

Auf einem Transparent war zu lesen: „Die Kassen von HABAŞ sind mit Arbeiterblut gefüllt – sie werden Rechenschaft ablegen.“ Die Teilnehmer:innen skandierten unter anderem „Wir wollen nicht bei der Arbeit sterben“, „Die Regierung schaut zu, die Arbeiter sterben“ und „Das ist kein Schicksal, sondern Mord“. Neben dem HABAŞ-Konzern wurde auch die Regierungspartei AKP in Sprechchören für die Todesfälle verantwortlich gemacht.




Anwalt berichtet von wiederkehrenden Todesfällen




Der Rechtsanwalt Lütfi Sabri Batı, der Beschäftigte aus der Bergbau-, Metall-, Hafen- und Logistikindustrie in der Industrieregion Aliağa vertritt, schilderte die lebensgefährlichen Arbeitsbedingungen in den dortigen Betrieben. Er habe am Vortag gemeinsam mit einer Delegation das HABAŞ-Werk aufgesucht, in dem sich die Explosion ereignet hatte.


„In diesem Walzwerk sterben Arbeiter, weil sie in Schmelzpfannen mit tausend Grad heißem Stahl stürzen und verbrennen. Deshalb sind die Arbeiter heute nicht mehr identifizierbar“, erklärte Batı. Nach seinen Angaben komme es in dem Werk nahezu jeden Monat zu einem tödlichen Arbeitsunfall, bei dem Beschäftigte verbrennen. Wie viele Menschen dort in den vergangenen 20 Jahren ums Leben gekommen seien, werde nicht einmal systematisch erfasst. 

Batı machte politische und wirtschaftliche Verflechtungen für die ausbleibende Aufarbeitung verantwortlich. (…)




Mindestens 1.930 Beschäftigte bei der Arbeit gestorben




In einer gemeinsamen Presseerklärung riefen die beteiligten Organisationen dazu auf, das Schweigen über die tödlichen Arbeitsbedingungen zu durchbrechen. Hinter den Todesfällen in Fabriken und anderen Betrieben stünden überhöhte Produktionsvorgaben, die Profitgier der Unternehmer und mangelnde Kontrollen. Die Regierung sichere das durch Privatisierungen, Leih- und Subunternehmerarbeit entstandene Ausbeutungssystem gesetzlich ab, hieß es in der Erklärung. Statt ihrer Verpflichtung nachzukommen, sichere Arbeitsbedingungen durch wirksame Kontrollen in Fabriken, Bergwerken und auf Baustellen durchzusetzen, würden die zuständigen Ministerien neue Gesetze zur Verschärfung der Angriffe auf die Arbeiterklasse erlassen.




Unter Berufung auf Daten des unabhängigen Rats für Arbeitssicherheit und Gesundheitsschutz (ISIG) verwiesen die Organisationen darauf, dass im laufenden Jahr bereits mindestens 1.930 Beschäftigte bei der Arbeit ums Leben gekommen sind. (…)




Forderung nach unabhängiger Untersuchung und Rücktritt des Arbeitsministers




Die Protestierenden verlangten eine umfassende Untersuchung der Explosion und der Todesfälle im HABAŞ-Werk. Sämtliche Versäumnisse, die zum Tod oder zur Verletzung von Beschäftigten geführt hätten, müssten offengelegt werden. Eine Vertuschung von Beweisen oder der Schutz der Verantwortlichen dürfe nicht zugelassen werden. Neben Konzernchef Mehmet Rüştü Başaran müssten auch sämtliche beteiligten staatlichen Verantwortlichen zur Rechenschaft gezogen werden. Die im Betrieb zuständige Gewerkschaft Türk Metal wurde ebenfalls scharf kritisiert. Sie habe ihre Verantwortung für den Schutz der Beschäftigten nicht wahrgenommen und sich stattdessen an den Interessen der Unternehmensleitung orientiert. Die Organisationen forderten Türk Metal auf, sich ihrer Mitverantwortung zu stellen.


Zugleich verlangten sie den Rücktritt des türkischen Arbeits- und Sozialministers Vedat Işıkhan, dem sie vorwarfen, die anhaltenden Todesfälle in den Betrieben tatenlos hinzunehmen

…“ 

ANF-Bericht vom 11 November 2026

 

 

 mit Fotos und Video




19 Arbeiter waren ums Leben gekommen: Festnahmen bei HABAŞ – Arbeiter forderten Trauerurlaub




„

Nach der Explosion bei HABAŞ Demir Çelik in Aliağa bei İzmir, bei der 19 Arbeiter ums Leben kamen, protestierten die Arbeiter, die gezwungen wurden, auf den Trümmern weiter zu produzieren und Waren zu versenden. Mehr als 20 Arbeiter, die fünf Tage bezahlten Trauerurlaub forderten, wurden nach einem Eingreifen der Gendarmerie festgenommen.




Nach der Explosion in der HABAŞ-Eisen- und Stahlfabrik in Aliağa bei İzmir, bei der 19 Arbeiter ums Leben kamen, begannen die Arbeiter vor dem Werk zu demonstrieren, um sowohl um ihre Kollegen zu trauern als auch sichere Arbeitsbedingungen zu fordern. Als die Arbeiter in der Frühschicht aufgefordert wurden, ihre Mobiltelefone abzugeben, eskalierten die Proteste vor dem Werk.


Die Arbeiter, die sich gegen die Anweisung wehrten, ihre Mobiltelefone beim Sicherheitsdienst abzugeben, während die Aufräumarbeiten auf dem Werksgelände noch andauerten, forderten fünf Tage bezahlten Trauerurlaub.  Bei der Demonstration wurden Slogans wie „Management, tritt zurück!“ und „Türk Metal, tritt zurück!“ skandiert. Die Gendarmerie griff ein, als die Arbeiter mit den Worten „Wir wollen nicht mehr sterben“ die Straße vor der Fabrik blockierten. Bei dem Einsatz wurden mehr als 20 Arbeiter festgenommen.




Am vierten Tag nach der Explosion wehrten sich die Arbeiter, die zur Fabrik kamen, gegen die Forderungen des Arbeitgebers, indem sie sich weigerten, ihre Handys abzugeben. Die Arbeiter, die ihre Kollegen verloren hatten und angaben, nicht an deren Beerdigungen und den Beileidsbekundungen ihrer Familien teilnehmen zu können, forderten fünf Tage bezahlten Urlaub und erklärten, diese Zeit mit Trauer verbringen zu wollen. Die vor der Fabrik versammelten Arbeiter kündigten an, so lange zu warten, bis ihre Forderungen erfüllt seien, und blockierten die Straße.




Einer der Arbeiter schilderte die Arbeitsbedingungen in der Fabrik und ihre Forderungen wie folgt: „Als die Arbeiter morgens an ihren Arbeitsplatz kamen, wurden sie auf Anweisung des Arbeitgebers aufgefordert, ihre Handys draußen zu lassen. Daraufhin leisteten unsere Kollegen hier Widerstand. Sie beschlossen, ihre Handys nicht abzugeben. Gleichzeitig stellten sie eine rechtmäßige Forderung. ‚Unsere Kollegen sind gestorben, wir konnten nicht einmal zu ihren Beerdigungen gehen und ihren Familien unser Beileid aussprechen. Deshalb wollen wir fünf Tage bezahlten Urlaub erhalten und diese Zeit als Trauerzeit anerkennen lassen“, sagten sie. Drinnen dauern die Aufräumarbeiten noch an. Während diese Arbeiten andauern, weiß niemand von außen, was dort vor sich geht. Einerseits werden die Arbeiter zur Arbeit gezwungen, andererseits finden die Aufräumarbeiten statt. Es ist ganz klar, dass die Arbeiter kein Vertrauen mehr in die HABAŞ-Geschäftsführung haben

.“…“ türk. 

Artikel von Aycan Karadağ vom 14.11.2026 in BirGün Gazetesi

 

 (maschinenübersetzt) mit Fotos und dazu:







Im System des Palastes ist dem Arbeiter der Tod beschieden




„

Die Tatsache, dass die Produktion bei HABAŞ nicht unterbrochen wurde, die gegen den Arbeitgeber verhängte Hausarreststrafe und die Festnahme der Arbeiter haben einmal mehr das Ausbeutungsrad des Kapitals offenbart, das Menschenleben auf Gewinnberechnungen reduziert. Während die Familien auf den Hausarrest des Arbeitgebers Başaran mit den Worten „Diese Strafe ist zu hart, gebt ihm lieber eine Belohnung“ reagierten, erhob sich bei der Beerdigung von Abdullah Kılıç der Aufschrei: „Sagt den Reichen endlich ‚Stopp‘!“


Während die Forderungen nach Gerechtigkeit für die Arbeiter, die bei der Explosion in der HABAŞ-Eisen- und Stahlfabrik in Aliağa bei İzmir ums Leben kamen, immer lauter werden, hat die HABAŞ-Explosion den Charakter des Arbeitsregimes offenbart, das die AKP in Zusammenarbeit mit dem Kapital geschaffen hat. Während das Palastregime angesichts des Todes der Arbeiter in Schweigen verharrte, wurde die Produktion in der Fabrik, die 19 Arbeitern zum Grab wurde, fortgesetzt.


20 Arbeiter, die sich weigerten zu arbeiten und vor der Fabrik für ihr Recht auf Leben eintraten, wurden nach einem Polizeieinsatz festgenommen. Der Arbeitgeber Mehmet Rüştü Başaran wird die gegen ihn verhängte Hausarreststrafe in seiner Villa verbüßen

…“ türk. 

Kommentar von Ebru Çelik vom 14.11.2026 in BirGün Gazetesi

 

 (maschinenübersetzt) 










Die Gendarmerie griff die vor der Fabrik demonstrierenden HABAŞ-Arbeiter an; zahlreiche Arbeiter wurden geschlagen und festgenommen




„

Nach der Explosion am 9. November in der HABAŞ-Eisen- und Stahlfabrik im Bezirk Aliağa in İzmir griff die Gendarmerie Arbeiter an, die vor der Fabrik demonstrierten und gegen das Verbot protestierten, Mobiltelefone mit in die Fabrik zu nehmen; zahlreiche Arbeiter wurden geschlagen und festgenommen




Nach der Explosion, die sich am 9. November in der HABAŞ-Eisen- und Stahlfabrik im Bezirk Aliağa in İzmir ereignete, stieß das von der Werksleitung verhängte Handyverbot bei den Arbeitern auf Ablehnung. 

Den Arbeitern wurde am Morgen bei Arbeitsantritt über eine Lautsprecherdurchsage mitgeteilt, dass sie ihre Mobiltelefone auf Anweisung von Mehmet Rüştü Başaran, dem Vorstandsvorsitzenden von HABAŞ, der im Rahmen der Ermittlungen zur Explosion unter Hausarrest steht, am Sicherheitskontrollpunkt abgeben müssten. Die Arbeiter reagierten darauf mit Protest, sperrten die Straße vor dem Werk für den Verkehr und begannen einen Sitzstreik. Die Gendarmerie griff in die Aktion ein; zahlreiche Arbeiter sowie Yücel Memiş von der Ege-Arbeitergewerkschaft wurden geschlagen und festgenommen.




Auch Journalisten wurden von der Gendarmerie angegriffen




Die Reporter der Zeitung „Evrensel“, Hatice Çoruk und Emirhan Durmaz, die über die Aktion der Arbeiter berichteten, sollten ebenfalls von der Gendarmerie festgenommen werden. Dabei wurde Durmaz der Arm verdreht; dank des Eingreifens anderer Journalisten, die den Vorfall beobachteten, kam es jedoch nicht zur Festnahme durch die Gendarmerie.




Forderung der Arbeiter nach bezahltem Trauerurlaub und unabhängiger Überprüfung




In einer Erklärung, die die Arbeiter während ihres Sitzstreiks abgaben, forderten sie fünf Tage bezahlten Trauerurlaub für ihre bei der Explosion ums Leben gekommenen Kollegen, eine Überprüfung der Fabrik durch unabhängige Institutionen wie die Kammer der Maschinenbauingenieure sowie die Aussetzung der Produktion, solange die erforderlichen Arbeitsschutzmaßnahmen nicht getroffen sind. Es wurde betont, dass Arbeitnehmer aus allen Abteilungen der Fabrik in die Prüf- und Arbeitsschutzprozesse einbezogen werden müssten, und darauf hingewiesen, wie wichtig es sei, bei der Ermittlung von Risiken am Arbeitsplatz auf das Wissen und die Erfahrung der Arbeitnehmer zurückzugreifen. author: ACG
title: Resistance to Data Centres in Ireland
content:
From a correspondent  in the Republic of Ireland.




On November 7

th 

over 2,000 participated in a protest march in Dublin. The action was against data centres. There was a range of ages and organisations represented, from children to grandparents, environmental and community groups as well as political parties.  It was part of a co-ordinated Europe-wide response to a growing problem.




There are a number of reasons to oppose data centres and those at the protest voiced a variety of objections. One of the most commonly expressed complaints is their massive consumption of energy, often 24 hours a day. They compete with houses, schools and hospitals in this regard and the figures for the past decade show the increase they have made in consumption.




In the case of Ireland the Central Statistics Office (CSO) shows that data centres accounted for just 5% of consumption in 2015, but this had skyrocketed to 23% in 2025 (CSO.ie). This resulted in Irish households paying an estimated 715 Euros more in electricity bills from 2015 to 2023. This trend is likely to continue under current conditions. Campaign group Friends of the Earth predicts in a report that if that is the case, costs on households could mean an additional 1.43 billion Euros in electricity bills by 2034 (friendsoftheearth.ie).




oplus_32




Environmental concern can be found in their use of water. Data centres use huge amounts for their cooling systems. This puts pressure on local water supplies, especially during periods of drought or water restrictions. This is not a purely theoretical point in the case of Ireland. An indication of the general governmental attitude towards water usage can been seen in this year’s 2 and a half month ban on the use of hosepipes during summer. This was applied in Dublin and a number of other areas. However, an exemption was made for business during the ban (RTE, 22nd July 2026).




To put water use in perspective, total data centre water usage in Ireland was around 1 billion litres in 2025. Academics from universities in Ireland and Catalonia estimated in a recent joint report that this was equivalent to 18.5% of the consumption of occupied households in the Republic during that period (Irish Times 24/9/26). Over 95% of this water was consumed by the Mark Zuckerberg controlled Meta (Facebook, Whatsapp) alone.




Another reason sometimes forwarded in favour of data centres is the job creation that supposedly results. Its true they may employ workers during the construction phase of a project, but once up and running, data centres don’t need many people on an ongoing basis. Even those who remain once a data centre is established, don’t stay in the jobs very long. Data centre operations in Europe and Ireland show a low employee retention rate paired with a relatively short median tenure of 1.8 years. Linkedin data shows a high job turnover, with a minimum of 1,100 professionals changing jobs in a year (Savillis.ie). There is also the increase in AI services, which data centres’ enable. This deskills labour and puts human jobs at risk.




oplus_32




A further concern is the way the data centres are tied-in to the military-industrial complex. The ones in Ireland operated by Google, Microsoft and Amazon host cloud and AI infrastructure that support digital economies and military-connected cloud systems (KPMG.com). Human rights organisations such as the Irish Council for Civil Liberties have raised complaints about this, including the fact that Irish-based storage of data is tied to military and surveillance operations linked to foreign occupations and wars (ICCL.ie). Officially the Irish state claims to be neutral, but ever since World War 2, this has been more a form of neutrality that leans towards certain powers rather than others. The updating of technology is therefore really a continuation of a long-standing approach to intelligence gathering and geopolitics.




Data centres are clearly problematic. Those who have joined the opposition to them hold a combination of motivations, as can be seen in the broad demographics and organisational diversity of those who took part in the recent demonstrations. Along with this multiplicity of people, there is a variety of tactics that can be applied to the issue. At one end of the spectrum, there is the signing of a petition or marches like the ones held in Dublin. A march has its place. It at least raises greater awareness that a problem exists. The difficulty is often that petitions and marches ultimately only reinforce people’s sense of passivity, since they entail appealing to politicians to fix the very ill they created in the first place.




Further along the continuum is a perspective that argues ordinary people should directly own and control resources in society. Existing community-based groups certainly have the potential kernel of this view within them. This is something that should be encouraged. With ownership and self-management of what is produced, we can decide if we want data centres, where, when and how. In such circumstances the environment we are all part of will not be put under strain, workers and communities will decide what work needs to be done and whether we really want to support the mass killing of ordinary people elsewhere.




As for tactics, direct action is a more empowering approach. This is one where we intervene directly to change a particular situation. Instead of asking others to fix something for us, we do it ourselves here and now. There is not much sign of such activity in Ireland to be honest, but it has happened elsewhere in relation to data centres. As part of the same weekend of continent-wide initiatives, activists from the direct action group Geef Tegangas physically occupied a Microsoft data centre in Westpoort, Amsterdam. They drew attention to the use of its services by the Israeli military and Trump’s Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency (The Guardian 6/11/26). It’s a small contribution compared to the much bigger series of actions required to achieve deeper change, but it does point to a method and aim that is likely to be more effective in the long run.




To sum up, the march in Dublin was a small component of a much larger move to oppose data centres. Due to the complex mix of participants, motivations and tactics of the wider movement, we can say it should be supported, but with a critical eye towards some aspects of what is happening. Get involved if you can.

author: Corey Larocque
title: Let’s hope ‘build, baby, build’ doesn’t overshadow environmental protection
content:
We’re starting to see what it means to be “masters of our destiny,” to “build Canada strong” and to “build, baby, build.”




Those are expressions associated with Prime Minister Mark Carney’s bullish approach to strengthening Canada’s economy in the face of uncertainty by building big infrastructure projects — and building them fast.




Two recent Nunavut-related steps signal a willingness to ease off conventional safeguards in the interest of stimulating the economy. Carney’s Liberal government is considering 

lifting the moratorium

 on oil and gas exploration in the Western Arctic. And its adviser on the impact of proposed developments in Nunavut says the proposed Iqaluit Nukkiksautiit Hydro Project does not require a 

public review

.




In 2016, a Liberal government under then-prime minister Justin Trudeau imposed a ban on offshore oil and gas exploration in the Western Arctic. The risk of spillage could be disastrous to a delicate ecosystem and pristine wilderness.




But when Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne unveiled the 2026-27 budget on Nov. 5, it included funding that will be used to consider lifting that ban. Since taking over as prime minister in 2025, Carney has relaxed his party’s environmental protection standards in favour of strengthening the economy by building so-called “nation-building” infrastructure projects.




Coincidentally, a day before the budget’s release, the Nunavut Impact Review Board issued its screening decision that the proposed hydroelectricity generator near Iqaluit does not require a public review.




The Iqaluit Nukkiksautiit Hydro Project is a proposal to build a $500-million hydroelectricity generator near Iqaluit. It would generate up to 30 megawatts of power and reduce Iqaluit’s reliance on burning diesel fuel to produce electricity.
















The federal government referred the hydro project to its Major Projects Office, making it eligible to be fast-tracked through the regulatory process.




But the Qikiqtani Inuit Association — whose own business development arm, Qikiqtaaluk Corp., owns Nunavut Nukkiksautiit Corp., the company pitching the project — said it’s concerned about not having a “full public review.”




Go figure! The proponent of a multimillion-dollar construction project wants a review, but the review board that advises the government doesn’t. It seems a little backwards.




The hydro project is still in the planning stage, and its size, location and design are being finalized, the board said. Environmental, socio-economic and technical studies are underway, and it’s undergoing other reviews, including by the Nunavut Planning Commission. Federal permits will still be needed for specific activities, the board said.




NIRB did note the project will reduce diesel use, support Inuit jobs and business opportunities.




You have to wonder if NIRB would have taken that stance if it had screened the hydro proposal before Carney started talking about “nation-building” and created the Major Projects Office.
















Or is the board taking its cue from Ottawa — the government wants to move quickly on what it calls “nation-building projects” like the hydro plant — and not getting in the way?




In any case, Nunavut has recently and quickly encountered two big economic projects with the potential to generate both jobs in Nunavut and government revenue. But they also bring the risk of adverse environmental impacts.




We need to hope that the enthusiasm for building big and fast doesn’t cancel out the safeguards that have traditionally been in place to prevent environmental disasters.

author: Keerti Gopal
title: The scientists fighting to help Maui wildfire survivors heal
content:
Early on a Saturday morning in May, Ruben Juarez took the 45-minute flight from Oʻahu to Maui, just like he’d done dozens of times over the past three years. 




This one felt different. 




Juarez landed in Kahului Airport with his partner, Alika Maunakea, and drove on a long winding highway beside the piercing blue ocean until they reached the Lahaina Comprehensive Health Center.




A cool breeze wafted in from the Pacific less than half a mile below as they set up stations for blood collection, lung function tests, and mental health check-ins, directing a team of Ph.D. students and local healthcare providers. Then they waited for the fire survivors to arrive.




Ruben Juarez, left, and Alika Maunakea are professors at the University of Hawaiʻi and co-leads of the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study.

 

Keerti Gopal




On August 8, 2023, Maui was hit with the deadliest wildfires the U.S. has seen in over a century. They killed at least 102 people, displaced nearly 13,000 residents, and destroyed more than 2,200 buildings. Three years later, just 15 percent have been rebuilt. 




Juarez, an economist, and Maunakea, a biomedical scientist, never expected to focus on disaster recovery. But after the fires, they were thrust into the space by the overwhelming scale of need. The two University of Hawaiʻi professors dreamed up the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, or MauiWES, as a form of rapid response: an effort to track the impacts of the fires on survivors’ health. 




Three years and 2,500 participants later, the study has blossomed into a combination of research and intervention, a web of community organizations working together to give participants not just free testing but also therapy, food assistance, cash support, and help connecting with doctors and insurance. Some even say the study saved their lives.




The researchers hope MauiWES could become a national blueprint for public health response after disasters. Experts across the country are paying attention. One longtime disaster researcher, David Eisenman at the University of California, Los Angeles, said the study’s holistic approach is “singular.”




Alika Maunakea checks wildfire survivor Nilsson Panis into the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study at the Lahaina Comprehensive Health Center in May.
 

Keerti Gopal




But critical federal support to keep the effort going for at least a decade was running out, and its renewal was uncertain — grant applications had been met with silence for months. And just two weeks before Juarez and Maunakea landed on Maui, state funding they were counting on fell through. 




Now, here they were at what might be their last big event to understand how survivors were doing and what help they needed. 




Juarez was distraught: It felt like the end. But Maunakea, usually the pessimist of the pair, refused to believe it. He felt the study had to continue. The need was too great. They would find a way.




At the health center that Saturday morning, Maunakea greeted Lisa and Nilsson Panis, a pair of siblings born and raised in Lahaina. As he checked them into the study, he explained what they’d do that day. Urine samples to track environmental exposures. Saliva collection for biomarkers of stress and aging. Blood tests for metabolic function. Two assessments of lung health. Recordings of blood pressure, height, and weight. A mental health screener. 







At the end of it all, they’d meet with a volunteer physician who would help them understand their test results, and they’d each walk away with $100, compensation for their time.




“We’re trying to do this every year,” Maunakea told the Panises. 




He was determined to make that happen.







The lobby of the health center had a dark stain on its ceiling where water had leaked in just a month before. 




The building — run by the state’s Department of Health and loaned to MauiWES for the weekend — sits near the base of the sprawling West Maui mountains. That weekend, the foothills above the center were covered in dry, yellowing grass that was nonetheless much greener than usual, courtesy of recent Kona low storms.




The storms swept water damage into construction sites and homes that had just been rebuilt. They busted up highways and caused torrential flooding, triggering millions of dollars in damage across the county. They also kicked off an unusually verdant spring, with flowers blooming on the trees outside the center and along the highway below. Wetness that early can heighten the fire risk later in the year, fueling grass and brush growth that dries out and becomes plentiful tinder, susceptible to heat and strong winds.














































Lisa Panis, a participant in the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, has struggled with her mental and physical health since the fires, and her family is still in temporary housing. 

Keerti Gopal​​













Lisa Panis had an appointment with MauiWES that day, but she was hoping they’d have room for her older brother, too. In a fluorescently lit room just beside the center’s main lobby, she introduced Nilsson to Maunakea and explained that he had been a first responder after the wildfires, cleaning up debris in the burn zone. Maunakea immediately instructed the Ph.D. students working the check-in desk to sign him up, along with Nilsson’s girlfriend, another survivor.  




MauiWES had limited resources, especially with funding so up in the air. But on an island already suffering from a severe healthcare provider shortage, Maunakea and Juarez didn’t like turning anyone away. 




Maunakea listened to Nilsson explain what his life looked like in the months after the fires:12-hour days, seven days a week, clearing the burn zone for a construction company. He wore full-body gear to keep as much of the dust out as possible, but he still ended each day coated in grime. Though he’d never been tested, Nilsson felt confident the constant inhalation of ash and the debris that covered his body as he worked had impacted his health.







“We 

tried to push all the dust down with water,” Nilsson said to Maunakea, describing the cleanup. “But you cannot get everything.”




“Are you still doing that, or 

pau

?” Maunakea asked.




“

Pau

,” Nilsson replied. Finished. Now he was working as a mason, bringing his sister on whenever he could. It wasn’t steady. He hoped jobs would pick up in the summer.




The Panis siblings’ father is descended from Filipino immigrants who came to the island to work on the sugar plantations more than a century ago, during a period when American and European companies brought indentured laborers from the Philippines to work under brutal conditions for extremely low pay. The plantations, established before Hawaiʻi’s illegal annexation by the United States and continuing another century after, sucked water out of Lahaina’s once green and fertile hills. 




Kelly Panis, Lisa and Nilsson’s mother, sits in her FEMA-built temporary home in May. Three years after the fires, she still does not have permanent housing.
 

Keerti Goapl




That set the stage for modern-day wildfire risks, now worsened by climate change, and cemented a pattern of local disenfranchisement that continued as the tourism industry took hold. 




For years, the Panises had experienced the harder realities of life in Lahaina, like gentrification and unstable housing and employment. On the day of the fires, Nilsson was meant to fly back from Las Vegas to spread the ashes of two siblings who had passed away just weeks apart that spring. Lisa was living with an aunt whose home would not survive. She remembers standing on the field next to the post office where she and her brothers played football as kids, watching as flames engulfed the town above and below her. 




After they finished checking into the study, the Panis siblings moved through the stations, a sort of medical assembly line: urine samples, then blood tests, then blood pressure, then spitting into a tube. A few feet away, Juarez coached another participant on how to blow into a spirometer to test lung function. 




























Ruben Juarez explains to a participant in Spanish how to take the lung function test.




Keerti Gopal































Amy Jackson, a former trauma nurse, credits MauiWES with saving her life after her hemoglobin was so low she had to go to the hospital.




Keerti Gopal



















“

Sigue, sigue, sigue

,” he said, reminding the man to keep breathing out. Throughout the day Juarez greeted Spanish-speaking participants, acting as one of a handful of interpreters who walked people through the study’s tests in English, Spanish, and Tagalog.




Juarez was pulled into Maui’s recovery because of his connections to Lahaina’s abundant immigrant community. One-third of Lahaina residents were born outside the U.S., many in Asia or Latin America. Juarez moved from Mexico to Houston for a doctorate at Rice University, then to Oʻahu for a job at the University of Hawaiʻi. There, he met Maunakea, and as neighbors in the university’s faculty housing, they fell in love. 




When they met, Juarez’s research was focused on social networks and Maunakea’s on health disparities in disease. After the fires, Maunakea was drawn to Maui by his connections with people working to address the disproportionate public health burdens faced by Native Hawaiians across the islands. Although he lives on Oʻahu, his great-grandmother, a Native Hawaiian healer, was born in Kula, an upcountry Maui community that was also badly impacted by the 2023 fires.




Mikey, left, and Rob Burke stand outside of their rental home. Their home burned down in the 2023 wildfires, and three years later they are just beginning their rebuild.

 

Keerti Gopal




He and Juarez met with community leaders and healthcare workers on Maui soon after the fires. They became part of the MauiWES advisory board, consulting on design and implementation. For many study participants, that grounding made a big difference.




Mikey Burke, a Native Hawaiian mother of four who grew up in West Maui, remembers an influx of mental health practitioners from the continent who swarmed to Maui after the fires. They roamed the lobbies of hotels where she and other displaced families were sheltered. But though they were well-intentioned, they felt largely unapproachable. She gravitated toward local organizations like Maui Medic Healers Hui, which was working with MauiWES. It was something in their mannerisms, the way they spoke to her, the normalcy and familiarity they offered.




In the months after they lost their home, Burke, her husband Rob, and their four young sons were shuttled between temporary shelters, family homes, and rental properties. She could see that her twin boys, just 8 years old when the fires hit, were struggling. But it wasn’t until they got screened by MauiWES that addressing their mental health shot to the top of her lengthy to-do list. The study team told her that both boys were showing serious signs of post-traumatic stress disorder, and got them connected with a free therapist right away. 




The Burkes aren’t an anomaly. The study found widespread 

emotional distress and trauma

 in adults and children, and connected many with therapists.














































During a weekend collection event in May, the Lahaina Comprehensive Health Center was bustling with families, healthcare workers, and researchers. MauiWES has seen 2,500 participants in three years. 

Keerti Gopal​













On an island with a severe shortage of physicians, MauiWES was also most early participants’ first time seeing a doctor after the fires. Over the past three years, the team made some big saves. 




In August 2024, one year after the fires, a former trauma nurse named Amy Jackson had such a low hemoglobin count that it wasn’t registering on MauiWES’ testing system. The team urged her to go to the emergency room immediately. Jackson had signed up for the study because the cash would be a good birthday present for her daughter. If it wasn’t for that, she wouldn’t have gotten checked out at all.




At the hospital, she remembers a doctor telling her he was amazed she was still alive. She was admitted and treated, and she credits MauiWES with saving her life.




Lisa and Nilsson Panis wait for their test results at the Lahaina Comprehensive Health Center.
 

Keerti Gopal




In February 2024, another participant presented with symptoms suggesting a serious lung infection. Volunteer physicians were concerned and said she needed medical attention right away. But she was an undocumented immigrant and one of the 10 percent of study participants who had both lost their jobs in the fire and weren’t eligible for state insurance. 




Juarez coordinated with Roots Reborn — a local organization supporting Maui’s immigrant community — and reached out the next day to ask an insurer with a charitable health coverage program to consider an emergency enrollment. 




She got the insurance and then the treatment she needed. She’s one of more than 200 participants Juarez estimates have been connected with private insurance via Kaiser Permanente because of interventions from MauiWES and Roots Reborn. He was happy to see her now, in good spirits and good health, coming in for her follow-up at the May collection event. He thought the immigrant population had the most to lose from the study ending.




The team still had so much to do.




Alika Maunakea walks MauiWES participant Ekolu Lindsey through his test results, including a panel on heavy metals.
 

Keerti Gopal




After her lung test, Lisa Panis stood underneath the stain on the lobby’s ceiling and waited for her brother. The Panis siblings stay strong for one another. But she’s experienced depression since the fires, like many other survivors, and her tests revealed elevated levels of several toxic metals in her body.




In their first, smallest cohort, about six months after the fires, Juarez, Maunakea, and their colleagues 

found

 that about half of study participants were experiencing breathing problems that suggested ongoing, residual impacts from wildfire smoke. They’ve also found that poor lung function was linked to 

elevated levels of heavy metals

 in participants’ urine, including some of the same metals the health department found in the burn zone.




After looking at so many test results, Maunakea can guess with considerable accuracy what neighborhood a participant lives in just by seeing the distribution of metals in their body. Some of that contamination may predate the fires. But the health implications are the same.




Lahaina residents lay flowers at a memorial for the at least 102 people who were killed in the 2023 fires, the deadliest the U.S. has seen in more than a century.
 

Keerti Gopal




Before Nilsson Panis left for the day, Juarez gave him a T-shirt with the MauiWES logo — a sun rising behind the island — and a hundred-dollar bill. Then he ushered him over to the front desk, where a case manager who works for the Department of Health was waiting.




She asked Nilsson if there was anything he might need help with. 




He paused for a moment before answering. Maybe some assistance with food, he said. He also asked about opportunities to volunteer and help other survivors.




The case manager took down his email.







The next day Maunakea supervised a group of staff and volunteers administering lung function tests. A participant wearing a neon-yellow baseball hat and flower-patterned shorts walked in and took a seat. 




“It’s unfortunate that you guys didn’t get more additional funding from the legislative session this time,” Ekolu Lindsey said to Maunakea as he took a break from breathing hard into a plastic mouthpiece. 




It had been MauiWES’ most recent funding attempt: A bill sponsored by the state senator for West Maui, Angus McKelvey, would have allotted $3 million to keep the study going and expand the number of children it could serve. But at the last minute, the bill 

failed

 to make it through. 







“I get it, they went for the bigger-ticket items, but the health part is also a big-ticket item that didn’t take precedence,” continued Lindsey, who is the president of a 

grassroots land trust

 organization on Maui. “I don’t think they understood, because probably none of them went through it.”




Maunakea agreed. He had thought that public health would be more of a priority in the wildfire recovery, especially in a state with a doctor as a governor. But funding MauiWES has been an ongoing challenge.




The study’s first cohort, in early 2024, began with charitable funding from the Hawaiʻi Community Foundation and Kaiser Permanente, while the researchers pursued government support. That summer, they got $2.3 million from the state. And almost one year after the fires, they received a 

$1.4 million grant

 from the National Institutes of Health’s minority health disparities program. 




That support quickly turned precarious after Donald Trump retook office and slashed funding for programs focused on diversity or health disparities, along with a wide swath of academic research. 




Since the 2023 wildfires, the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study has tested more than 2,500 participants for a range of physical and mental health impacts.
 

Keerti Gopal




The MauiWES researchers hoped to renew their federal funding and keep the study going for at least a decade. But heading into the May event, applications they submitted to the agency had been languishing without a decision for more than a year. By that time, the NIH had lost 23 percent of its staff under the Trump administration, almost double the reduction across the entire federal government, according to an analysis by Inside Climate News.




The MauiWES researchers started getting national recognition in the disaster recovery space, speaking on panels and presenting at conferences on the mainland, hoping that might drum up more cash. But private funding wasn’t enough to keep the study going, and the speaking engagements had yet to pay off. More state funding seemed like Juarez and Maunakea’s best hope.




Initially, the team had strong backing from the state’s Department of Health, which wrote enthusiastic letters of support for federal grants. But as the study progressed and the researchers began publicizing their results, the agency pushed back.




The Department of Health had earlier screened 557 West Maui residents for lead in their blood, saying in May 2024 that so few had elevated levels that it was not necessary to screen the general population for toxic substances identified in the burn zone. 




Christopher Knightsbridge leads the mental health portion of the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study. He worries about study participants who are still facing acute, ongoing trauma due to fallout from the fires.
 

Keerti Gopal




“On the basis of these results with lead as an indicator of exposure, we do not expect to find health impacts caused by toxins in the wildfire ash,” agency director Kenneth Fink said in a 

statement

 at the time.




But lead is just one of the toxic substances the department found at elevated levels in burn zone ash, and it’s undetectable in people’s blood relatively quickly after exposure, unlike some other substances found in the burn zone. Environmental health experts questioned why the department used a limited sampling of lead to draw broad conclusions about the burn zone as a whole. 




Then MauiWES found elevated levels of heavy metals associated with heart and lung issues and cancer risks in a cohort of more than 1,200 fire survivors.




As of early October 2026, more than 360 Maui families are still living in temporary FEMA housing, and another 169 are receiving rental assistance from the federal agency. MauiWES researchers have found that temporary or unstable housing is a strain on survivors’ health.
 

Keerti Gopal




The findings seemed to contradict the Department of Health’s assertion that the burn zone was safe. Emails and letters Inside Climate News obtained through public records requests suggest that agency staff quickly moved into damage-control mode. 




The day after Honolulu Civil Beat 

published a story

 about the preliminary findings last year, a naturopathic doctor on Maui emailed state toxicologist John Jacob for information about the effects of heavy metals like arsenic, 

nickel

, cadmium, mercury, and lead on psychological function. Her clients had been tested by MauiWES and registered high levels of those metals, she wrote.




Jacob forwarded the email to colleagues at the Department of Health.




“I don’t want to affirm what UH is stating,” he wrote, referring to the University of Hawaiʻi. “The panic has begun!”




A few days later, agency staff discussed whether to stop assisting MauiWES with data collection. Fink, the director, said staff could continue for now, but he felt the department’s recommendations on study design had been either inadequate or disregarded. “If the latter, I would need to reevaluate our involvement,” Fink wrote to colleagues.




In October, the Department of Health 

sent a letter

 to the University of Hawaiʻi, criticizing MauiWES’ reliance on sampling survivors who showed up — as opposed to a randomized cohort — and its findings of elevated heavy metals in their urine. 










Read Next




























Long after the Maui fires, toxic metals linger in residents’ bodies













Joseph Lee

 



















The university defended the research in its 

response

 and explained that MauiWES was not claiming a definitively causal relationship between the fires and the heavy metals. 




Although the team remained committed to working with the state, Juarez said he saw the Department of Health’s letter as an attempt to censor their research. Academics not involved with MauiWES told Inside Climate News the exchange seemed unusual for a university and a state agency, and they did not think the health department’s dismissal of burn-zone dangers was warranted based on the limited information it had collected.




The agency’s director said in a statement to Inside Climate News that discussions about the best way to approach research “are a normal and healthy — and often essential — aspect of scientific collaboration.”




“While our perspectives may differ, both DOH and UH remain committed to respectful dialogue and evidence‑based inquiry,” Fink wrote in his statement. “Most importantly, the public needs clear, accurate, and consistent information about how the wildfires may have affected their health. Residents deserve timely communication they can trust — free of speculation and grounded in the best available data.”




In an emailed statement to Inside Climate News, Jacob acknowledged that the researchers’ approach was acceptable but said that not disclosing limitations could “result in confusion among the general public.”




In defense of the agency’s own approach to quantifying post-wildfire health risks, a department spokesperson said in an email that a structured soil sampling technique allowed staff to use the lead screening as a “reasonable indicator for population exposure.”




In internal emails in January, agency staff discussed a bill with funds earmarked to keep MauiWES alive. They agreed to keep a close watch on the effort. “Especially since we are not satisfied with their science,” wrote Jacob, the toxicologist.




In the end, a department subagency was among those 

submitting testimony

 in support of the funding. But that wasn’t enough to push it through. When the bill fell short with still no word on federal money, it looked like the end of MauiWES.







At nearly 5 p.m. on Sunday, the team packed up while finishing tests for the last few stragglers. Most of the staff and volunteers had to catch a flight back to Oʻahu in a couple of hours, but Christopher Knightsbridge, a therapist working on the study’s research team, would stay on Maui a few more days to see patients in person. 




Knightsbridge was overcome with pure frustration. All weekend, he’d done mental health check-ins with participants still focused on getting by, day by day. He felt certain the study was having an impact. He saw it every week. And he was still concerned about what he’d been hearing in his sessions. He wanted his patients to wake up and feel like they were living, not simply fighting to survive. For that, they needed more support, not less.




Knightsbridge poured everything he had into supporting survivors’ mental health in recovery. He spent half of most weeks away from his wife and young children on Oʻahu to see patients still dealing with ongoing crises: survivors in temporary housing and unstable employment, people with cancer diagnoses, young children whose lives were turned upside down by the fires. He’s seen serious PTSD symptoms, depression, and even suicidal ideation from kids as young as 6.




That same week, he sat in his video gaming group for kids at the health center with two of Mikey and Rob Burke’s sons, the twins dealing with PTSD. Knightsbridge was seeing both boys for therapy and organized the gaming group as another form of support, a low-stakes place for kids to open up. But the federal emergency grant supporting his position — separate from MauiWES’s funding — was also about to run out. 










Read Next




























First came the wildfire. Then came the scams.













Naveena Sadasivam

 



















On the other side of the lobby, Juarez stood in a doorway, gutted. The study had made painfully apparent the gaps in healthcare access on the island, and it felt like their work was just beginning. The thought brought him to the brink of tears. Throughout the weekend, he heard from worried participants who asked if the study was going away. He didn’t want to let them down.




Near the entrance to the courtyard, Maunakea carried a table from the hallway back into one of the offices, tired but heartened by how many people had come through. Sitting with returning participants, learning about their recovery journeys and watching how they were putting the pieces back together was energizing for him. Healing is a communal task in Lahaina. The study leaned into that. 




Maunakea knew the next disaster was just around the corner. He believed Maui could adapt and offer a model to the rest of the world for building resilience to the steep challenges climate change brings. 




Maybe, he thought, that would be the ultimate lesson from the study: that documenting and addressing health inequities in the wake of a disaster helps communities withstand what they cannot escape. 




Toward the end of the day, more survivors arrived without appointments after hearing about the study from family and friends. By closing, he estimated the team had turned away more than a dozen new people, taking down their names in case funding came through. Maunakea met people that weekend who said they’d known about the study for several years but hadn’t felt ready to participate until now. It hammered home to him how crucial it was for their work to go on.




The team would find a way to continue the study, Maunakea felt certain. He didn’t know how, but he saw no other choice. If his great-grandmother was alive, she would have said: 

‘O ka pono ke hana ‘ia a iho mai nā lani

. Continue to do good until the heavens come down to you. 




He believed that this study is 

pono

, and that the community wanted and needed this service. So, somehow, 

iho mai nā lani

. The heavens would come down.




Inside Climate News’ Peter Aldhous contributed to this story. 




This story was originally published by 

Grist

 with the headline 

The scientists fighting to help Maui wildfire survivors heal

 on Nov 14, 2026.

title: as someone who has severe sensory issues re: my own hair but who also KNOWS THINGS ABOUT MISOGYNY, I…
content:
creekfiend

:

creekfiend

:

creekfiend

:

as someone who has severe sensory issues re: my own hair but who also KNOWS THINGS ABOUT MISOGYNY, I always want to respond to “I shave/wax for sensory reasons” with “me too, but I was encouraged to do that with the hair on my legs, whereas when I removed the hair on my eyelids, eyebrows, and scalp, it got me institutionalized. can you think of any reasons why that might be, bc I have a hypothesis”

people do not like when you say things such as this. i think its a conversation which needs to be had, though!!! like what hair is it considered appropriate and desirable for women to remove? what hair is it considered inappropriate and pathological for women to remove? WE HAVE SOME VERY OBVIOUSLY ANSWERS HERE we just choose not to look at them

“I do it for sensory reasons” is, CHARITABLY, not the end of a conversation. i say charitably because it often is not even fucking relevant. but assuming that it is, ok. and how did those around you react when you began doing this. were you encouraged or discouraged? what would the reaction be if you stopped? what if you removed hair from other areas? what if a man removed his hair for sensory reasons? what would the reaction be? what social pressures might he need to overcome in order to take that action that don’t exist for those of us for whom this is expected? 

LET’S GO ON A THOUGHT JOURNEY TOGETHER. 

less generously and more straightforwardly because I think many people are missing my point here

“I do it for sensory reasons” is almost never fucking relevant to an existing conversation about the expected removal of body hair in women and is 100% never a relevant response to an existing conversation about SOCIETAL MISOGYNY. 

and I would like for those who deploy it as such to do some serious reflecting on why they think it is a reasonable counterpoint in said discussions, rather than a segue into another related discussion about what behaviors are rewarded and encouraged in what people and whether those same behaviors are discouraged and punished in other people. and what someone’s experiences seeing reflected in the world around them might prime them to see certain things as normal (and therefore no big deal to engage in) and others as abnormal (and therefore something that would require an unusually strong individual motivation to engage in)

В маленькой редакционной комнате еженедельной пропагандистской газеты мы с наслаждением предавались дружеской беседе между товарищами, как вдруг вошёл рослый парень с ремнём за плечами.

Он весело поздоровался с присутствующими, расстегнул ремни, поставил ящик на пол и сел на него, вытирая пот.

Пока мы ждали, что он заговорит, мы молча рассматривали его. Это был высокий, широкоплечий юноша с чёрными усиками на смуглой, загорелой коже и живыми, искрящимися глазами, как пенистое вино. Одет он был в деревенскую одежду, с некоторыми городскими штрихами или отголосками города.

Наконец, с улыбкой, очень непринуждённо, гость назвал своё имя.

Администратор газеты прекрасно знал его как неутомимого активиста, который очень часто писал ему – то из одного населённого пункта, то из другого – и с дьявольской энергией распространял брошюры. Где бы он ни проходил, люди массами подписывались на газету. Если он не был коммивояжёром, то уж точно был Вечным жидом[1]… – Вечным жидом пропаганды, – сказал парень с ящиком, широко и довольно улыбаясь.

И поскольку на наших лицах откровенно разливалась жадная любопытность, он принялся в общих чертах рассказывать о своей кочевой жизни.

В городе он был механиком и уже зарабатывал хорошую зарплату. Но, будучи человеком читающим и стремящимся к знаниям, завсегдатаем собраний, жадно ловившим каждое слово из дискуссий, которые велись в помещении профсоюза, он вскоре воспламенился нашим прекрасным идеалом человеческого освобождения. И тут же его охватила ненасытная жажда обращать в свою веру, тут же его озаботила великая проблема сельской пропаганды, сеяния за пределами промышленных центров – по этим обширным невозделанным полям провинции, тревожным и полным тайны. Далеко ли может зайти любая попытка городского рабочего, одинокого и встречающего враждебность? Почему бы не последовать прекрасному примеру русских революционеров, которые идут жить и работать среди крестьян?

Молодой и крепкий, без семейных обязательств, в один прекрасный день наш парень отправился по этим землям. Он запасся полезными и дешёвыми предметами, которые продавал с минимальной прибылью. Он изучил основы различных ремёсел и был на селе услужливым умельцем на все руки. В деревенских хижинах не было мебели или утвари, которую он не сумел бы починить или даже изготовить. Он даже чинил грубую обувь, за неимением сапожника, и нередко видели, как он вносил свой изобретательный вклад в ремонт или строительство домов…

При этом он довольствовался малым. Есть и спать – как придётся: иногда лучше, иногда хуже; иногда за несколько грошей, иногда в уплату за работу. В жаркое время он не брезговал спать под открытым небом, на гумнах или под скирдами. Умирать – не умирал. В общем: жил помаленьку – и со здоровьицем…

Таким образом он быстро завоёвывал сердца и доверие людей из деревень и маленьких городков, которые внимательно слушали его беседы и публичные чтения, охотно принимали его брошюры и газеты, задумчиво следили за ясными и светлыми картинами будущего, будущего с большей свободой и большим довольством.

Мы с волнением смотрели на доброго сеятеля, запоминая его облик и черты, словно пытаясь увидеть воплощение той благороднейшей страсти и того животворящего героизма.

— Вот уже пять лет веду эту жизнь, – просто заключил он.

Мы предположили, что он имеет в виду холеру и месть властей. Нет; мы поняли неправильно: речь шла об узах любви. Случаев и соблазнов ему не хватало; и не то чтобы он хвастался, но о многих он знал, что они не сказали бы ему «нет»… Но, честно говоря, решение не казалось ему из самых лёгких, как и не находил он лёгким найти женщину, которая бы ему подошла. Ужасная проблема…

И когда доблестный парень собрался уходить, уже приготовив свой запас печатной бумаги, мы захотели проводить его до окраины города.

Мы попрощались в том месте, где дорога, огибая последние дома, устремляется в великолепную прямую линию, теряющуюся из виду, обсаженную возделанными землями. На полях мужчины и женщины занимались посевами.

Наш друг попрощался с нами с искренней улыбкой, энергично пожав нам руки, и весело пустился в путь; его тяжёлые башмаки гулко били по земле, в сопровождении окованной палки.

Мы оставались там, пока его тёмный силуэт не исчез на горизонте. Белая дорога, бесконечная, сверкала на солнце. С полей доносились звуки работы. И вдали чёрный силуэт, покачивая рукой, казалось, делал благословенный жест сеятеля.

[1] Имеется ввиду легенда о Агасфере, которого Бог проклял на вечные скитания без отдыха и смерти за отказ помочь Иисусу, который шел на Голгофу. В переносном смысле «странник», употребляется в шутливой форме, без отрицательных коннотаций, которые приобрело слово «жид» в русском языке.

title: Özgür Özel: Seçimi kazanacak cesarete ve ülkeyi yönetecek maharete sahibiz
content:
YENİ Parti Genel Başkanı Özgür Özel, partisinin Ankara’da düzenlediği 1. Olağan Kurultayı’nda konuştu.




“Türkiye Yenileniyor” sloganıyla toplanan kurultayda Özel, partinin kuruluş sürecini, parti içi demokrasiye ilişkin düzenlemelerini ve ekonomi, adalet, dış politika ile toplumsal barışa yönelik hedeflerini anlattı.




“Müesses nizamın çarkları tepedeki bir azınlık için dönmektedir. İşte biz, o düzenin çarkına çomak sokanlarız” diyen Özel, partisinin “seçimleri kazanacak cesarete ve Türkiye’yi yönetecek maharete sahip olduğunu” söyledi.



















YENİ Parti 1. Olağan Kurultayı çalışmalarına başladı




Bugün  13:00










Özel, 24 Temmuz’da kurdukları YENİ Parti’nin siyasi kuruluş sürecini kurultayla tamamlayacaklarını söyledi. Partinin ortaya çıkışını, CHP yönetimine yönelik yargı kararları ve müdahalelerle ilişkilendiren Özel, iktidarın siyasi rekabeti engellediğini savundu.




CHP’nin önceki kurultaylarına ilişkin kararları ve genel merkezine yönelik polis müdahalesini eleştiren Özel, bu gelişmelerin ardından yeni bir parti kurma kararı aldıklarını anlattı.




Özel, konuşmasında tutuklu İstanbul Büyükşehir Belediye Başkanı Ekrem İmamoğlu’na ve cezaevindeki belediye başkanlarına da değindi. Beşiktaş, Beykoz, Şişli, Büyükçekmece, Bayrampaşa, Ataşehir ve Adalar belediye başkanlarının YENİ Parti’ye katıldığını duyurdu.



















Tutuklu yedi belediye başkanı YENİ Parti’ye geçti




Bugün  12:00










“Genel başkanı sadece üyelerimiz belirleyecek”




Özel, parti içi demokrasiyi güçlendirmek amacıyla ilçe başkanlarını, il başkanlarını ve genel başkanı doğrudan üyelerin seçmesini sağlayan bir sistem kurduklarını söyledi.




Eylül ayında ilçe, ekim ayında il başkanlığı seçimlerini gerçekleştirdiklerini belirten Özel, 8 Kasım’daki genel başkan ön seçimine ilişkin şu bilgileri verdi:







Tam 2 bin 502 sandıkta, 800 binden fazla üyemizin yüzde 82’sinin rekor katılımıyla Genel Başkan ön seçimini tamamladık.







Özel, mahalle, ilçe ve il meclisleri kuracaklarını, Siyaset Akademisi ve Dijital Katılım Platformu aracılığıyla üyelerin karar süreçlerine katılımını artıracaklarını söyledi.




Parti Meclisi’nin yapısını da değiştirdiklerini anlatan Özel, bu organın Parti Yasama Grubu, Parti Örgütü Grubu ve Politika Geliştirme Grubu olmak üzere üç bölümden oluşacağını açıkladı.







Asgari ücret, emekli aylığı ve sosyal konut vaatleri




Konuşmasının ekonomi bölümünde hayat pahalılığını, gelir dağılımındaki eşitsizliği ve barınma krizini ele alan Özel, YENİ Parti’nin ekonomik vaatlerini sıraladı.




Özel, asgari ücreti açlık sınırının üzerine çıkarmayı, ücret artışının işverenler üzerindeki yükünü devlet desteğiyle hafifletmeyi ve en düşük emekli aylığını asgari ücret düzeyine yükseltmeyi hedeflediklerini söyledi.




Barınma sorununa karşı sosyal konut stokunu artıracaklarını belirten Özel, sosyal konutlarda kira tutarını hane gelirinin yüzde 25’iyle sınırlama vaadinde bulundu.




Vergi politikalarına da değinen Özel, dolaylı vergileri azaltacaklarını, ücretlilerin gelir vergisi yükünü hafifleteceklerini ve vergilendirmede gelir ile serveti esas alacaklarını anlattı.




Tarım politikalarında ise çiftçilere alım garantisi vermeyi, mazottaki vergileri kaldırmayı ve çiftçi borçlarının faizlerini silerek borçları beş yılda yapılandırmayı hedeflediklerini söyledi.







“Bir daha kimsenin ele geçiremeyeceği bir yargı sistemi kuracağız”




Özel, konuşmasında yargı bağımsızlığına ve tutuklama uygulamalarına geniş yer ayırdı. İmamoğlu ve diğer tutuklu siyasetçiler hakkındaki davaların siyasi amaç taşıdığını savunan Özel, tahliye çağrısı yaptı.




“Tutuklama bir ön infaz yöntemi değildir. Son tedbirdir,” diyen Özel, iktidara gelmeleri durumunda yargının bağımsızlığını ve tarafsızlığını güvence altına alacaklarını söyledi.




Özel, “Biz iktidara geldiğimizde yargıyı ele geçirmeye asla çalışmayacağız. Bir daha kimsenin ele geçiremeyeceği bir yargı sistemi kuracağız” dedi.




Gazetecilere yönelik soruşturma ve tutuklamaları da eleştiren Özel, basın ve medya kuruluşlarının siyasi müdahalelerden bağımsız faaliyet yürütmesini sağlayacak bir düzen kurmayı vadetti.




Özel, adalet anlayışlarını dört başlıkta topladıklarını belirterek, “Mahkemede adalet, gelirde adalet, vergide adalet, sosyal hayatta adaleti sağlayacağız” dedi.







Eşit yurttaşlık ve barış çağrısı




Özel, YENİ Parti’nin sosyal demokrat bir parti olduğunu belirterek farklı kimliklerin, inançların ve siyasi görüşlerin eşit haklara sahip olacağı bir düzen hedeflediklerini söyledi.




Başörtüsü ve cemevi meselelerini eşit yurttaşlık hakkı çerçevesinde değerlendiren Özel, şu ifadeleri kullandı:







Bu ülkede başörtüsü meselesiyle cemevi meselesi, aynı eşit yurttaşlık sorununun iki farklı yüzüdür. 15 Temmuz nasıl hain bir darbe girişimiyse; 27 Mayıs, 12 Eylül, 28 Şubat nasıl demokrasimize yapılmış müdahaleler, darbelerse; 19 Mart 2025 de 21 Mayıs 2026 da birer siyasi darbedir. “Senin darbecin kötü, benim darbecim iyi” anlayışından kurtulduğumuz gün, gerçek demokrasiyi kurabiliriz.




Abdullah Tayyip Olçok'la Berkin Elvan'a birlikte ağladığımız gün gerçekten barışabiliriz. Selahattin Demirtaş, Figen Yüksekdağ, Tayfun Kahraman, Osman Kavala, Can Atalay, Ekrem İmamoğlu ve daha niceleri için adalet talebinde birleşebildiğimiz gün, gerçek çözümün kapısını aralayabiliriz. Biz AK Parti’nin suni barışına değil, milletin samimi barışına talibiz. Milletin hasret kaldığı barışı, milletin elleriyle kuracağız.







YENİ Parti’nin farklı siyasi geleneklerden ve toplumsal kesimlerden insanlara açık olduğunu belirten Özel, “Türkiye İttifakı” çağrısını yineledi.







Kadın, çocuk ve işçi haklarına ilişkin vaatler




Özel, iş cinayetleri ve işyerlerindeki denetim eksikliğini eleştirdi. Madenlerde ve diğer işyerlerinde uluslararası iş sağlığı ve güvenliği standartlarını uygulamayı hedeflediklerini söyledi.




Kadına yönelik şiddetle mücadelede İstanbul Sözleşmesi’ni yeniden yürürlüğe koymayı vadeden Özel, çocuk işçiliğine ve Mesleki Eğitim Merkezlerindeki (MESEM) uygulamalara yönelik eleştirilerini dile getirdi.







Okullarımız için yeni güvenlik reformları öneren, MESEM'lerde çocuk işçiliğine karşı çıkan, uyuşturucu ve yasadışı bahis illetine karşı acil önlem paketi hazırlayan, kadına şiddetle mücadelede İstanbul Sözleşmesi'ni savunan, geri getirecek olan, sağlıkta şiddetin önlenmesi için caydırıcı cezalar teklif eden, madenlerde ve bütün işyerlerinde uluslararası iş sağlığı ve güvenliği tedbirlerini yazılı hale getiren YENİ Parti kadroları var.










“Biz bölmeye değil birleştirmeye talibiz”




Özel, konuşmasının son bölümünde YENİ Parti’nin iktidar hedefini yineledi. Daha önce AKP ve MHP’ye oy veren seçmenlere de seslenerek partilerinin politikalarından herkesin yararlanacağını savundu.




“Biz bölmeye değil, birleştirmeye; kırmaya değil, onarmaya; kanatmaya değil, bu milletin yaralarını sarmaya talibiz,” diyen Özel, şunları kaydetti:







Görüyorsunuz ki bu çürümüş, köhnemiş, kibrin sahibi olmuş iktidarın artık adım atacak mecali kalmamıştır. Bunlar eskimiştir, yaşlanmıştır, yorulmuştur. Erdoğan, eskinin temsilcisidir. Eski gitmelidir, değişmelidir. Yorgun durmalıdır, çekilmelidir. İnananlar, çalışanlar, başaracak olanlar göreve gelmelidir. Tüm bu baskılar, haksızlıklar, zulümler, gitmekte olan bir iktidarın son çırpınışlarıdır. Artık eskiyenler, milletin istikbalini karartamayacak. Milletin kaderi, milletin elleriyle yeniden yazılacak. Biz AK Parti’nin kara düzenini değiştireceğiz. Milletin yeni düzenini kuracağız.







(VC)

author: Unknown
title: Cumartesi Anneleri/İnsanları 1129. haftada sordu: Bekir Demir nerede?
content:
Cumartesi Anneleri/İnsanları, zorla kaybedilen yakınlarının akıbetini sormak ve sorumluların yargılanmasını talep etmek için 1129. hafta buluşmasında Galatasaray Meydanı’nda bir araya geldi.




Kayıp yakınları ve hak savunucuları bu hafta, 13 Ekim 1993’te gözaltında kaybedilen Bekir Demir’in akıbetini sordu.




Cumartesi Anneleri/İnsanları adına açıklamayı Zeynep Yıldız okudu.




Askerler Bekir Demir’i helikopterle götürdü




Yıldız’ın anlatımına göre Bekir Demir, kaybedildiğinde 29 yaşındaydı ve dört çocuk babasıydı. Batmanlı Demir, Adana’da otogarda taksicilik yaparak ailesinin geçimini sağlıyordu.




Demir, birlikte çalıştığı arkadaşı S.T.’nin daveti üzerine eşi ve bir buçuk yaşındaki çocuğuyla Diyarbakır’ın Kulp ilçesine bağlı Alacakepir köyünün Badı mezrasına gitti. Aile, burada bal ve ceviz gibi kışlık yiyecekler satın almayı planlıyordu.




O dönemde General Yavuz Ertürk komutasındaki Bolu Tugayı bölgede askerî operasyonlar yürütüyordu.




Açıklamaya göre askerler, 13 Ekim 1993’te Badı mezrasına operasyon düzenledi ve yaklaşık 30 kişiyi köy meydanında topladı. Kimlikleri kontrol eden askerler, Demir’in köyde yaşamadığını belirledi. Ardından “Komutan istiyor” diyerek Demir’i askerî helikoptere bindirip götürdü.




Demir’in eşi ve köylüler bu olaya tanık oldu. Ailesi, o tarihten sonra Demir’den bir daha haber alamadı.







Tanık ifadelerine rağmen dosya kapandı




Demir’in ailesi, valiliğe, jandarmaya ve savcılıklara başvurarak kayıp yakınlarının akıbetini öğrenmeye çalıştı. Ancak aile, başvurularından sonuç alamadı.




Aile, 1995 ve 2002 yıllarında yeniden savcılığa başvurdu. Yetkililer, Demir’in kaybedildiği tarihte bölgede askerî operasyon gerçekleşmediğini bildirdi. Cumartesi Anneleri/İnsanları ise daha sonra ortaya çıkan resmî belgelerin, Bolu 2. Komando Tugayı’nın o dönemde bölgede operasyon yürüttüğünü doğruladığını belirtti.




Açıklamaya göre Askerî Savcılık, 6 Kasım 2011’de Bolu 2. Komando Tugayı Komutanlığı’ndan operasyonda görev alan rütbeli personelin kimlik bilgilerini istedi. Tugay Komutanlığı, arşivin bulunduğu binayı su bastığını ve kayıtlara ulaşamadığını ileri sürerek bilgileri paylaşmadı.




Kulp Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı, tanık anlatımlarına rağmen 3 Kasım 2014’te zamanaşımı gerekçesiyle kovuşturmaya yer olmadığına karar verdi. Diyarbakır 3. Sulh Ceza Hâkimliği de ailenin itirazını 5 Mart 2015’te reddetti.




Aile, iç hukuk yollarından sonuç alamayınca Anayasa Mahkemesine, ardından Avrupa İnsan Hakları Mahkemesi’ne başvurdu.




“Bekir Demir dosyası, tanıklıkların nasıl görmezden gelindiğinin ve cezasızlığın nasıl üretildiğinin açık örneklerinden biridir,” diyen Yıldız, etkili bir soruşturma yürütülmesi ve sorumluların yargı önüne çıkarılması talebini yineledi:







Bekir Demir dosyası, zamanaşımı gerekçesiyle kapatılamaz; zorla kaybetme suçuna ilişkin uluslararası hukuk yükümlülükleri gözetilerek etkili soruşturma ve kovuşturma yürütülmeli, Bekir Demir’in akıbeti ortaya çıkarılmalıdır.










33 yıl önce gözaltına alınarak askeri helikopterle götürülen Bekir Demir’e ne oldu? #CumartesiAnneleri1129Hafta https://t.co/uji60nqKTQ


— Cumartesi Anneleri (@CmrtesiAnneleri) 

November 14, 2026







Osman Demir: “Çocukluğumuz o gün bitti”




Bekir Demir’in oğlu Osman Demir, buluşmaya gönderdiği mesajda babası kaybedildiğinde altı yaşında olduğunu anlattı. Dört kardeşin en büyüğü olduğunu belirten Demir, “Babam gittiğinde evden yalnızca bir insan eksilmedi. Evin düzeni, kahkahası, geleceği eksildi. Çocukluğumuz o gün bitti,” dedi.




Annesinin dört çocuğuyla tek başına kaldığını belirten Demir, kardeşleriyle birlikte babalarının nerede olduğunu bilmeden büyüdüklerini anlattı.




Demir, ailesinin 33 yıldır belirsizlik içinde yaşadığını şu sözlerle dile getirdi:







Bir düşünün. Ölenin yası tutulur. Bir toprağın başında dua edilir, bir taşa dokunulur. Peki gözaltında kaybedilen biri için ne yapılabilir? Biz yas bile tutamadık. 33 yıldır yarım bir yasın içinde yaşıyoruz.







“Bu dosyayı yeniden açın, tanıkları dinleyin”




Osman Demir, soruşturmanın yıllarca farklı savcılıklar arasında dolaştığını, tanıkların ifadelerine rağmen babasının akıbetinin ortaya çıkarılmadığını söyledi.




Adalet Bakanlığına ve savcılıklara seslenen Demir, “Bu dosyayı yeniden açın. Tanıkları yeniden dinleyin. Zamanaşımının arkasına saklanmayın, esastan inceleyin” dedi.




Demir, Millî Savunma Bakanlığı ile Jandarma Genel Komutanlığından da 1993’te bölgede görev yapan askerî birliklerin ve komutanların kimliklerini açıklamalarını, arşivleri erişime açmalarını istedi.




Meclise ve karar vericilere geçmişle yüzleşme çağrısı yapan Demir, “Biz adalet istiyoruz. Babamıza ne olduğunu, kimlerin onu aldığını, nereye götürüldüğünü bilmek istiyoruz. Sorumluların hukuk önünde hesap vermesini istiyoruz. Bu bizim en temel insani hakkımızdır” dedi.







(VC)

author: Redação
title: Vitória: um cartão postal manchado de pó preto
content:
Há mais de meio século, a população da Grande Vitória enfrenta uma poluição carregada pelo vento que causa transtornos tanto à sua rotina quanto à sua saúde – o Pó Preto. O material particulado de cor escura, popularmente chamado de pó preto, é produzido a partir de processos industriais com minério de ferro, carvão e outros metais pesados que acontecem no complexo industrial de Tubarão, onde estão instaladas a mineradora Vale e a siderúrgica ArcelorMittal.




No segundo episódio de Big Problema, vamos viajar até o litoral capixaba para investigar de onde vem o pó preto que cobre a cidade de Vitória e por que, mesmo após décadas de denúncias, a poluição causada pela indústria ainda faz parte da vida de quem mora na cidade.







O Big Problema é uma série de podcast narrativo idealizada pela primeira turma de 

trainees da 

Agência Pública

, que investiga como grandes empreendimentos têm transformado a cultura, o cotidiano e a relação das pessoas com as cidades brasileiras.
