author: Fikayo Akeredolu
title: Nigeria's petrol subsidy was also an electricity policy
content:
As long as households and businesses in Nigeria depend on generators and cannot rely on the grid for electricity, some form of fossil fuel subsidy will always be necessary. Despite the costs, and despite what the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund (IMF), and the climate research community say. This is because fossil fuel subsidies, in my opinion, are the country’s largest and most decentralized electricity access program, and any attempt at reform without explicitly accounting for this will fail. This essay explains why.

As a starting point, I need everyone to read Dr. Neil McCulloch’s book 

Ending Fossil Fuel Subsidies

. The book explains how subsidies are effectively a political prosthetic. Imagine you run a developing country with weak administrative capacity. You cannot reliably deliver schools or clinics, but you need to give citizens something that shows you are on their side and ensures you stay in power. Cheap energy through fossil fuel subsidies is the one thing you can deliver somewhat easily. Weak states, like Nigeria, lean on subsidies because a subsidy is a substitute for the public goods the state cannot otherwise provide.

Citing a Nigerian study, he shows that the subsidy mostly benefits the rich — the bottom 40 percent of households consumed only 3 percent of petrol, while the richest fifth captured around 27 times more benefit than the poorest fifth. By 2018, Nigeria was spending roughly $300 million a month on the petrol subsidy, more than its entire budget for basic education. Considering all of this, anyone can see that the subsidy is a bad political and economic deal.

Beyond the numbers, there is the climate change literature. McCulloch notes that fossil fuel subsidies are sometimes a key blockage to the wider development of renewable energy. Cheap petrol and diesel weaken the incentive to switch to cleaner alternatives. The reformist logic follows rationally — remove the subsidy, allow prices to reflect the true cost of fuel, and households and businesses should begin moving toward cleaner energy. And this logic from the literature is intuitive. But it makes assumptions that anyone who truly understands Nigeria will tell you just do not apply.

It assumes grid electricity already exists and the question is simply how it should be generated. But for many Nigerians, electricity means a petrol generator. Remove the subsidy and the choice is not necessarily dirty electricity versus clean electricity; it is instead between some electricity versus none.

The reformist logic also assumes a certain level of demand elasticity. The assumption here is that people can meaningfully reduce their demand when prices rise. But if petrol is running the generator that powers your home or business, there is only so much consumption you can cut before you have a bigger problem. It also assumes a substitute is readily available. A higher petrol price only pushes someone toward solar and electric vehicles if solar and electric vehicles are actually affordable, available, and accessible. It assumes subsidy removal mainly hurts a powerful fossil fuel industry. In Nigeria, it also hurts households and small businesses that rely on petrol generators because the grid does not work. And probably most importantly, it assumes a state government capable of capturing the savings from subsidy removal and redirecting them transparently, efficiently, and effectively into the transition.

If the assumptions do not hold, how exactly is the price signal of subsidy removal supposed to work? Post subsidy removal, what was the immediate short-term plan for providing electricity? If you make petrol for running generators more expensive, yes, the price signal should move people to cleaner sources, but are the cleaner sources within a price range that allows everyone to make the switch?

As someone who has lived in Nigeria, sat through more blackouts than I care to number and then gone on to do a PhD on this topic, I think that there was a key part of this debate that analysts, international financial institutions, and policymakers did not seem to fully reckon with. And it is this — on a not insignificant note, Nigeria’s subsidy was about generating electricity just about as much as it was a fiscal matter. Effectively, Nigeria’s petrol subsidy was a key part of its electricity policy.

And recommending and enacting its removal without explicitly accounting for this made the average Nigerian’s life worse. I say the average Nigerian because following the subsidy’s removal, some people did make the switch to solar. But it was mostly the wealthy households and larger businesses concentrated in wealthy urban areas with poor grid access.

Removing the subsidy in May/June 2023 did not end a regressive transfer. It sorted the country by those with enough wealth to exit a failing system by going solar and stabilizing their costs and those without who were left with neither cheap fuel for their generators nor the means to replace them. The subsidy removal worsened energy inequality/poverty.

Yes, the subsidy was terrible for the budget and for the country’s long-term prospects and it benefited mostly the rich. But it was all most people, especially the poor, had. The grid reaches too few and works too rarely, and the generator economy — the so-called “shadow grid” — grew in the gap. Expensive, dirty, and improvised, but a system that tens of millions got their power from. The subsidy for the most part held it together. Removing it the way it was done broke the system further, and the breakage fell hardest on the people the subsidy reform claimed to be for.

On page 98, Dr. McCulloch writes, “the trick is not to stop subsidies — it is to swap them for something people value more.” And yes, this is the way successful subsidy reform happens. But it exposes the Nigerian problem. The swap only works if there is something people value more than what the subsidy was giving them. So what do Nigerians want more than electricity? Cheaper food, maybe, or cash. But every one of those runs into the same wall: the state has to be able to deliver it. A swap is only as good as the government’s capacity to hand over the other side of the trade. Could the Nigerian government reliably hold up its end of the subsidy removal deal per assumption?

The answer is a resounding no. Per 

the government’s own numbers

, the conditional cash transfer scheme reached only 5.5 million households, about 37 percent of the 15 million it targeted. 

The Auditor General of the Federation later reported

 that ₦33.75 billion paid to 3.29 million households in 2023 could not even be authenticated. So it is not just that the amount was too small, it is also that part of what did go out cannot be traced.

A state that cannot transparently deliver targeted transfers is not in a position to remove a subsidy that only targeted transfers could soften. A state that is not actively investing in improving the grid and public electricity supply should not be removing the subsidy that allows the people to self-supply their electricity.

The IMF

 said the subsidies “are costly, and do not reach those that most need government support.” The World Bank, in the December 2022 

Nigeria Development Update

, called the subsidy “unsustainable, opaque, wasteful and regressive expenditure on the premium motor spirit, PMS or petrol, subsidy” and said “richer Nigerians benefit significantly more from it than poorer Nigerians.” Both institutions are right on these counts. They go on to recommend the phase-out of the subsidies. Each institution is careful to say that there must be compensation. Both institutions asked the government to remove the distortion caused by the subsidy but to make sure to protect the poor. In fact, the IMF asks that the safety net should be built and working before the subsidy is removed. There are two problems with this.

First, both institutions are assuming a level of state capacity everyone knows the Nigerian government does not have. In the same December 2022 

Update

, the World Bank refers to Nigeria’s “legacy of weak governance and poor track record of macroeconomic policies” twice. In the June 2022 

Update

, the World Bank, using Afrobarometer data, concludes Nigerians do not trust the government to use any resources saved from removing the petrol subsidy for causes that would benefit the population at large. How can we ask a distrusted state with a “legacy of weak governance and poor track record of macroeconomic policies” to credibly deliver this kind of reform?

It should shock no one that the government appears to have done the opposite of what the IMF recommended. It removed petrol subsidies in May 2023 and the safety net still had not reached most of its targets years later.

Second, both institutions, in my opinion, insist on seeing the subsidy mainly as a fiscal problem. The World Bank estimated that keeping the petrol subsidy will cost Nigeria ₦4.8 trillion in 2022, equivalent to roughly 2.5 to 2.7 percent of gross domestic product in forgone government revenue. They argue that money spent keeping petrol cheap was money not going to schools, clinics, or roads.

But this framing misses something important because it does not replace the electricity the subsidy was helping people produce for themselves. Because like I keep explaining, the petrol subsidy in Nigeria is also an electricity subsidy.

You can see the gap in the IMF’s own language. In its 

2024 Article IV Consultation

 it refers to “fuel and electricity subsidies” as two separate items on three occasions. And on paper they are, but in everyday life, they are not. Millions of Nigerians rely on petrol generators because the grid is unreliable or unavailable. To the IMF’s credit, they recognize the need to protect electricity access, including through a “lifeline tariff” for poorer consumers. But that only helps people who have a working grid connection. What is the equivalent for the 

85 million Nigerians without grid electricity access

, or for households that get only a few hours of grid power a day?

So what should have been done to remove the subsidy without worsening energy poverty? Before there was even talk of removing the subsidy, there should have been a focus on bringing down the cost of household and business solar power and financing it for people who cannot pay cash, getting installers and supply chains into the regions that have none, and setting up the payment and identification systems and proving they work at scale for cash transfers to poorer households. There should have been significant investment in the grid to replace privately generated electricity with public supply.

Instead of this, the government went the other way. In March 2025 it 

announced plans

 to ban the importation of solar panels, arguing this would build up local manufacturing. The problem is that local production can meet only a small share of national demand, so the practical effect of a ban is scarcity and higher prices. 

Analysts warned

 it could push the cost of a solar installation up by as much as 150 percent. The subsidy that made generators affordable was mostly gone, and the state’s response to the alternative that could have filled the gap was to make it more expensive.

Despite how it is titled and how it reads, this essay is not a defense of fossil fuel subsidies. The subsidy in Nigeria is regressive, corrupt, expensive, and overdue for reform. This essay is instead asking that before we talk about reforming the subsidy, we need to do a better job of understanding what exactly the subsidy is doing and the ways government failure makes it a necessary evil.

Any attempt to reform the subsidy that does not start by accounting for its role in electricity generation is most likely to fail. It is Nigeria’s largest and most decentralized electricity access program, delivered through the pump thanks to a failing power sector.

Carol Andersonprofessor of African American studies at Emory University.

Black voters in Georgia on Tuesday said, “Not today, Satan,” according to professor Carol Anderson, professor of African American studies at Emory University. Despite the Trump administration’s efforts to disenfranchise Black voters in the South this election cycle and the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act, she says there was “massive turnout” that propelled Democrats to victory. Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated billionaire Republican healthcare executive Rick Jackson, becoming the first Black woman ever elected governor in the United States. Incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff also handily won his bid for reelection.

Carol Andersonprofessor of African American studies at Emory University.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman, with Anjali Kamat.

ANJALI KAMAT: We turn now to Georgia, where former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms has defeated billionaire Republican healthcare executive Rick Jackson to become the state’s next governor. Jackson spent more than $200 million in his losing bid. Bottoms becomes the first Black woman ever elected governor in the United States. This is Keisha Lance Bottoms in her victory speech Tuesday night.

GOV.-ELECT KEISHA LANCE BOTTOMS: This win is for the caregiver who can’t afford healthcare and needs Georgia to finally expand Medicaid. It is for the entrepreneur who is seeking to grow her small business. This win is for the farmer who is trying to hold on to his family land. It is for the teacher who’s working two jobs so that they can educate our children. And this win is for the child who deserves every opportunity to succeed. Georgia, this win is for all of us.

AMY GOODMAN: Keisha Lance Bottoms in her victory address last night. Again, she becomes the first Black woman governor in U.S. history. Also in Georgia, Senator Jon Ossoff cruised to reelection early Tuesday night. Many people wonder if this is now just ushering in his run for president in 2028.

For more, we’re joined by Carol Anderson, professor of African American studies at Emory University, the author of many books, including One Person, No Vote: How Voter Suppression Is Destroying Our Democracy.

Professor Anderson, thanks again for joining us today. As we talked to you last night in our midterm special, you had just finished driving people to the polls. The significance of the voter turnout, the Black woman voter turnout? The significance of this history that has been made, not only with Keisha Lance Bottoms, but with the attorney general of Georgia and the secretary of state, all three Black women?

CAROL ANDERSON: Yes, I mean, this is monumental. And I think what we’re really seeing here is this is basically the result of over a decade of organizing, of being in the community. So, when you’re looking at Governor-elect Bottoms, Lance Bottoms’ vote, you’ll see that it went all the way from Augusta through Macon and through to Columbus, so you get this belt of voters in those counties that we don’t often think of as — and so, this, again, is — like I said, this is part of the work that Stacey Abrams has done over a decade ago in terms of being in those counties, doing that kind of relationship, doing that kind of organizing, building the kind of capacity that can get that massive voter turnout.

And it’s about framing this election for all of us. It’s recognizing that in a state that has systematically refused to expand Medicaid, even when there was money on the table in order to do that, instead being willing to have rural hospitals shut down, instead being willing to have some counties that have no OB-GYN, so that somebody who is pregnant will have to go over like a hundred miles in order to get to a doctor — it is recognizing the absolute inhumanity of that. And that’s what we’re seeing in this vote. We’re seeing in this vote this quest for humanity, this quest for dignity, this quest in order to live our lives fully.

ANJALI KAMAT: And, Professor Anderson, I mean, you’ve talked about the long history of organizing in Georgia, but this is also coming at a time when the Trump administration was trying to redistrict, to gerrymander so many districts across the South, and to disenfranchise Black voters. Can you talk about how that pushed more people to the polls?

CAROL ANDERSON: Oh my gosh! It was like — and so you see this massive push, where it’s like, “Oh, you want to take away my voting rights? Not today, Satan. Not today.” And so you see this kind of — the anger. So, when Governor Kemp made the decision to have a special session to basically redraw the boundaries, the way that Abbott did in Texas, there was this massive organizing that happened throughout the community, where you began to see people just fill up the state House as the Legislature is beginning this special session. And when they saw all of those people in the state House, they backed off. They said, “Oh, we’re not going to do this right now. We know this will not be a good thing.” And so, this is where that organizing comes in. This is where that kind of sense of “You’re trying to steal my ability to have my citizenship rights. You’re trying to steal one of the key components of being an American. You’re trying to steal that from me. I’m not going to let you take it.”

AMY GOODMAN: We’re talking about the Deep South. Whether we’re talking about Georgia or we’re talking about South Carolina, where Dr. Annie Andrews has just flipped a Senate seat, we are seeing in the South a massive change, why the Republicans poured millions into the reddest of red states. If you can talk about the significance, going beyond Georgia, of what has taken place, with what some are calling not just a blue wave, a blue tsunami, a “bluenami,” that has taken place?

CAROL ANDERSON: I mean, so, you see it, for instance, in Louisiana, where you had this massive Black voter turnout in terms of early voting. You see it in South Carolina, where you had this massive Black voter turnout. You’re seeing it here in Georgia. And what that is talking really — what that’s really signaling is this sense of what Callais did. So, the Supreme Court’s Callais decision was really about diluting the power of the Black vote. It really was about saying, “OK, so, we can just gerrymander you and put you into districts where you can vote, but you will not have any kind of power to choose your representatives.” And that is so Jim Crow. That is so — Georgia used to have a thing called the county unit system, which was about minimizing the power of the Black vote in the urban areas and increasing the power of the white conservative vote in the rural areas. And so, you see this hearkening back to those good old days of Jim Crow. And you had the Black community saying, “We’re not having it,” and that kind of turnout in South Carolina, in Louisiana, in Mississippi.

Think about this. In Mississippi, where you’ve got — the race is really close between Cindy Hyde-Smith and Colom, right? It’s really close. And it’s that close because of the power of that Black vote. And remember, in Mississippi, where you had the Legislature basically carve out a district, a policing — a judicial district in Jackson, so that Black folks in Jackson would have no kind of power, no kind of authority in that area, in their own city. And so, this is what we’re looking at. We’re looking at Black folks just standing up and saying, “Not today. You will not take away my rights. We will have representation. We will vote,” and again, that massive voter turnout. So, it was almost twice as many African Americans voted early in 2026 than they did in 2018, almost doubled. This is what we’re seeing here.

AMY GOODMAN: Do you think it’s also a wake-up call, Professor Anderson, for the Democratic Party? I mean, many people felt the lack of resources that were poured into the Democratic candidates in the South, not believing that there would be this blue wave, right through to Florida, where it looks — I mean, Angie Nixon, where she had so little support from the Democratic Party, the DSA Senate candidate. Yes, she was defeated, but it was such a close race against Ashley Moody. And then you’re talking about Scott Colom. That is still too close to call, African American in Mississippi taking on Cindy Hyde-Smith. We’ll see what happens with the votes still to be counted. If you can end up talking about what is the message to the Democratic Party right now?

CAROL ANDERSON: The message to the Democratic Party is believe us when we talk about we have the power. We just need the resources in order to be able to exercise that power. It is actually asking them to be very strategic and listen to the people and listen to the kinds of candidates that really resonate with the people. And that’s where the resources should go. It’s not going, “OK, who is electable?” “Who is electable” becomes a really kind of standard to just get the same old same old. And that same old same old will not work. We know that. And it is like — it is saying to basically have the resources to be able to lead, have the resources to be able to support these incredible candidates.

So, what happened in Florida, she deserved better than that. That was a fierce, fierce warrior. And when she said, “I am an organizer, not a politician,” and so that means that she’s going to get up and continue to work. And because that is a two-year term that they’re looking at here, it means that the Democratic leadership needs to begin to invest in these folks that can really speak to the people.

AMY GOODMAN: And isn’t this also a message about class? I mean, Rick Jackson, who Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated, poured over $200 million of his own personal fortune into his campaign, one of the largest self-funded candidates in Georgia politics. We have five seconds.

CAROL ANDERSON: Yes, it is. It is about that. It is about data centers. It is about really listening to the people and not having billionaires basically trying to buy this democracy.

AMY GOODMAN: Carol Anderson, professor of African American studies at Emory University, author of many books, including One Person, No Vote: How Voter Suppression Is Destroying Our Democracy.

That does it for our show. Visit democracynow.org and our YouTube channel to watch our four-hour election night special last night.

Oh, and Steal This Story, Please!, the documentary about Democracy Now!, is now available on many streaming platforms, from Amazon Prime to YouTube to Apple TV. Go to StealThisStory.org to see where you can watch it.

Democracy Now! produced by an amazing group: Mike Burke, Deena Guzder, Anjali Kamat, Messiah Rhodes, Nicole Salazar, Nermeen Shaikh, María Taracena, John Hamilton, Sara Nasser, Charina Nadura, Sam Alcoff, Tey-Marie Astudillo, Robby Karran, Hany Massoud. Special thanks to Julie Crosby, Denis Moynihan. I’m Amy Goodman, with Anjali Kamat.

title: Bakirhan li Kandirayê, Hatimogullari Edîrneyê daxûyanî dan
content:
Hevserokê Giştî yê DEM Partiyê Tuncer Bakirhan serdana Fîgen Yuksekdag kir û Hevseroka Giştî ya DEM Partiyê Tulay Hatimogullari jî serdana Selahattîn Demîrtaş kir.




Li gorî nûçeya Ajansa Welat piştî serdanan li ber girtîgehan daxuyanî hate dayîn û hevserokan diyar kir ku hevalên wan ên siyasetmedar bi awayekî neqanûnî di zindanan de girtî ne û bang kirin ku demildest werin berdan. 




Di 4ê Mijdara 2016an de li dijî HDPê û siyasetmedarên Kurd êrişeke hate destpêkirin. Di çarçoveya vê derbeya siyasî de 9 siyasetmedar hatibîn girtin. Di qonaxa yekem a vê derbeya siyasî de hevserokên giştî yên berê yên HDPê Fîgen Yuksekdag û Selahattin Demîrtaş jî di nav de gelek parlamenter hatibûn girtin.







Cezayên ku di 

Doza Kobanê 

de li siyasetmedaran hatibû birîn




22emîn Dadgeha Cezayê Giran a Enqereyê di 16ê Gulana 2024an de di dozê de biryara cezayan da. Her weha biryara hêcetê jî di Hezîrana 2025an de hatibû aşkerekirin.




Selahattin Demirtaş: 

42 sal




Fîgen Yuksekdağ:

 32 sal 9 meh




Gultan Kişanak, Sebahat Tuncel, Emine Ayna: 

12 sal




Ahmet Turk: 

10 sal




Ali Urkut:

 13 sal 4 meh




Alp Altınors:

 18 sal




Ayla Akat Ata, Aynur Aşan: 

9 sal 9 meh




Mesut Bagcik, Nezir Çakar, Ayşe Yagci, Meryem Adibelli: 

9 sal




Bulent Parmaksız: 

23 sal




Gunay Kubilay, Îsmaîl Şengul: 20

 sal 6 meh




Nazmi Gur, Pervin Oduncu, Zeki Çelik, Zeynep Karaman:

 22 sal 6 meh




Cîhan Erdal, Dîlek Yagli:

 16 sal







Bi boneya 10emîn salvegera darbeya 4ê Mijdarê Hevseroka Giştî ya DEM Partiyê Tulay Hatimogullari li Girtîgêha Edîrneyê serdana Selehattîn Demirtaş kir. Hevserokê Giştî yê DEM Partîyê Tuncer Bakirhan jî li Girtîgeha Tîpa Fyê ya Kandirayê serdana Fîgen Yuksekdag kir.




Piştî serdanan hevserokan li ber girtîgehan daxuyanî da. Serokên giştî yên partiyên siyasî yên pêkhateyên DEM Partiyê, rêveberên partiyên siyasî, rêxistinên DEM Partî û gelek welatî tev li daxuyaniyê bûn. Di daxuyaniyan de de pankarta “Ji bo aştî û demokrasiyê azadî bo girtiyên siyasî” hate vekirin û dirûşmeyên “Bijî berxwedana zindanan” hate berzkirin.




"Divê hemû girtiyên siyasî demildest werin berdan"




Tuncer Bakirhan li pêşiya Girtîgeha Kandirayê axivî û daxuyanî da. Tuncer Bakirhan bi bîr xist ku îro salvegera 4ê Mijdarê ye û ev roj di dîroka siyasî ya Tirkiyeyê de rojeke reş û birîneke kûr e û wiha axivî:







“Berî 10 salan, di 4ê Mijdara 2016an de, bi rakirina parêzbendiyan û girtina hevalên me Fîgen Yuksekdag û Selahattîn Demîrtaş jî di nav de 10 parlamenterên me, darbeyeke siyasî li dijî demokrasiyê hate kirin. Ev birîna ku 10 sal berê hate vekirin, bi demê re mezin bû û hemû Tirkiye xist bin bandora xwe. Îro ne tenê siyasetmedarên Kurd û DEM Partiyî, lêbelê bi hezaran kesên ku fikrên xwe tînin ziman, rexne dikin û muxalefetê dikin ji Girtîgeha Kandirayê bigire heta hemû girtîgehên welêt bi neheqî di girtinê de ne. Di nava van 10 salên borî de hiqûq hat rawestandin û di warê edaletê de qelsiyek mezin çêbû. Niha li pêşiya me du rê hene: Em ê bitirs û tirsên borî bi rêbaza bêhiqûqiyê bidomînin, an jî em ê birînên borî bi hiqûqeke demokratîk derman bikin. Em aştiyeke ku tê de birînên borî bên dermankirin dixwazin. Pêvajoya aştiyê ji bo dermankirina van birînan e. PKKê xwe fesix kiriye û li sînorên Tirkiyeyê tu kampên ku ‘tehdîdê’ çêbikin neman. Niha divê gavên yekalî yên dîrokî bersivekê bibînin.




Di vê serdema ku em hewl didin serdema şer biqedînin. Divê pêşî Hevserokên me Fîgen Yuksekdag û Selahattîn Demîrtaş û hemû girtiyên siyasî yên wekî Can Atalay, Selçuk Kozagaçlı, girtiyên Geziyê û Kobaniyê demildest werin berdan. Ev ne lutif e; ev deynê dewletê yê li hemberî hiqûqê ye. Divê biryarên Dadgeha Destûra Bingehîn (AYM) û DMMEyê bê şert û merc bên cîbicîkirin û qeyûmên ku li şûna îradeya gel hatine danîn werin rakirin. Di heman demê de, divê rê li ber darizandina bêgirtî ya şaredar û rêveberên bajêr jî vebe. Bêyî azadiya raman, çalakî û rêxistinbûnê, em nikarin aştiyê qezenc bikin û demokrasiyê ava bikin. Ji ber wê em bi dengekî bilind dibêjin: Azadî ji bo hemû girtiyên siyasî!”







"Heya ku yek girtiyê siyasî hebe wê têkoşîna me bidome"




Hevseroka Giştî ya DEM Partiyê Tulay Hatimogullari jî pişti serdana Demîrtaş, li peşîya Girtîgeha Edîrneyê daxuyanî da.




Tulay Hatimogullari diyar kir ku piştî hevalan wan hatin girtin rejîmeke nû, ango ‘rejîma qeyiman’ li welat dest pê kir û wiha got:







“Qeyim li Wanê û li gelek bajarên Tirkiyeyê hatin danîn. Li zanîngeh û cihên kar jî rejîma qeyûman xwe nîşan da. Ev yek ne tenê bi qadên Kurdan re sînorkirî ma, li hemû mûxalefetê belav bû. Ev rêbaz, ne tenê di dîroka HDP’ê de, lê li hemû mûxalefetê hat sepandin. Niha Serokê Şaredariya Stenbolê yê hilbijartî birêz Ekrem Îmamoglu û gelek şaredarên hilbijartî di girtîgehê de ne. Ev yek nîşan dide ku ew rejîma ku di 4ê Mijdarê de dest pê kir, niha li hemû Tirkiyeyê belav bûye. Em rejîma qey,man qebûl nakin. Bila Selahattîn Demîrtaş, Fîgen Yuksekdag û hemû girtiyên Kobaniyê tavilê bên berdan. Çimkî hevalên me deryasayî di girtîgehan de ne. Birêz Selahattîn li ser pêyan e û dibêje, ‘Silav û hezkirina xwe ji hemû gelên Tirkiyeyê re dişînim’. Wî diyar kir ku ew ê di şert û mercên girtîgehê de piştgiriya xwe ya ji bo Pêvajoya Aştî û Civaka Demokratîk bidomîne û dibêje, ‘Me li ser vê axê bedelên giran dan, lê çi dibe bila bibe em ê hewldanên aştiyê qut nekin’. Heya ku hemû girtiyên siyasî azad bibin, wê têkoşîna me bidome. Hevalên me yên li hundir têkoşîna xwe didomînin, em ê jî li derve ji bo avakirina sîstemeke demokratîk têkoşîna xwe bidomînin. Heya ku yek girtiyê siyasî hebe, wê têkoşîna me bidome.”










Doza Kobaniyê




Serdozgeriya Komarî ya Enqereyê di lêpirsîna derbarê çalakiyên Kobaniyê de biryara desteserkirina 82 kesan dabû. Akademîsyen Cîhan Erdal, Prof. Dr. Beyza Ustun û Can Memîş di 25ê Îlona 2020an de polîsan ew desteser kiribûn.




Cîhan Erdal û endamên berê yên Lijneya Rêveberiya Navendî yên HDPyê jî di nav de tevlî 17 kesan di 2yê Çiriya Pêşiyê ya 2020an de girtibûn. Buroya Lêpirsînên Sûcên Terorê ya Serdozgeriya Komarî ya Enqereyê ji bo 108 kesan îdianame amade kiribû û Dadgeha Cezayê Giran a Enqereyê ya 22yan ev îdianame qebûl kiribû.




Di îdianameyê de dozgerî 22 jê girtî, 6 jê bi şertê kontrola edlî serbest, ji bo her yek ji 108 kesan 38 caran cezayê miebeta girankirî xwestiye. Biryara zeftkirina 75 kesan dabû.




Selahattîn Demîrtaş, Hevserokê Giştî yê kevn yê HDPyê jî di nava wan kesan de ye ku dozgerî ceza jê re dixwaze.




Daîreya Bilind a Dadgeha Mafên Mirovan a Ewropayê (DMME) di 22yê Kanûna Pêşiyê ya 2020an de ji bo Demîrtaşî biryarek dabû û gotibû ku “divê demildest tehliye bikin”. Piştî wê bi heşt rojan, di 30ê Kanûna Pêşiyê ya 2020an de îdianameya navborî amade bûbû.

author: Jana Hoger
title: Nach Wiedereröffnung von Tötungsstation: Proteste gegen Behördenentscheidung
content:
Zahlreiche Tierschützende gingen vor der Nationalen Behörde für Veterinärwesen und Lebensmittelsicherheit (ANSVSA) in Bukarest auf die Straße. Anlass war die Entscheidung der Behörde, die zuvor geschlossene und durch ein Unternehmen geführte 

Tötungsstation

 „Vetmedan“ von Tierarzt Lazaar in Suraia wieder für den Betrieb zuzulassen. Die Einrichtung war zuvor durch erschütternde Bilder und Berichte über die Zustände dort in die Schlagzeilen geraten. Auf den Aufnahmen ist zu sehen, wie Hunde auf grausamste Weise illegal getötet und massiv misshandelt wurden. Die Demonstrierenden forderten deshalb Konsequenzen für die Verantwortlichen und einen grundlegenden Kurswechsel im Umgang mit 

heimatlosen Hunden

 in Rumänien.  




Gemeinsam mit der Nationalen Föderation für Tierschutz (FNPA) kritisieren wir von PETA Deutschland die Wiedereröffnung der Einrichtung scharf. Wir sehen darin ein weiteres Beispiel für ein System, das seit Jahren versagt und unzähligen Hunden schlimmstes und unwiederbringliches Leid zufügt.  




Der Fall Vetmedan: Ein Symbol für ein größeres Problem 




Die Zustände im „

Tierheim

“ Vetmedan sorgten in Rumänien für große Empörung. Versteckte Aufnahmen zeigen mangelnde Versorgung der dort untergebrachten 

Hunde

, schlechte Haltungsbedingungen und massives Tierleid, auch bei der Tötung. Diese Bilder lösten in der Öffentlichkeit eine Welle der Kritik aus. Für viele Tierfreund:innen ist die Entscheidung zur Wiedereröffnung der Einrichtung deshalb nicht nachvollziehbar. 




Doch der Fall Vetmedan ist nach Ansicht von PETA und der FNPA weit mehr als ein Einzelfall. Er macht auf ein strukturelles Problem aufmerksam, das Rumänien seit Jahrzehnten begleitet: den Umgang mit heimatlosen Hunden und das korrupte System dahinter. 




Über eine Milliarde Euro ausgegeben – und das „Problem“ besteht weiterhin 




Eine von FNPA und PETA ausgewertete Analyse für den Zeitraum von 2001 bis 2025 zeichnet ein alarmierendes Bild: In diesen 25 Jahren wurden schätzungsweise 2,76 Millionen Hunde eingefangen. Rund 1,28 Millionen Tiere starben in Einrichtungen oder wurden getötet. Gleichzeitig flossen etwa 1,01 Milliarden Euro öffentlicher Gelder in das bestehende System.  




Trotz dieser enormen Ausgaben gibt es weiterhin Hunderttausende heimatlose Hunde in Rumänien. Ein klares Zeichen, dass der bisherige Ansatz des Fangens und Töten nicht nur tierquälerisch, sondern auch vollumfänglich gescheitert ist.  







Straßenhunde leiden unter den untragbaren Umständen in Tötungsstationen in Rumänien.







Statt die Ursachen nachhaltig durch tierschutzgerechte Mittel, wie der 

Kastration

 anzugehen, wird ein Kreislauf aufrechterhalten, der Jahr für Jahr neue Leben hervorbringt und neues, massives Leid verursacht. 




Wenn Tierleid zum Geschäftsmodell wird 




Im Mittelpunkt der aktuellen Problematik mit heimatlosen Hunden in Rumänien stehen kommerzielle „Tierheime“. 




Viele Unternehmen unterhalten diese sogenannten Tierheime und erhalten öffentliche Gelder für das Einfangen, Unterbringen und Verwalten von Hunden. Dadurch entsteht ein offensichtlicher Interessenkonflikt: Solange weiterhin Hunde auf der Straße leben, fließen auch weiterhin öffentliche Mittel – im großen Stil. 




Das Einfangen und Töten von Hunden ist mittlerweile landesweit zu einem lukrativen Geschäft geworden, welches aus Steuergeldern finanziert wird. Solange ein wirtschaftlicher Anreiz besteht, wird sich auch das „Problem“ der heimatlosen Hunde nicht verändern.  




Aus Sicht des 

Tierschutzes

 muss endlich jeder eingesetzte Euro dazu beitragen, die Zahl der heimatlosen Hunde nachhaltig und human dauerhaft durch Kastrationen zu reduzieren. Langfristig spart dies viele öffentliche Gelder ein – und das Leid der Hunde wird auf nahezu Null reduziert. Denn innerhalb von zehn Jahren gäbe es nahezu keine heimatlosen Hunde mehr, wenn in Kastrationen statt in Einfangen und Töten investiert werden würden. 




Heimatlose Hunde entstehen nicht von allein 




Immer wieder wird so getan, als seien Straßenhunde ein eigenes „Phänomen“. Tatsächlich ist der Grund für ihr Leid jedoch immer menschengemacht. 




Unkastrierte Hunde mit und ohne Halter:in vermehren sich dauerhaft unkontrolliert. 

Welpen

 werden einfach auf den Straßen entsorgt und ausgesetzt, ohne dass eine langfristige und tierschutzgerechte Lösung gefunden wird. Solange diese Ursachen nicht bekämpft werden, gelangen immer neue Hunde auf die Straßen. 




Aus diesem Grund ist es dringend an der Zeit endlich zu handeln: weg von Fang- und Tötungsstrategien, hin zu wirksamer Prävention. 






















Kastrationskampagnen helfen nachweislich, um das massive Tierleid einzudämmen.

























Sinnfreie Tötungen stattdessen, lösen die Problematik nicht.

























Die Lösung liegt in Kastration, Kennzeichnung und Aufklärung 




Rumänien verfügt bereits über gesetzliche Regelungen zur Kastration bestimmter Hunde. Es müssen alle Hunde kastriert werden, auch die bei Menschen lebenden. Ausgenommen sind nur Hunde, die zur Zucht registriert sind.  Bis heute wird dieses Gesetz nicht ausreichend umgesetzt. 




Viele Menschen, insbesondere in ländlichen Regionen, haben keinen Zugang zu kostengünstigen oder kostenlosen Kastrationsangeboten. Zudem wissen viele nicht, dass das Gesetz besteht. Genau hier muss die Politik ansetzen. 




Aus diesem Grund fordern wir von PETA und der FNPA: 







landesweite kostenlose Kastrationsprogramme,




eine konsequente Kennzeichnung und Registrierung von Hunden,




stärkere Maßnahmen und Strafen gegen das Aussetzen von Tieren,




umfassende Aufklärung der Bevölkerung,




die Förderung von Adoptionen,




eine stärkere Unterstützung seriöser Tierschutzorganisationen. 







Studien und internationale Erfahrungen zeigen seit Jahren, dass nachhaltige Kastrationsprogramme die Zahl herrenloser Tiere langfristig deutlich wirksamer reduzieren können als reine Fangmaßnahmen. [1]  




Tiere brauchen Schutz statt Verwahrung 




Der Fall Vetmedan zeigt, welche Konsequenzen entstehen, wenn Kontrolle, Transparenz und Tierschutz nicht konsequent durchgesetzt werden und Korruption im Land weiterhin herrscht. 




Aus diesem Grund fordern wir, gemeinsam mit der FNPA, dringend unabhängige Untersuchungen der Einrichtung sowie eine Überprüfung vergleichbarer Tötungsstationen. Die Öffentlichkeit hat ein Recht darauf zu erfahren, wie mit den Tieren umgegangen wird und wofür öffentliche Gelder eingesetzt werden. 




Vor allem aber muss sich die politische Debatte verändern, wobei nicht die Frage, wie heimatlose Hunde möglichst schnell von den Straßen verschwinden, hierbei im Mittelpunkt stehen darf. Entscheidend ist vielmehr, wie verhindert werden kann, dass sie überhaupt dort landen und was wir langfristig für sie tun können. 
















 

Jetzt lesen













Adoption







Hunde aus dem Ausland adoptieren | Alle Infos & wichtige Tipps




Sie möchten einen Hund aus dem Ausland adoptieren? Diese Dinge sollten Sie vor der Adoption eines Tierschutzhundes wissen!




Jetzt lesen
















 




Ein Neuanfang für Rumäniens Hunde 




Der Protest vor der ANSVSA steht stellvertretend für den Wunsch vieler Menschen nach einem grundlegenden Wandel. Nach mehr als 25 Jahren, über einer Milliarde Euro öffentlicher Ausgaben und mehr als einer Million verstorbener Hunde ist klar: Das bisherige System ist weder tierfreundlich noch erfolgreich. 




Eine moderne und mitfühlende Gesellschaft misst ihren Fortschritt nicht daran, wie viele Tiere sie einsammelt oder tötet. Sie zeigt ihn dadurch, dass sie Leid verhindert, Verantwortung übernimmt und nachhaltige Lösungen schafft. 




Genau dafür setzen sich wir uns vor Ort ein: Für ein Rumänien, in dem Hunde nicht länger Opfer eines gescheiterten Systems werden, sondern endlich den Schutz erhalten, den sie verdienen. 




Helfen Sie Tieren in Rumänien 




PETA HELPS ROMANIA hilft mehr als 12.000 Tieren im Jahr. Wir kastrieren, registrieren und versorgen diese mit medizinischer Hilfe und lebensnotwendigen Sachspenden. Unsere politische Arbeit und die Bildungskampagne treiben wir mit viel Engagement stetig voran. 




Bitte unterstützen Sie uns dabei, den Tieren in Rumänien mit unserem nachhaltigen Projekt zu helfen! Jede Spende rettet Leben. Auf unserer Spendenseite finden Sie verschiedene Hilfspakete und Patenschaften für Tiere in Not.








		Jetzt helfen!

agement: A Systematic Review,

title: "The Earth Shook Last Night": Talarico Wins Senate, Hinojosa Becomes First Latina Governor in Texas
content:
Texas Democrats have shattered more than three decades of Republican dominance in the state, winning races for U.S. Senate, governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general and even railroad commissioner. They are also poised to possibly take control of the Texas House of Representatives for the first time since 2003. The Republican governor of Texas, Greg Abbott, lost his bid for a fourth term to Democratic state Representative Gina Hinojosa, who defeated him by nearly 700,000 votes. She will be Texas’s first Latina governor. And James Talarico will be the first Democrat to represent Texas in the U.S. Senate since 1993.




“We’re celebrating these wonderful candidates who won office, and we’re also starting to think about what it means to hold power,” says Mike Siegel, a city council member from Austin, Texas, who founded Ground Game Texas, a statewide voter turnout organization. “We need to start thinking very quickly about how we will protect public education, how we will stop data centers and the encroachment of AI on our society, how we will protect public schools, how we stop collaboration with 

ICE

.”

author: EDRi
title: EU governments call it ‘simplification,’ but their Data Omnibus deal considerably weakens our rights
content:
EU governments have agreed on their position on the Digital Omnibus, retaining changes that threaten fundamental rights to privacy and data protection. With negotiations moving to the European Parliament, MEPs must reject the proposed weakening of GDPR safeguards for AI and pseudonymised data, protect individual rights, and defend ePrivacy against new tracking exemptions. Genuine simplification should make our rights easier to exercise and enforce, not give companies more freedom to exploit our data.

When the European Commission presented its Digital Omnibus in November 2025, it promised to simplify Europe’s digital rules without weakening fundamental rights. Yet, as EDRi and others warned at the time, a majority of its proposals, particularly those regarding General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and ePrivacy, went far beyond reducing administrative burdens. They are part and parcel of a broad deregulatory wave that is devouring most of our rights and safeguards in the name of empty promises of competitiveness and sovereignty.

On 21 October 2026, EU governments agreed on their negotiating position, which has timidly corrected some of the Commission’s most questionable choices, but has mainly endorsed changes that could make exploiting personal data easier while making abuses even harder to challenge.

The result is a deal that weakens important safeguards and makes redress harder. There is also little evidence that weakening these protections will improve Europe’s competitiveness. Some changes may instead reinforce the advantages of Big Tech companies that already control and abuse enormous volumes of information about us and the people around us.

One of the most worrying changes concerns the use of personal data for AI.

The Council retained a dedicated provision, Article 88bis (Article 88c in the Commission’s proposal), explicitly recognising the possibility of relying on the GDPR’s ‘legitimate interest’ legal basis to use personal data when developing or operating AI systems. Under the GDPR, companies can already use this legal basis in certain circumstances, provided they demonstrate a legitimate interest, prove that processing is necessary, and establish that people’s rights do not override that interest.

The Council clarifies that AI development does not automatically constitute a legitimate interest and that existing conditions still apply. But if legitimate interests can already justify certain AI processing, why introduce a special provision?

The concern is that Article 88bis could tilt the legitimate interest assessment in favour of AI companies, giving preferential treatment to a vaguely defined set of technologies primarily owned by autocracy-supporting billionaires, regardless of the exact purpose for which our personal data is going to be used. As recent legal analysis explains, this risks changing how the existing balancing test between legitimate interest and data protection safeguards is applied, even without formally removing its requirements.

Companies could invoke this legislative endorsement to justify extensive data reuse, even when people never reasonably expected their information to be used for AI training. And who benefits most? The same dominant Big Tech corporations that have spent decades accumulating the most intimate information about billions of people.

The Council also retains an exception for sensitive personal data appearing incidentally in AI datasets (proposed Article 9(2)(k) and 9(2)), including information revealing health, political opinions or religious beliefs. Companies must try to avoid collecting and, where collected, remove such data, but may retain them under safeguards when removal proves technically impossible or requires manifestly disproportionate effort.

These conditions might look important, but risk turning difficulties in cleaning datasets into a justification for retaining highly sensitive information. In opaque AI systems, verifying whether such data have genuinely been isolated may often be impossible. In this regard we should bear in mind that companies are mandated to protect our data and rights, and technical choices should not determine how far our fundamental rights extend.

There is some, even if limited, good news. The Council has rejected the Commission’s attempt to rewrite the GDPR’s definition of personal data in Article 4.1 and dropped its proposed Article 41a, which would have allowed the Commission to specify when certain pseudonymised information could fall outside GDPR protection – which would likely be an unconstitutional move.

However, the underlying problem remains. Under a new Article 25a, pseudonymised data, where direct identifiers have been replaced or separated, could be considered non-personal for third parties unable to identify the individuals concerned.

Consider how information travels through websites, analytics companies, cloud providers and advertising intermediaries. Each organisation possesses different information and different capacities to link, single out or identify people, and very recent history is full of examples where re-identifying individuals from large datasets has been shockingly simple (it’s been done to Netflix film rating data, NYC cab drivers data, Australian health data, many more areas). The appearance of modern re-identification methods suggests that ‘even heavily sampled anonymized datasets are unlikely to satisfy the modern standards for anonymization set forth by GDPR and seriously challenge the technical and legal adequacy of the de-identification release-and-forget model.’

The Council position includes safeguards concerning processors and onward disclosures, and recognises that identifiability depends on the circumstances. Yet its approach still focuses heavily on whether an individual recipient can identify someone, rather than fully accounting for the wider context in which data are processed, linked and shared. The Court of Justice has called for a contextual, case-by-case assessment, not a general blanket assumption that pseudonymised data fall outside the GDPR whenever one recipient cannot identify someone.

This distinction has real consequences for rights protection: organisations could claim that information is non-personal, leaving people without the transparency and access rights needed to challenge its use, and supervisory authorities could face lengthy technical investigations just to establish whether the GDPR applies, particularly across complex data chains. Instead of simplifying compliance, the Council risks creating more uncertainty for everyone involved.

Several other changes proposed by the Commission have been taken on by the Council.

Companies would have more room to reject or charge for access requests considered abusive. Yet access rights are often the only way to uncover unlawful surveillance, discriminatory profiling or misuse of personal information.

The Council also retains a new exemption from GDPR transparency obligations for certain limited, low-risk processing activities, such as a sports club collecting members’ contact details to manage memberships or organise activities. Where organisations have reasonable grounds to believe that people already know who is processing their personal data and why, they may be exempted from providing the information normally required under Article 13 GDPR. Although considerably narrowed, the exemption still allows organisations to assume that people already have essential information about how their personal data are processed, rather than requiring them to provide it.

The Council also introduces a new exception allowing companies to process biometric data for identity verification without explicit consent or another existing exception to processing sensitive data foreseen in the law, provided the data or means of verification remain under the person’s ‘sole control.’ While this includes safeguards, the concept of sole control remains problematic, particularly when biometric verification becomes a condition for accessing essential services. It risks normalising the collection of highly sensitive personal information instead of encouraging less intrusive alternatives.

On automated decision-making, the Council preserves Article 22’s basic protection against certain solely automated decisions. However, it also clarifies that such decisions may be considered necessary for a contract even when a human could have made them. This gives companies greater room to justify automated decisions with significant consequences, while leaving human intervention primarily as a safeguard after the wrongful decision has been made.

The Council also adds useful methodological and ethical criteria to a new definition of scientific research in Article 4(38) GDPR. Nobody denies that commercially funded research can genuinely advance scientific knowledge, and should not be excluded simply because it has commercial applications. The concern, however, is that the proposed definition, combined with easier data reuse and reduced information duties for research, could allow activities such as routine product optimisation or commercial AI development without genuine scientific objectives or sufficiently rigorous methodologies to claim privileges intended for scientific inquiry.

One significant improvement is the Council’s decision to keep rules protecting access to our phones, computers and connected devices within the ePrivacy Directive, rather than transferring them to the GDPR. This preserves a crucial distinction, even more so when considering the attacks against this different fundamental right from so many different angles: ePrivacy protects the confidentiality of our devices regardless of whether the information accessed qualifies as personal data.

However, the Council introduces additional exemptions allowing access without consent, including audience measurement and measurement of contextual advertising.

Contextual advertising can provide a less intrusive alternative to behavioural ad targeting. But displaying an advertisement based on a webpage’s content does not necessarily require accessing information on someone’s device. Why, then, should measuring its performance justify a new consent exemption? It is true that the Council includes restrictions on profiling and reuse, but it still permits certain device-level data collection. In addition to this, its definition of contextual advertising also covers advertising based on a single search query. A query about abortion, debt or political beliefs can reveal highly sensitive information. Using one query instead of a longer browsing history does not automatically make the practice harmless.

The Council also allows companies to ask for consent again four months after someone refuses. This may reduce repeated requests, but people will still have to keep saying no.

Worse, it deletes the Commission’s proposed system of automated, machine-readable privacy signals. That proposal offered a genuinely rights-respecting way to simplify people’s lives: allowing them to express their tracking preferences once through browsers, operating systems, apps or connected devices, and requiring services to respect those choices. Instead, parts of the industry continue demanding more exemptions from consent to get rid of cookie banners. But eliminating annoying cookie banners should not mean eliminating the right to refuse tracking.

The Council has also introduced provisions that could trigger further revisions before the current negotiations have even finished.

Within six months, the Commission would have to report on GDPR Chapter IV, potentially reopening central accountability obligations for controllers and processors for discussion, particularly smaller organisations carrying out low-risk processing. It is true that smaller organisations deserve better support, but guidance, templates and better-resourced authorities can reduce compliance burdens without weakening safeguards. An organisation’s size is no reliable measure of the risks its processing creates for people.

The Council also requests a review of privacy-enhancing technologies (PETs) within twelve months, particularly regarding access to our devices. PETs can reduce risks, but technologies such as pseudonymisation do not necessarily prevent tracking, singling out, or harmful data reuse. Other references to PETs throughout the text raise similar concerns about using technical measures to justify narrower legal protections. One thing that was central to the essence of GDPR is that technical safeguards should help organisations meet their obligations, rather than become arguments for removing them.

The European Data Protection Board and European Data Protection Supervisor – all EU’s data protection watchdogs – have already warned that parts of the Digital Omnibus could reduce protection and increase legal uncertainty.

The Council has corrected some important problems, particularly concerning ePrivacy and the definition of personal data. But its position still makes extensive data reuse easier, weakens safeguards, and introduces legal exceptions that will generate further uncertainty.

The European Parliament must now address these problems. This means rejecting Article 25a’s approach to pseudonymised data, deleting the AI-specific Article 88bis and the new exception for sensitive data in Article 9(2)(k), and preserving meaningful safeguards for access, transparency and automated decision-making.

MEPs should also resist further consent exemptions under ePrivacy and restore legally binding, machine-readable privacy signals that allow people to refuse tracking without confronting endless cookie banners. With more than 1,800 amendments tabled, Parliament has an opportunity to prioritise genuine simplification that makes compliance easier for smaller organisations and rights easier to exercise and enforce.

Meanwhile, the promised competitiveness gains remain speculative. Giving companies that already control vast amounts of data more flexibility will hardly solve the EU’s dependence on dominant technology providers. The EU can simplify its digital rules without weakening fundamental rights. And if its competitiveness strategy increasingly depends on doing the latter, perhaps it is the strategy, rather than our rights, that needs reconsidering.

title: Abdul El-Sayed Becomes First Muslim Senator as Democrats Rout GOP Across the U.S. in Rebuke to Trump
content:
In a stunning repudiation of President Trump, Democrats regained control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections, flipping seven Senate seats: Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina. Meanwhile, progressive Democrat Dr. Abdul El-Sayed defeated former Republican Congressmember Mike Rogers for an open Senate seat in Michigan with over 52% of the vote. El-Sayed campaigned on a platform of Medicare for All, tackling economic inequality and getting big money out of politics — as well as ending military aid to Israel. He is the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. El-Sayed faced vitriolic, Islamaphobic attacks by top Republicans throughout the campaign.




“Last night wasn’t just about Dr. Abdulrahman being a Muslim, winning and going to the United States Senate,” says Palestinian American organizer and author Linda Sarsour, who has been campaigning for El-Sayed. “It demonstrated that progressives can win in states like Michigan” and that “we can win on standing up for the human rights of the Palestinian people.”

author: Harriet Williamson
title: Palestine Action Protesters Arrested for Quoting Wife of Prime Minister’s Advisor
content:
Twenty-five peaceful protesters were arrested under terror legislation outside the supreme court in London on Wednesday, as the controversial ban on Palestine Action undergoes its final legal challenge on British soil. 




Retirees, health workers, the children of Holocaust survivors, a CBE and a professor held signs quoting the writer Sarah Helm, who posted on X last month, “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action” . They swapped the word “authors” for their own descriptor, such as “Jews”, “physiotherapists”, “son of a Holocaust survivor”, “gardeners” or 

“normal people”

. 




Everybody who held these signs was arrested on suspicion of supporting a proscribed terrorist organisation under section 13 of the Terrorism Act. 




Helm is married to the prime minister’s national security advisor, Jonathan Powell. The Metropolitan police 

chose not to take action over her post 

, saying it “did not meet the criminal threshold”.




Many of those outside the court decried this apparent “double standard” in the enforcement of the Palestine Action ban. Officers seemed initially confused about what they should do. Novara Media heard some debating the meaning of the protesters’ placards and whether or not they should make arrests. 




The majority of those protesting outside the supreme court were over the age of 50, as has been the case at all demos against the ban organised by Defend Our Juries (DOJ) over the 15 months of the proscription being in force. 




Actor Alfie Enoch and Massive Attack frontman Robert Del Naja were outside court in support of the protesters. Enoch, who played Dean Thomas in seven Harry Potter films, told Novara Media that the arrests of peaceful protesters happening around him were “chilling and frightening”. He held a sign reading: “This is democracy, not terrorism.” 




Del Naja said he hopes “common sense prevails” at the supreme court, telling Novara Media: “Direct action is not terrorism. These are people acting on conscience to prevent lethal drones destined for the civilian population of Gaza – that to me is a patriotic duty.” 




Among those arrested were Jonathon Porritt CBE, a former advisor to the government, and academic Peter Hallward. Professor Hallward organised a letter delivered to the president of the supreme court, which was signed by 150 leading professors – including dozens of UK law professors – and 1,500 members of the public. It read: “We oppose genocide so we support Palestine Action.”




Porritt, a professor with the Centre for Research in Modern European Philosophy, told Novara Media that preventing genocide is an “absolutely moral obligation and legal duty” and compared defying the ban on Palestine Action to the historic actions of the suffragettes and the abolitionists. 




Trudi Warner, a 71-year-old retired social worker and DOJ co-founder, told Novara Media, that the ban is a “complete mess” and “we’ve managed to show what a mess it is”. “It’s cost the police and the taxpayer millions of pounds to enforce a law that’s obviously ridiculous – it has to stop.”




Warner was arrested for holding a sign that read, “God help us artists who support Palestine and Palestine Action” as she enjoys art in her retirement. 




Tom Southerden, Amnesty International UK’s law and human rights director, called the arrests “appalling” and said that people being arrested for using the same language as Sarah Helm “shows how dangerously vague our terrorism laws are”.




A DOJ spokesperson said: “Now we understand what the Met meant when they said Sarah Helm’s message ‘did not meet the criminal threshold’. If you say you support Palestine Action and you’re married to the national security advisor that doesn’t meet the criminal threshold. But if you’re not married to the national security advisor it does.




“Let’s hope the supreme court takes into account the blatantly discriminatory application of this crazy law.”




A Met spokesperson said: “

Officers have arrested a total of 25 people outside the Supreme Court on suspicion of expressing support for a proscribed organisation. The policing operation is ongoing and officers will continue to arrest those who break the law.”




Why is Palestine Action in court?




Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori is challenging whether the UK government’s decision to proscribe the direct action group as a terrorist organisation last summer was lawful. 




It’s Ammori’s last chance to appeal in the UK, and she was granted permission to do so on one ground: whether the proscription of Palestine Action is compatible with Articles 10 (the right to free expression) and 11 (the right to freedom of peaceful assembly) of the European Convention of Human Rights (ECHR). 




Ammori has confirmed that if her appeal to the supreme court is unsuccessful, she will take her case to the European Court of Human Rights.




Justices will hear arguments over two days (4 and 5 November). This includes interventions in support of Ammori’s case from writers’ associations PEN International and English PEN, Amnesty International UK and Liberty, a UK Jewish Bloc, and UN special rapporteur Ben Saul. 




The Jewish Bloc, made up of 11 Jewish and Jewish-led groups, seeks to challenge the “fundamental fallacy” that Palestine Action targeted or otherwise posed a threat to the Jewish community, or that it was in any way motivated by antisemitism. It also highlights the particular impact of the proscription of on the Article 10 and Article 11 ECHR rights of the pro-Palestinian Jewish community.




Ammori first took the UK government to court 

in November 2025

, marking the first time a banned group has been able to legally challenge its proscription via judicial review in British history. The high court 

decided in February this year

 that the decision to ban Palestine Action was unlawful because it was incompatible with articles 10 and 11 of the ECHR and that then-home secretary Yvette Cooper breached her own policy in the proscription process. 




The government appealed the high court’s decision, and the court of appeal – the next court up the chain – sided with the government, 

ruling the ban on Palestine Action lawful

 in June.




Since Palestine Action was proscribed, approximately 4,000 people protesting the ban have been arrested under the Terrorism Act 2000, causing 

a record-breaking spike

 in terror-related arrests.

author: anred
title: Mendoza: cárcel al abusador Mauro Aguirre, basta de impunidad patriarcal
content:
En 2018, estudiantes de la Facultad de Ciencias Políticas y Sociales (FCPyS) de la Universidad Nacional de Cuyo (UNCuyo), en Mendoza, denunciaron al profesor y dirigente de la Agrupación Universitaria Nacional (AUN), Mauro Aguirre, por abuso sexual, violaciones y violencia de género. Sin embargo, después de casi ocho años, la justicia patriarcal todavía no lo juzgó. Aguirre es un peso pesado de la política mendocina. En 1994 fue convencional constituyente por el partido derechista Modin, del golpista carapintada Aldo Rico. Antes había militado en el Frente de Izquierda Popular, de Jorge Abelardo Ramos. Tras el retroceso electoral del Modin volvió al peronismo, donde participó de la creación del Movimiento de Integración Nacional (MIN) y llegó a integrar la conducción provincial del Partido Justicialista. 

Por Isadora e Izquierda Socialista Mendoza.







En agosto de 2024, la Universidad Nacional del Litoral le entregó una medalla y un diploma por su participación en la reforma constitucional de 1994. El reconocimiento a un denunciado de múltiples abusos sexuales provocó el repudio del movimiento de mujeres y de la propia UNCuyo. La universidad tuvo que dar marcha atrás, revocar la distinción y exigirle que devolviera ambos reconocimientos.




Las denuncias se hicieron públicas en diciembre de 2018, durante una asamblea de mujeres e identidades disidentes de la facultad. Seis estudiantes denunciaron hechos ocurridos entre 2010 y 2015, cuando algunas tenían apenas 18 y 19 años. Según sus testimonios, Aguirre aprovechaba su posición como docente y dirigente político para ejercer violencia sexual y psicológica.




Las denunciantes también señalaron el papel de la agrupación peronista AUN, donde se desarrollaban prácticas de aislamiento y manipulación. Integrantes de la agrupación habrían colaborado para alejar a las jóvenes de sus vínculos personales y facilitar los abusos. Por estos hechos también fueron imputados Leandro Fontán, Lucía Fernández y Mario Codoni, acusados de actuar como partícipes primarios.




En mayo de 2019, Aguirre fue detenido. Durante la pandemia obtuvo prisión domiciliaria y en 2022, tras el pago de una fianza, recuperó la libertad. Aunque la UNCuyo lo exoneró en abril de 2021 por violencia patriarcal, la causa penal continuó acumulando demoras. El abogado defensor de Aguirre, Carlos Varela Álvarez, también es conocido por representar a la monja Kumiko Kosaka en la causa por los abusos a menores con discapacidad en el instituto Próvolo.




Recién en mayo de 2025, la Justicia confirmó que Aguirre y los otros tres imputados debían enfrentar un juicio oral. El 27 de octubre de 2026 comenzó la audiencia preliminar, que pasó a un cuarto intermedio hasta mediados de noviembre. Mientras tanto, Aguirre continúa en libertad.




Las sobrevivientes llevan casi ocho años reclamando justicia. Tuvieron que enfrentar las consecuencias de los abusos denunciados, el poder político del acusado y un sistema judicial que prolonga su sufrimiento con dilaciones interminables. La impunidad también se sostiene en estas demoras, que obligan a las denunciantes a seguir esperando mientras los acusados permanecen libres.




Desde Isadora e Izquierda Socialista Mendoza acompañamos la lucha de las sobrevivientes y denunciamos la responsabilidad de esta justicia patriarcal, que después de ocho años todavía no llevó a Aguirre al banquillo de los acusados. Exigimos que se realice de inmediato el juicio oral, que se juzgue a todos los responsables y que Aguirre y sus cómplices vayan presos.




Basta de impunidad patriarcal. Justicia para las sobrevivientes. Cárcel a los abusadores y sus cómplices.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Cómo fue el ataque a las trabajadoras sexuales trans en los Bosques de Palermo
content:
En la madrugada del domingo, un grupo de ciclistas atacó a mujeres trans que estaban realizando trabajo sexual en los Bosques de Palermo. La violencia que crece.







En la misma semana en que la Ciudad de Buenos Aires se prepara para la 

35 Marcha del Orgullo

, un grupo de varones que participaba de una bicicleteada nocturna atacó a trabajadoras sexuales travestis y trans en los Bosques de Palermo el domingo en la madrugada. El hecho se difundió y viralizó a partir de los videos que los agresores subieron a las redes sociales. Y desataron el repudio de gran parte de la sociedad.










 


































Ver esta publicación en Instagram






































































 




Una publicación compartida por Presentes (@presenteslatam)











Una mujer trans que estuvo presente cuando ocurrió la agresión contó a 

Presentes 

lo que vivió esa madrugada. A las chicas “las cercaron. Fue así como un torbellino, un huracán. Las rodearon a todas ellas en la esquina de Ombúes y Bello. No podías entrar a defenderlas porque eran más de 150 ciclistas”, dijo Leticia . “Fue como a las tres de la mañana. Pude zafar porque cuando vi que ellos venían con esa intención, que empezaban a insultar, a gritar y tenían cosas en la mano, me metí en el bosque”.




Desde la 

Defensoría del Pueblo de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires

 informaron a esta agencia que, tras la agresión, hay varias mujeres trans heridas. “Lo que pudimos saber es que por lo menos hay seis compañeras lesionadas. Una bastante grave. No corre peligro de vida, pero tiene muy afectada una de sus orejas”, sostuvo María Rachid, titular del Instituto contra la Discriminación de la Defensoría del Pueblo de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires.




“Estamos trabajándolo y hablando con la fiscal Andrea Verónica Scanga, la fiscal especializada en discriminación, quien ya abrió de oficio una investigación. Vamos a aportar el testimonio de las compañeras que presenciaron la agresión, los videos y print de pantalla que tenemos”, agregó Rachid.




Qué se sabe de los hechos




Algunos de los agresores, luego de subir los videos, cambiaron la privacidad de sus cuentas mientras que otros difundieron versiones que tendrán que probar en la Justicia. Por ejemplo, “sugerir” que reaccionaron a un ataque, cuando, hasta ahora, no existe un solo video que registre el supuesto ataque. Por el contrario, varios muestran desde distintos ángulos las agresiones a las personas trans.




También dijeron que un grupo se separó del recorrido central de la bicicleteada organizada para la noche de Halloween que recorrió la Ciudad.




Desde la Federación Argentina LGBT+ (FALGBT+) presentaron una denuncia penal. “No vamos a tolerar la violencia ni la impunidad. Por eso, presentamos una denuncia penal exigiendo justicia y el esclarecimiento inmediato de los hechos. Frente al odio y los ataques, nuestra respuesta es la organización y la presencia en las calles”, expresaron a través de sus redes y convocaron a marchar el 7/11: “Que el orgullo en las calles sea nuestra resistencia”.










 


































Ver esta publicación en Instagram






































































 




Una publicación compartida por Federación Argentina LGBT+ (@falgbt)













Violencia permanente




No es la primera vez que las trabajadoras sexuales de esa zona de la Ciudad sufren ataques. Hace más de un año que vienen denunciando en distintas oportunidades situaciones de hostigamiento y persecución por parte de la Policía de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires.




Los videos se conocieron horas antes del 

Paro de Trabajadoras Sexuales 

en el que, entre otros reclamos, plantearon los ataques y agresiones que se agudizaron en los últimos meses. “Estamos frente a una situación de violencia de manera permanente. Todo el tiempo nos llegan videos, mensajes, audios, denunciando violencia por parte de la policía y de los vecinos. En Palermo, en los bosques, los jóvenes van a la zona de trabajo sexual a violentar a las compañeras, filman con los celulares y suben ese contenido a TikTok o a sus redes sociales”, describió Georgina Orellano, secretaria general de la 

Asociación de Mujeres Meretrices de Argentina

 (Ammar).  Ella misma fue detenida en varias oportunidades




Por el hecho interviene el 

Ministerio Público de la Ciudad

, a través de la Unidad de Flagrancia Norte, a cargo de Ángel Palopoli, que dispuso iniciar actuaciones por “averiguación de lesiones”. Fuentes vinculadas con la investigación informaron a 

Presentes

 que el caso se está investigando para determinar qué pasó. En el proceso se hizo un pedido para acceder al registro de las cámaras de la zona y a testigos.




Artistas y referentes culturales se solidarizaron con las trabajadoras sexuales travestis y trans agredidas, desde sus redes sociales. Entre ellas, María Becerra -que integra el line up en el escenario principal del Orgullo el sábado-, Tini, Lali y Emilia Mernes.




 

 




Desde la política, la senadora provincial Mónica Macha (expresidenta de la comisión de mujeres y diversidades de la cámara baja) también se expresó. “Filmaron y difundieron la agresión como un modo de disciplinamiento. Los discursos de odio matan y Milei y Jorge Macri son responsables de sembrar odio ,escalar y profundizar la violencia”.







Varones transfóbicos atacaron a travestis por su identidad de género y filmaron la agresión como una performance para disciplinar.


Ya lo dijimos: los discursos de odio matan y el Estado es responsable.


Este 7 marchamos porque nadie debería tener miedo de ser quien es.




— Mónica Macha (@MoniMacha) 

November 3, 2026







El ataque se produce en un contexto nacional de desfinanciamiento de políticas de inclusión a colectivos travestis y trans, de persecución a trabajadoras sexuales y criminalización de personas LGBTIQ. Entre agosto y octubre fueron asesinadas cuatro trabajadoras sexuales en contexto de trabajo. Según el observatorio Adriana Zambrano de la Casa del Encuentro en lo que va del año se produjeron 9 transfemicidios; mientras en 2025 de acuerdo al informe de la Falgbt hubo 227 crímenes de odio.




También en medio de una campaña  del gobierno de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires, encabezado por Jorge Macri de “Ley y Orden”, que persigue a trabajadores de economías informales, y hostiga con grandes operativos a vecines de barrios populares -como denunciaron en la última Marcha del Orgullo Villero y Trans Diverso en la Villa 31 de Retiro.




Mientras Clara Muzzio, vicejefa de gobierno, ataca constantemente a las diversidades sexuales e instala la falsa idea de “ideología de género” para atacar la Educación Sexual Integral. En una ocasión, incluso, habló de que sólo “hay dos sexos, el masculino y el femenino”. A raíz de esto, el diputado Esteban Paulón la 

intimó a retractarse

, con el apoyo de Falgbt. Lejos de hacerlo, ratificó sus dichos.




Si también te indignó: cómo podés ayudar




Si esta noticia despertó tu indignación, podés sumar tu repudio y dejar de compartir el video reproduciendo el ataque. Si tenés registros que puedan ayudar a esclarecer los hechos, acercalos a la Fiscalía.




Los colectivos travestis y trans necesitan de la solidaridad de toda la sociedad. Una manera es apoyando el pedido de reparación integral trans, exigiendo el cumplimiento del cupo laboral travesti trans, y participando de las marchas y actividades.







Fuente: 

https://agenciapresentes.org/2026/11/03/como-fue-el-ataque-a-las-trabajadoras-sexuales-trans-en-los-bosques-de-palermo/




La entrada 

Cómo fue el ataque a las trabajadoras sexuales trans en los Bosques de Palermo

 se publicó primero en 

Indymedia Argentina Centro de Medios Independientes (( i ))

.
